The PERMAS documentation mainly consists of the PERMAS User’s Reference Manual, the
PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU), manuals of the built-in interfaces, the so-called Doors, and
the PERMAS Programmer’s Manual.
Throughout all PERMAS documents external hyperlinks appear blue and internal links appear
in red color.
Chapter 1 of this document gives an introduction to PERMAS.
The PERMAS User’s Reference Manual reflects the separation of analysis control (UCI) and model description (DAT),
which is a basic concept of PERMAS.
The Element Atlas describes the available element types including physical properties and applicable element loads.
Design elements for optimization are documented in the following chapter.
Available results are documented followed by description of
the supported export formats.
The final chapter contains a short theoretical overview on material properties.

In chapter 2 the commands of the User Control Interface are
documented according to their menu structure. For each section, the commands are listed in alphabetical order. To look up
a specific command, one may use
• the bookmarks bar of the PDF reader as shown left
• the UCI Index, if the command name is known
• the Global Index
• the search function of the PDF reader

Together with the description of the command, each page contains the following additional
information together with embedded links.

Model Quality Assurance
Basic module of PERMAS including all basic functions like the Data Object Management System, the PERMAS data input and export, various
element types and the task scanner to qualify the model for each kind
of analysis to be performed. The scanning process may be performed
for each program module, regardless whether it is licensed or not at the
current site. This module is the basis for the utilization of other modules.
Linear Static Analysis
Module to perform linear elasto–statical analyses.
Contact Analysis
Very efficient handling of contact problems including orthotropic friction.
It allows the calculation of the correct changes of the force distribution
in parts gaining or losing contact.
Extended Contact Analysis
High performance algorithms for large contact models and friction problems
Contact Analysis Multigrid solver
High performance acceleration for large contact models based on update and contact multigrid coarsening strategies
Contact Geometry Update
Update of contact partners in geometrically linear and nonlinear analysis.
Nonlinear Static Analysis
Nonlinear material behaviour and geometric nonlinearities with large
displacements but small strains. Calculation of elasto-plastic, viscoplastic and creep material behaviour as well as nonlinear elasticity including contact analysis.
Nonlinear Static Analysis Advanced
Large strain elements and hyperelastic material
Extended Nonlinear Material Laws
Cast-iron and nonlinear kinematic hardening
Buckling Analysis
Computation of buckling modes and load scale factors for linear buckling problems.
Heat Transfer Analysis
Field problems. This module allows the calculation of heat conduction
and analogous field problems such as potential flow, seepage and lubrication. Not only steady–state and linear analysis but also transient
problems and nonlinear material behaviour are covered in this module.
Nonlinear Heat Transfer Analysis
Calculation of nonlinear steady–state and transient heat conduction
and convection problems

Special Features of PERMAS
• Easy to Use
By a convenient user control interface (UCI) command language
• Integrated Interfaces
allow for direct communication with the pre- and postprocessing system.
• High Efficiency
The algorithms within PERMAS are designed to be highly efficient, even for extremely
large models.
• Parallelization
PERMAS has been parallelized by a unique and general concept dealing with message
passing as well as with multithreading.
• Optimum Management of Computer Resources
The central memory may be adapted to any hardware or a certain calculation. Moreover,
the database may be distributed to several physical locations, due to special needs.
• Low resource requirements
Even very large models may be solved with few central memory (e.g. 3 Mio. unknowns
with 150 MB central memory)

1.1 Brief Description

– Independent modelling of parts
without the need for matching meshes at the interface.
– Fast change cycle of virtual prototypes
Studies of different design variants are highly accelerated, leading to a better feedback in the layout design phase.
– Accurate mesh transition without bad elements
by concentrating the transition to a small region.
– Based on incompatible meshes
– Fixed coupling for lines and surfaces
– Weld coupling
– Contact
• Substructure Analysis
In addition to the part handling described above, PERMAS allows the decomposition of
a model into substructures. Substructures can be assembled the same way as single
elements and are therefore often called superelements. The assembly process may be
performed on an arbitrary number of levels. The most important advantages of this analysis technique include:
– Generally, any substructure may be arbitrarily large and complex, thus allowing the
overall model to assume a size which has so far been impossible in practical applications.
– Decomposition into substructures is good way to cope with large analysis projects.
Any substructure may be constructed and verified separately before it is inserted into
the model.
– Elements may be used on every substructure level, i. e. they may be introduced
even in assembled components.
– Identical substructures may be inserted repeatedly — thus leading to considerable
savings in computation time.
– Much computation time may also be saved as far as design variations or non–linear
analyses are concerned, provided that the modifications respectively the iterations
can be concentrated onto one of several substructures.
• Element Types
PERMAS includes comprehensive element families offering a wide range of elements for
all fields of application:
– more than 50 element types for static and dynamic calculations including linear and
nonlinear spring and damper elements.
– nonlinear shells

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

1-5

Intro

• Part handling with PERMAS
The ability to use parts as independent computational models is a technology to speed-up
the analysis process especially during the design layout phase, where a lot of modifications occur in a short time frame. The available functionality is subsequently summarized
briefly.

1 Introduction to PERMAS
– threedimensional gasket elements
– plot elements for visualization purposes
– more than 40 element types for heat transfer calculations
– axisymmetric elements for harmonic analyses

Intro

– specific element types for performing calculations of fluids and their coupling to structural elements.
– semi-infinite elements for electromagnetic or acoustic problems.
– radiating boundary condition elements.
– about 25 element types support the calculation of electromagnetic field problems.
• Model Size in Calculations with PERMAS
The data management and the built–in solution algorithm in PERMAS are suitable for the
calculation of very large models. Projects with well over 20.000.000 unknown degrees of
freedom can be solved with the standard software. By optionally using the substructure
analysis, models of this size may be built up of substructures that are simple and easy to
handle. Such large models can always be calculated on computer systems of any size —
on workstations as well as on servers. The only limitations are the performance and disk
storage capacity of the computer system available and the time available for performing
the analysis.
• PERMAS is an Open Software System
PERMAS offers the user numerous solution process controls and internal data access
facilities. In particular, the analysis tools available (e. g. for matrix calculation) may be
applied for flexible in–house user requirements. For standard applications a comfortable
command language — the User Control Interface (UCI ) — is available.

1.2 Basic Definitions
1.2

Basic Definitions

The component is an environment for the administration and analysis of a physical system. It
corresponds to the finite element model of the entire physical system or of a part of the system.
That is in general, the component corresponds to the finite element model in the preprocessor.
A component is identified by a name, see page 3-5.
Contents of a component are the mesh definition, boundary conditions and loads, the definition
and assignment of physical properties and the assignment of material data. Furthermore definitions for parameter and topology optimization may belong to a component. The definition of
material data is completely independent of the component description.
To each component a discretization type is assigned, which may be discrete (default), or axisymmetric. The discretization type defines the way how the physical system is represented.
In discrete components, all structural elements are useable, but no axisymmetric or Fourier
elements. In axisymmetric components only axisymmetric or Fourier elements may be used.
In order to perform analyses in different physical domains (e.g. mechanical, thermal, etc.) a
component may carry different degree of freedom types, see page 1-22. They are selected by
the DOFTYPE parameter. By default, mechanical degrees of freedom are available.
Using the substructure technique, components may be assembled to a so called configuration
(see figure F1-1) in order to model a more complex physical system. Dependent on their
position in such an assembly, there are several types of components:
Basic Component:

(single component) is a component that is no longer divided into
subcomponents.

Subcomponent:

is a component which may be inserted into another component.

Assembled Component:

(hypercomponent) is a component that is made up of subcomponents.

Top Component:

is the highest component in the assembly hierarchy.

Since each component is independent from any other one, the model description (e.g. node
numbers, elements, loads) may be done in a completely independent way. The coupling points
are identified by the definition of external degrees of freedom in the subcomponent and the
corresponding connectivity definition in the hypercomponent.
A configuration defines the range of components to be analyzed in the current computation. It
is identified by the name of the highest component in the assembly hierarchy. This component
is called the top component. The simplest case of a configuration is a single component,
where the component corresponds to the configuration. A component may be a part of several
configurations.
Figure F1-1 shows an example for a simple configuration. The configuration is defined by
activating component COMP_5 as the top component. All subsequent computations are after-

wards performed within this configuration. There are no restrictions concerning the number of

1.2.2

Variants and Situations

PERMAS offers the possibility to provide input for different variants of a model and to examine
them within one calculation.
Invariant data of the model description are collected in the so-called structure bracket. The
main contents of the structure bracket are:
• nodal point coordinates
• element topology
• element and node sets
• reference coordinate systems
• global rotated node basis definitions
(i.e. assignment of displacement coordinate systems)
• invariant linear multipoint constraints
Variants may be defined with respect to boundary conditions, loading, physical properties, material assignment and other attributes of the model. Variants are indentified by a name. They
can be seen as a container to organize data by their physical meaning. The following types of
variants are available:

1-8

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

1.2 Basic Definitions
System Variant:

Holds a set of physical properties and related data. The most important
contents are:
• element property definitions and assignments
• material assignments (not definitions!)

Intro

• element local systems
• global damping parameters
Constraint Variant:

The variant contains a specific set of boundary conditions, mainly:
• suppressed degrees of freedom
• prescribed degrees of freedom
• linear multipoint constraints
• coefficients of general linear multipoint constraints
• local system definitions indicating a rotated node basis (displacement coordinate system).
• contact boundary conditions

Loading Variant:

Serves to organize different loading conditions, e.g. in case of different
constraint variants or several dynamic load cases. One loading variant
may contain an arbitrary number of static load cases.

Modification Variant: Contains data related to design optimization, like design constraints, design variable limits or the like.
Result Variant:

Holds the specification of result requests (e.g. excitation frequencies,
load steps) and the definition of references to existing results (e.g. result
combination rules).

These contents are allowed for each component level (basic or assembled component).
A specific combination of variants for which an analysis is performed is called a situation. A situation is identified by a name and is the main link between model description and analysis control.

1.2 Basic Definitions
1.2.3 Coordinate Systems

1. The component system is a cartesian coordinate system within each substructure. It
serves as the reference for all other coordinate systems of the component.
2. Reference systems may be used for coordinate input, the transformation of nodal point
vector quantities and the definition of a rotated node basis or local element systems.
3. The rotated node basis is an optional cartesian coordinate system assigned to a nodal
point to modify the directions of the degrees of freedom. Also often called a displacement
coordinate system or analysis coordinate system.

The Component System
Each component carries a basic coordinate system, called the component system. The component system is the default for:
1. the specification of nodal point coordinates
2. the output of nodal result vectors
3. the directions of the degrees of freedom

Reference Systems
In the structure bracket of each component, an arbitrary number of reference systems may be
defined as local coordinate systems. The reference systems may be cartesian, cylindrical or
spherical coordinate systems. Also special purpose conical, helical and toroidal coordinate
systems are available. They can be used:
1. for the definition of further reference coordinate systems
2. as reference systems for coordinates
3. for the definition of a rotated node basis.
4. for the orientation of local element systems
A reference system is defined by three points, either by specification of nodal point identifiers
or by specification of their coordinates (which may refer to a reference system, too).

The reference points and axes of $RSYS TOR and $RSYS TORMAX are identical and both
establish the very same toroidal system. The difference only applies to the generation of local
cartesian systems via $ROTB or other definitions that establish a local system based on a given

the r0 ring while TORMAX will use a projection to the opposite nadir point, resulting in a spindle
reference torus, see figure F1-12, e.g. useful for rollers or barrel chestlike surfaces.

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

1.2 Basic Definitions

Many applications require the possibility to define the loads and boundary conditions in directions other than the directions given by the component system. For that purpose a local
cartesian coordinate system may be assigned to each node. In PERMAS this coordinate system is called rotated node basis. Other terms are displacement coordinate system or analysis
coordinate system. There are several possibilities to define a rotated node basis, see $ROTB :
• A global rotated basis may be defined with the $ROTB statement in the structure bracket.
This definition is valid for all variants of the model.
• A variable rotated basis may be defined within the constraint variant using the $ROTB
statement. The freedom directions defined by this way may vary from constraint variant
to constraint variant.
• In both cases the definition may be performed by reference to a reference coordinate
system or by direct input of a cartesian system for the corresponding node.
The definition of a rotated node basis must be in accordance with the following rules :
1. If reference is made to a cylindrical or spherical system, the local x-axis at the node is
build from the radius vector. Hence this system may not be assigned to nodes on the
z-axis of a cylindrical or in the origin of a spherical reference system.
2. If a node carries external degrees of freedom, only a global rotated basis may be assigned.
3. A duplicate definition of a rotated basis at a node is impossible. Especially the (global) rotated basis of subcomponents must not be defined again on hyper-component level. The
definition is automatically taken over from the subcomponent to the hyper-component. It
is not allowed to specify the local system on hyper-component level for such nodes, since
the local system is transported only in a bottom-up way.
4. If a hyper-component node which was inserted via $SUBCOMP shall be assigned an
additional local system (and no rotated basis already exists), this may be done in the
constraint bracket.

1.2.4

Degrees of Freedom, Freedom Classes

Degrees of freedom are the state variables of a discrete system (i.e. finite element model).
PERMAS provides different degree of freedom types for the different classes of physical problems to be solved:

Intro

DISP
POTE
PRES
TEMP
MATH

mechanical analyses
electro-magnetic analyses
acoustic analyses
thermal analyses
optimization and coupled analyses

A component may carry several degree of freedom types in order to perform combined analyses.
The number of degrees of freedom at a particular node is determined by the elements (or
multipoint constraint conditions) which are connected to that node and the degree of freedom
type.

Degree of Freedom Type DISP
The degrees of freedom define the potential movements of a nodal point as well as the forces
that can be applied at that node. Thus, with each discrete degree of freedom a force and a
displacement vector component are associated that have the same direction in space. This
direction is defined by the node basis that assigns a direction to the corresponding degree of
freedom. The default directions of the degrees of freedom coincide with the component system.
Nevertheless, any other direction may be defined by assigning a rotated node basis to a nodal
point.
Table T1-2 summarizes the number of potential displacement degrees of freedom at a node for
different element families.

1.2 Basic Definitions
Freedom Classes

The actual degrees of freedom are those degrees of freedom which are elastically supported.
In contrast, degrees of freedom which are not elastically supported are called redundant degrees of freedom. They must be suppressed explicitly.
The actual degrees of freedom are partitioned internally into disjoint freedom classes. The freedom classes are defined by boundary conditions (like suppression of a degree of freedom, assignment of a prescribed value) which are defined within a constraint variant ($CONSTRAINTS)
or by linear constraint equations ($MPC). All degrees of freedom which are not explicitly assigned are called local degrees of freedom. The following table shows the freedom classes in
PERMAS and their description.
Class
L
E

Statement
$EXTERNAL

P

$PRESCRIBE

S

$SUPPRESS

D

$MPC

Explanation
Local degrees of freedom (usually no explicit definition)
External degrees of freedom. Coupling degrees of freedom
in a substructure analysis. The definition is done within the
structure bracket.
Prescribed degrees of freedom. The definition is done within the
constraint variant, the values for each loading pattern are defined in
the loading variant.
Suppressed degrees of freedom are specified in the
constraint variant.
Dependent degrees of freedom are declared with the DPDOFSparameter of the $MPC statement within the structure bracket or
constraint variant.

Each actual degree of freedom may be assigned to any freedom class. This assignment must
be unique, i.e. a degree of freedom can only be member of one class.
PERMAS distinguishes between degrees of freedom which are totally suppressed and degrees
of freedom which have assigned a specific (prescribed) value. Suppressed DOFs are neglected
when solving the system of equations, whereas prescribed DOFs are a part of the right hand
side (load vector). This allows to solve multiple load patterns with different prescribed values
with a single decomposition of the system matrix.

Intro

For all nodal point oriented matrices, the number of degrees of freedom at a node is determined
by the highest possible degree of freedom in a component in order to have a regular partitioning
of the matrices. Since these degrees of freedom are not always actually existing at each node,
they are called potential degrees of freedom.

DAT-file:

Is the PERMAS input file. If the input file shall be read automatically, it
must be located in the users working directory and follow the general
naming rule.

pre-file:

Specifies a foreign input format, like Abaqus input, NASTRAN input,
CAE-Databus or other supported preprocessing formats.

DFT-file:

The PERMAS default definition file holds permanent settings for the
analysis environment. The existing locations at your site may be asked
at your system administrator.

UCI-file:

Is the command file to control PERMAS. These commands may also be
submitted in an interactive way. It is read automatically if it is located in
the users working directory and follows the general naming rule.

PERMAS Data Base: The data base is organized as a direct access file, which may be partitioned into up to 40 single files to be stored in different directories, if
necessary. By default, the database is created in the users working directory.
PRO-file:

The protocol file provides a detailed protocol concerning progress and
contents of a PERMAS analysis. All steps from the UCI commands to
the individual procedures and processes with error reports and information concerning occupied disk space as well as computation times are
listed in this file.

1.3 Basic Files and Features

RES-file:

The result file includes the listings of input data, automatic output from
solvers and results requested by the user. It is located in the working
directory.

Post-files:

For all supported postprocessing systems like HyperView, I-DEAS, MEDINA, PATRAN,..., the results for postprocessing may be written directly
in the corresponding format. By default located in the users working
directory.

Central Data Management
PERMAS converts all input data (preprocessor files, PERMAS input files) into an internal format
and stores them on a database. This database is available during the analysis process as
backing storage. In this database, results as well as interim results are stored. It may be saved
and used for subsequent runs.
All read– and write–operations from this database to the central memory and vice versa are
controlled and monitored by a core management program (Data Object Management System
DMS), that is comparable to an operating system. The size of the central memory managed by
DMS is a dynamic quantity, chosen by the user. Its size is limited to 8GB for the D64 version
and only by the operating system for the S64 version. The database and the central memory
are divided into fixed–size–records (= pages). The typical page size is 512 kilobytes (D64) or
1024 kilobyte (S64). Its optimum value is hardware specific, since it depends on the ratio of
CPU speed to I/O speed. The data base size may vary — depending on the project volume —
from a few megabytes up to several terabytes. Only the pages currently required are loaded
into the central memory by DMS. Thus, merely the necessary disk accesses take place.
The communication between PERMAS and the database is made via data objects. A data
object is defined by:
• the structure of the data
• the possible operations on the object
• the access functions
PERMAS supports the following data objects:
1. tables
2. sequences
3. books
Tables and sequences serve to store the input data and control information. Books are used
to store matrices, e.g. the nodal coordinates, loads and displacements. The experienced user
may manipulate the books, e.g. by extracting specific information from the database for further
processing.

1.4

PERMAS Model Data

Although a finite element model is build mainly in a preprocessor, it is of importance that the
user gets familiar with the basic structure of the PERMAS input file.

Intro

Often complex boundary and loading conditions are more clearly arranged and faster modified
in an input file created by means of an editor. This file may then serve as an amendment to the
bulk of data created in the preprocessor. Furthermore, the popular preprocessors are not able
to fully support the extensive possibilities of PERMAS and thus the advanced user will have no
choice but to learn more about the input file structure.
Please refer also to the elaborated examples in the PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU).

1.4.1

Structure of the Input–File

The data input to PERMAS is arranged in data blocks, which are enclosed by brackets of
different level. Within a level, the data blocks may be arranged in an arbitrary sequence. The
data blocks represent the basic data structure presented in sections 1.2.1 and 1.2.2.
The high level brackets $ENTER ... $EXIT enclose data related to a component, as well as
component independent data, like material data. Medium level brackets $name ... $END name
enclose data blocks within high level brackets, e.g. variant definitions. The lines to close the
brackets ($EXIT, $END) are always optional. The input file is closed by the delimiter line $FIN.
The input structure is shown in the following schematic example:
$ENTER COMPONENT NAME=FRAME
$STRUCTURE
!
............ variant-independent input for current component
$END STRUCTURE
!
... comment sign
$CONSTRAINTS
!
............ input for constraint variant
$END CONSTRAINTS
$SYSTEM
!
............ input for system variant
$END SYSTEM
$LOADING
!
............ input for loading variant
$END LOADING
$RESULTS
!
............ input for result variant
$END RESULTS
$MODIFICATION
!
............ input for modification variant
$END MODIFICATION
$SITUATION
!
............ definition of situation
$END SITUATION
$EXIT COMPONENT

Intro

$ENTER MATERIAL
$MATERIAL
!
............ input of material data
$END MATERIAL
$EXIT MATERIAL
!
$FIN

The individual data items can be of the following types:
integer numbers, floating point numbers, names or text in quotation marks
The required type is documented together with the syntax description of the data block.
The syntax conventions are described more in detail in chapter 3.

Discussion of some Element Types
When selecting an element it should be taken into consideration whether it is suitable for the
problem, i.e. whether a model is capable of covering those points of the reality relevant for the
analysis. These include: shape, restraint conditions, material and load. Below some element
types are presented:

Intro

• Membrane Elements
FLA2, TRIM3, QUAM4 with linear shape functions and constant stress fields for modelling
of membranes. In order to obtain accurate stresses with these elements, the mesh must
be much finer compared to a mesh consisting of higher order elements.
FLA3, TRIM6, QUAM8, QUAM9 with quadratic resp. biquadratic shape functions for modelling of plane stress or plane strain problems with exact representation of linear stress
fields.
• Three–Dimensional Elements
TET4, PYRA5, PENTA6, HEXE8 with linear displacement fields and constant representation of stress field.
TET10, PENTA18, HEXE27 with quadratic, biquadratic and triquadratic displacement field
and representation of linear stress fields.
PENTA15, HEXE20 with parabolic curved edges, with nodes only on their edges (serendipity elements), not suitable for contact problems.
• Beam Elements
BEAM2 general beam with variable cross-section, optionally with eccentricity
BECOS centric or eccentric beam with solid cross section.
BECOC centric or eccentric beam with thin–walled, constant cross section.
BETAC centric or eccentric beam with thin–walled, tapered cross section.
BECOP centric or eccentric beam with thin–walled, open and constant cross section.
BEAM2W general beam with variable cross-section and warping dof, optionally with eccentricity
• Plate and Shell Elements
QUAD4, TRIA3 for thick and thin plates and shells.
TRIA3K for thin plates and shells, with better behaviour as TRIA3
QUAD4S, TRIA3S sandwich shell elements.
SHELL3, SHELL4 for thin laminated plates and shells.
QUAMS4, TRIMS3 for nonlinear analysis of thin or thick shells
QUAMS8,QUAMS9, TRIMS6 as higher order elements for nonlinear analysis of thin or
thick shells
• Three–Dimensional Gasket Elements
GKPNT6, GKHEX8 with linear displacement fields and constant representation of stress
field.
• Elements for Springs, Bearings and Supports
SPRING1 linear spring in space with single stiffness along its axis.

1-32

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

1.4 PERMAS Model Data
SPRING3 linear spring in space with three translational stiffnesses.
SPRING6 linear spring in space with three translational and three rotational stiffnesses.

• Axisymmetric Elements
TRIAX3, QUAX4 with linear resp. bilinear displacement fields.
TRIAX6, QUAX8, QUAX9 with quadratic resp. biquadratic displacement fields for general
applications.
In addition there are special purpose elements for thermal, acoustical and electro-magnetic
analyses. For a detailed description of the element library please refer to the Element Atlas.
Linear Multipoint Constraints
Multipoint constraints (see $MPC) can be defined in the structure bracket as well as in the
constraint bracket. PERMAS distinguishes between coupled degrees of freedom, rigid regions,
interpolation regions (also for volume–shell transitions) and general MPCs. Examples for some
types of constraints are shown below.
$MPC SAME DPDOFS = 2
1001
20 : 11 12 13 14 15

The $MPC SAME with identifier 1001 assigns the value at degree of freedom 2 at node 20
to degree of freedom 2 at nodes 11 to 15. Node 20 is the guiding node, nodes 11 to 15 are
dependent nodes.
$MPC JOIN DPDOFS= 1,2,3
1010 GSET : DSET

$MPC JOIN describes pairwise identical displacements. In this example the degrees of freedom 1, 2 and 3 at the dependent nodes in node set DSET are forced to have the same values as
degrees of freedom 1, 2 and 3 of the corresponding guiding nodes in set GSET. Node pairs are
determined according to smallest distance. Both sets must contain the same number of nodes.
Note that both types of MPC above do not take into account the location of the nodes or the
direction of the degrees of freedom ($ROTB).

MASS6 point–mass in space with translational and rotational inertia terms.

$MPC RIGID DPDOFS = 1,2,3
9001 20 : RIGSET

$MPC RIGID describes a rigid region. Degree of freedom 1, 2 and 3 of the dependent nodes
in the nodeset RIGSET are associated with the guiding degrees of freedom of node 20. Any
displacement or rotation of the guiding node moves the dependent nodes as a rigid body. The
guiding node carries always 6 potential degrees of freedom. If the dofs of the guiding node
are not determined by the dependent dofs or by connection to an element supporting these 6
degrees of freedom, the redundant dofs have to be suppressed.

Rules with respect to dependent and guiding degrees of freedom:
Guiding degrees of freedom may
• be loaded, if they are local or external;
• be constrained, i.e. suppressed, prescribed or dependent;
• be external;
Dependent degrees of freedom may
• be loaded;
• not be suppressed, prescribed or external, but may be guiding;
• may appear only once as dependent degrees of freedom.

Contact Boundary Conditions
In contrast to fixed boundary conditions, contact boundary conditions can open or close dependent on the deformation. Penetration of the contact partners is prevented. Definitions of
contact boundary conditions may be based on surfaces or nodes.

Z
Y

X

Figure F1-18: Contact boundary conditions
$CONTACT SURFACE SURFACE
PLATE2SPHERE
PLATE : SPHERE

Here $CONTACT SURFACE defines contact between two surface sets PLATE and SPHERE and
is mainly used for incompatible meshes like in figure F1-18. By default, the contact normal
direction (for which penetration is prevented) is given by the normal direction of the surface.
$CONTACT NODE
SHAFT2HUB

CONTSYS = 23
SHAFT : HUB

AXES = 1

$CONTACT NODE is defined between pairs of nodes and normally requires compatible meshes.
Here contact is specified between node sets SHAFT and HUB. Node pairs are determined according to smallest distance. Both sets must contain the same number of nodes. The normal
direction is defined by the first axis of reference system 23, which in this example is the radial direction of a cylindrical system. Compatible node-to-node contact has a higher accuracy
compared to incompatible surface contact, but requires the specification of the normal direction.
Please refer also to the related chapter in the PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU).

System Variant

The system variant is defined in a $SYSTEM bracket and is mainly used to:
• assign element and material properties
• define geometrical data (physical properties) for elements
• define damping data
• define system variant parameters like:
– mass model (consistent (default) / diagonal )
– reference frequencies for timehistory analysis
Since PERMAS allows to have several system variants with different sets of properties, there
is no strict hierarchy element → physical property → material.
Instead, in each system variant properties and materials are assigned to the elements, as
shown below for the example from figure F1-14:

1-38

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

1.4 PERMAS Model Data

The geometrical data are defined via $GEODAT. The header line specifies the following
data:
BEAM: Physical properties for beam elements
CONT: Describes the contents of the data line(s).
For the beam elements the area of cross section, the area moments of inertia for bending and torsion and the orientation of the cross section are defined.
Each new data line starts with the name of the geometrical data record (here BECOS_DAT), which
is used as reference by the $ELPROP statement, followed by the data lists as specified in the
header line. The different lists are separated by the colon (:).
The $ELPROP statement is used to assign the geometrical and material data to elements or
element sets (here BEAM_1). Finally, the system variant bracket is closed by the optional $END
SYSTEM statement.

1.4.5 Loading Variant
One loading variant contains the loading definitions for a specific analysis. Each loading variant
may consist of an unlimited number of loading patterns, in other terminology often called load
sets.
Each loading pattern may consist of different loads, e.g. concentrated loads, distributed loads,
prescribed freedom values or inertia loads. All loads with the same loading pattern identifier act
simultaneously. Example for a nodal force acting in local y-direction (dof 2) of node 5 in loading
pattern 4:
$CONLOAD LPAT=4 DOFTYPE=DISP
5 2: 10000.

Dependent on the element type and type of analysis, a multitude of distributed loads is available, for example pressure loads ($DISLOAD PRESS). Distributed loads may be specified in
different ways:
$DISLOAD:
$DISLOADN:
$DISLOADS:

distributed loads defined at elements
distributed loads defined at nodes
distributed loads defined at surfaces

Further distributed loads are available, see $LOADING, and the Element Atlas.
Also the properties of contact boundary conditions ($CONTACT LOAD) are defined in the loading variant.

A dynamic loading is defined in a straight forward way by combining each static loading pattern

examples in the analysis type specific chapters in the PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU).

1.4.6

Modification Variant

The modification variant ($MODIFICATION) contains input for parameter and topology optimization, as well as for reliability analysis. For these advanced topics please refer to the corresponding chapters of the PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU).

1.4.7

Result Variant

The result variant ($RESULTS) serves, among others, for the specification of result requests,
like excitation frequencies ($FREQUENCY) in dynamic analyses or time steps ($NLRESULTS)
in non-linear analyses. For these advanced topics please refer to the PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU).

1.4.8

data for an isotropic material are presented. Please note that no units are specified, so the

doftype, however SI units are always presented in the first column of each table.

1.5 Solution Control (UCI)
Solution Control (UCI)

PERMAS is controlled by a stream of commands submitted by the User Control Interface
(UCI). These commands may be submitted by one or several files or by interactive terminal
input. Command files may be included up to a depth of 10 files using the command INCLUDE.
Whenever an end-of-file mark is reached, control is returned to the next higher include level
(respectively the interactive command input as last part of the chain). The default extension for
such a control file is UCI.
The user control interface has a menu structure and is partitioned into several sections. The
main section of the UCI contains branches to the different (sub)sections.
A section provides specific section commands, which are available only within this environment
(command menu). A section is entered by typing the section name and may be left either by
the RETurn command, by entering a new section name or by terminating the PERMAS run
(STOP).
Figure F1-19 gives an overview about the available sections, which are listed below:
STARTUP: Provides the commands for the setup of the system and the system start.
INPUT:

Controls the input of model data.

EXEC:

Provides the commands to generate primary and secondary results. The time consuming operations of the analysis are managed within this section.

SELECT: Contains several utility functions, like transformation, summation and further processing of results.
PRINT:

Controls tabular output to the results file (RES).

EXPORT: Controls the output of data in various postprocessor formats.
USER:

Allows to activate user written solutions.

In addition to the section commands and transparent commands, which are available only in
specific sections, there are also global commands which are available everywhere.
Global Commands
DEFINE, REPORT, RETURN, SET, STOP, TASK ...

STARTUP

INPUT

EXEC

SELECT

PRINT

EXPORT

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

1-47

Intro

1.5

1 Introduction to PERMAS
The command interpreter of the user control interface works in two modes of operation:
1. The Direct Mode, where commands are executed directly.

Intro

2. The Task Mode, where the commands are queued to be checked first and to be executed
afterwards as a whole. The task mode is invoked and terminated by the global UCIcommand TASK (END). A task is valid for one configuration and the related situations of
a model. In case of several configurations, each configuration requires a separate task.
The task mode is intended to group commands with the possibility to check the consistency of
commands and data before the time–consuming execution of the analysis steps begins. This
operation mode helps to avoid errors at an early stage of the execution, saving computer time
and working hours. It is mandatory for all commands of the EXEC section.
An analysis is executed by a single command, a predefined solution step. As a rule of thumb,
each solution step is related to a situation of its own, which defines the combination of variants
to be analyzed and also provides an environment for the storage of results. On UCI level, the
solution step defines a computational task that in turn invokes a certain sequence of PERMAS
procedures which themselves activate all required processors and control functions.
PERMAS offers standard solutions for a great variety of computational tasks. Even a complex
task is defined by only a few UCI commands. As an example, a complete static analysis for all
components of a configuration (all substructures to be actually treated) is performed using the
UCI-command STATIC (to RESIdual):

NEW
! initialize database
INPUT
! input of model
READ PERMAS FILE = model.dat
READ PERMAS FILE = loadsBC.dat
RETURN
!
TASK
EXEC
ACTIVATE SITUATION = S1
! select a set of BC, loads, properties etc.
STATIC
! perform a linear static analysis
! including displacements and reactions
GENERATE ELEMENT STRESS
! calculate stresses
EXPORT
GO FILE = static_res
! write all results in standard
! postprocessor format
TASK END
STOP
! terminate the analysis
A detailed description of the UCI syntax and of the available commands can be found in the
PERMAS User’s Reference Manual, chapter 2.
The PERMAS Examples Manual (EDU) contains elaborated examples for all types of analyses.

1.6.1 PERMAS input files

[project.dat]

[project.uci]

Definition of system defaults
Is an ASCII file to set up permanent definitions like database file sizes
and location.
Model description
is an ASCII file with the model data (e.g. nodes, elements, boundary
conditions).
Solution control
is an ASCII file to select the type of analysis (e.g. linear statics) as well
as solution parameters and output requests.

Intro

PERMAS.DFT

Extra !#if...!#endif constructs in UCI/DFT/DAT:
The UCI/DFT and DAT syntax rules are described in great detail in UCI Syntax Rules and
Data Input (DAT) respectively. Moreover some extra !#if / !#else / !#endif constructs may
be used inside those input files in order to share them between different PERMAS versions
and/or servers with optionally different features, capabilities and/or settings. E.g.:
!#if (version > 14.10) then
DEFAULT SET VERIFICATION = MODEL
!#else
DEFAULT SET MODEL = VERIFICATION
!#endif

makes use of the VERIFICATION switch available with PERMAS V15 and falls back to the
corresponding MODEL switch in older PERMAS versions. Or a simple feature query by e.g.:
!#ifdef XPU then
! special settings for NVIDIA GPUs (i.e. Tesla K20/K40)
DEFAULT SET PAGESIZE = 2048. ! pagesize 2048 kB
DEFAULT SET NMATP = 4
DEFAULT SET NMATPv = 4
DEFAULT SET NMATP2 = 32
!#if ($PERMAS_XPU_DEVICE == P100-PCIE-16GB) then
! special improved settings for Tesla P100 GPU
DEFAULT SET PAGESIZE = 4096. ! pagesize 4 MiB
DEFAULT SET NMATP = 5
DEFAULT SET NMATPv = 5
DEFAULT SET NMATP2 = 68
!#endif
!#endif

sets an extra large page size plus some special DMS parameter if a XPU accelerator device is
used.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

1-49

1 Introduction to PERMAS
Currently the following constructs are available:

Intro

!#ifdef key [then]
!#if ( key cmp value ) [then]
!#else ifdef key [then]
!#else if ( key cmp value ) [then]
!#else
!#endif
With !#elifdef , !#elif & !#fi serving as additional shortcuts for !#else ifdef , !#else if
& !#endif respectively.
Currently supported cmp operators are: =, ==, >, >=, <, <=, <>, /=, !=
For key any system environment variable as well as UCI switches or UCI DEFAULT switches
can be used (plus the built-in parameter shared, cores, slots, bitspw, the PERMAS version
number and XPU feature as shown in the preceding examples and the (case-insensitive) defkeys permas and visper to check the current execution type). Environment variables may be
marked by $ and/or enclosed in braces, as shown in the following example:
!#if
( HOST
== server1) then
define dms dir = /scratch1/
!#else if ($HOST
== server2) then
define dms dir = /scratch2/dms/
!#else if (${HOST} == server3) then
define dms dir = "/scratch/%(user)/"
!#endif

Remarks:
1. The same mechanism – with #!if instead of !#if (comment starter # instead of !) – can
be used in the .permasrc resource file (however, querying a resource variable ahead of
its definition should be avoided and may end in unpredictable results).
2. Currently all cmp operations are based on simple lexical order, even if an integer/float
value is specified.
3. An additional !-prefix can be used to negate an if condition (e.g. #if !(HOST == hugo)
is identical to #if (HOST <> hugo)).
4. Keep in mind that earlier PERMAS versions may not support all !#-constructs shown
in this section. Hence – when setting up version aware UCI/DAT files – it might be
necessary to restrict !#-constructs to the former capabilities accordingly (i.e. the base
!#-functionality was introduced with PERMAS V14.00.365, so it won’t work with earlier
versions).
5. Since PERMAS V17.00.210 !#if... constructs may also be nested and/or indented
(this feature will not work with earlier versions).

[project.post]

1.6.3 Protocol File
The protocol file contains the echo of the UCI–commands with extensive information regarding
all individual steps performed during the analysis, e.g. error messages, diagnostics, list of
procedures, processors (basic computational operations), data objects, an echo of the switches
and control variables, statistics about computation and I/O-time, disk space and resources.
Start of protocol file
The protocol starts with a general information about the current program version, the site where
the job was running and some project information like: project-name, date and starting time. A
detailed explanation can be found in section 1.6.5.
At program start the standard settings of the PERMAS switches is reported. The switches are
documented under the UCI SET command.
The current time is printed as the leftmost information in the run protocol.
The protocol file contains an echo of all processed UCI commands. Input and output files are
reported in addition.

Is the record length for database transfers, indicated in KiByte. The

Statistics for each procedure step
As shown above, for each procedure step (major computational step) the following information
is indicated:
• Start of the solution step
The solution step name and purpose
• End of the solution step
The number of I/O Operations between memory and disk, if any, and the used CPU and
elapsed time. Furthermore a summary of errors, warnings and comments is given, if any
message occurs.
• Within each procedure, basic (arithmetic) operations are performed. These basic operations are done by the so called Processors. The processors (indicated by Proc) get some
data objects as input and modify or build new data objects. Watching the sequence of
processors makes the solution process transparent for the experienced user. The extended protocol including processors may be activated using the parameters -PROLOG(for processor message) and -PROARG- (for data objects) of the REPort command.
Special attention should be paid to messages within solution steps.
Procedures may write additional information to the protocol file. For example, step -SYACBKserves to perform the assembly and reduction of the stiffness matrix.

Error messages
Error messages are issued as soon as problems are encountered during the solution process.
If any error occurred during the analysis, an error summary is written at the end of the protocol
file:
ERRORS

0 *X*
1 *F*
ERRORS ERRORS ERRORS

1 *E*
ERRORS ERRORS ERRORS

0 *W*
ERRORS

The protocol file should then be examined from top to bottom to find the initial cause of the
problem.
The Error Severity is defined as follows:
*C*

Comment - no program termination,
intended for additional information.

*W*

Warning - no program termination,
hints to possible error conditions, should be carefully read.

1-56

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

*E*

Error, usually due to wrong or incomplete input data or wrong solution control. The
program continues execution as long as it is meaningful (e.g. to the end of data
consolidation)

*F*

Fatal error - leading to program termination
since a continuation is not possible. The reason may be a model error or a software
bug.

*X*

Internal error - program termination.
In most cases a software bug has been detected.

In case of syntactical errors in the data input file the corresponding line is echoed in the result file
together with the error message.

1.6.4 Log File
If the calculation is made in the background, a LOG file will also be created. It contains the
subset of the protocol file information which is output to the screen, i.e. the echo of the UCI
commands and parts of the protocol file already processed.

Remarks
1. The exact PERMAS Version number is an important item for all support queries.
2. Always try to run PERMAS on a dedicated machine.
3. Do not use more than ≈ 80 % of host memory for the PERMAS job
(e.g. using ≥ 90 % typically leads to heavy performance slow-downs due to swapping).
4. Do not use hyper-threading, i.e. verify that the number of cores matches the physical
number of cores/socket (ask your system administrator if you are not sure about this).
5. The process-id (PID) may be usefull to monitor or control the job with system tools like
e.g. top, kill or perf.

Remarks
1. Always check whether the job ended successfully before evaluating the simulation results.
2. The ’peak/avg sysload’ (host load info) should not exceed the ’peak/avg efficiency’ (parallel efficiency), as that would indicate that additional cpu-intensive processes were running
during the runtime of the PERMAS job, i.e. indicates a non-dedicated system.
3. Extremely long I/O-times and/or low I/O-bandwith and/or high System times may indicate
swapping (e.g. too much memory used) or may be due to network- instead of local DMSI/O (the DMS files should always reside on fast local disks).
4. Note that the average/peak parallel efficiency (pEff/Peak) refers to the parallel parts
(pTime) only, whereas the Total parallel efficiency applies to the whole job (including
all sequential parts). I.e. due to Amdahl’s Law the overall parallel efficiency may be heavily limited by the time spent in the sequential parts, even if the parallel parts alone show
excellent speed-ups.
5. Currently only CPU cores are taken into account when calculating the parallel efficiency.
Therefore, for runs with an XPU accelerator the parallel flops [GFlp/s] is a more usefull
performance parameter.

Result File

The result file contains information about the model input. This may be an optional echo of
header lines in PERMAS input files or information on the translation of data, if a foreign format
is read by a built-in interface (door).

Intro

In any case a summary of the characteristic component data (elements, nodal points, ...) and
for each situation a degree of freedom summary is given. Furthermore, solution steps will
output additional information like balance checks, calculated eigenfrequencies, contact results
or the like. Below the sum of applied loads from a linear static analysis is shown.
Finally the user may initiate ouput of results in tabular format by commands of the PRINT
section in the UCI file.

1.6.8 Progress File

1 Introduction to PERMAS
1.6.9

User Stop-File

Intro

With a <project>.stop file it is possible to explicitly break a PERMAS iteration (e.g. a contact/NL iteration or optimization loop) without loosing already computed results, i.e. stop further
calculations, but export all previously converged solutions. For this the stop-file must contain
the keyword BREAK (with an optional comment)* :
E.g.: myjob.stop
BREAK

! Break all iterations & proceed in UCI (export results so far)

If the user breaks a static contact calculation during the iteration of LPAT/TSTEP j, then all previously calculated LPATs/TSTEPs up to j-1† will be transformed and exported, i.e. the iteration
stops without error-termination and the rest of the UCI file is executed as if all iterations were
successfull.
The keyword KILL directly stops the job with a PERMAS error termination and without further
exports (but still closes/deletes the DMS-Files and gives a PERMAS job summary, i.e. is more
clean than a simple system ’kill pid’ command). With PAUSE the job can be set to hold and
the keyword TRACE can be used to print the current call-stack without stopping the job.
Beside the general BREAK command for all running iterations a specific stop request may be
given for a particular calculation step: E.g. STATIC, INERTIA, NLMATERIAL, NLTEMP, NLTIME,
OPTIM, TOPO or VIBRATION will break iterations within the specified UCI command only. Moreover CASOLV, CAU, MLLSOLV, NLEQUI or NLITER will break the corresponding iteration level only
(e.g. may stop the current CA-Iteration, but keep the above NL-Iteration running or vice versa).
Additionally a stop file may be used to apply one of the following UCI commands to a running
PERMAS job: DUMP, REPORT or SET (also see additional remarks on next page).
keyword

Table T1-12: List of Stop-File Keywords

For ’Break’ actions an additional break time may be specified, e.g.
STATIC TIME = 4.5

! Stop load history after reaching T = 4.5

will not break the currently running iterations, but will stop a static load history after reaching
(i.e. after convergence of) time step T = 4.5.

Additional remarks on DUMP and SET:
Keep in mind that changing UCI switch values right in the middle of a running job may cause
an unpredictable runtime behaviour depending on whether or not the underlying solution step
caches the corresponding switch value. Hence – inside a stop-file – only use DUMP or SET
with care. E.g. it is perfectly safe to in- or decrease the job’s verbosity (e.g. SET CAPRINT=4)
but don’t change critical control parameters of a running iteration.

1.7

Starting PERMAS

Usually PERMAS is started by the PERMAS Control Center
There may also be site specific solutions provided by the IT department, e.g. in case of batch
queuing systems.

Intro

It is possible to restrict the starting of the job on the condition that all required license modules
are available by setting a ! REQUEST.MODULES statement in the .uci, e.g.
! REQUEST.MODULES = MQA; LS; CAX
If one or more of the requested modules are not available at job starting time (because e.g.
already requested by another already running job), the job will wait for them.
The module names can be found at the end of a .pro file, which may also be generated by a
TASK / TASK STORE run.
Example:
License Resources Summary
License Type = Multi-Server, Module
Server:Port = srv5:56797
Used Threads = 4
Used Modules = LS;MQA;TOPO

options

Available options are:
-apc

file.f
Definition of a control program with a different name than project.f.

-memory

{R|text|all}
Explicit definition of the memory size. Optionally, the whole (process) memory may
be used by the -ALL- option. Real numbers are interpreted as MiB, a text string
may select the following units, based either on 1024 or 1000:
Base 1024 (IEC units): MI/MIB, GI/GIB, TI/TIB
Base 1000 (SI units): M/MB, G/GB/GBYTE, T/TB/TB
Examples: ’25.4 GIB’, ’2000.M’, ’1.2TIB’

-shared

n
Number of processes for a shared memory parallel PERMAS execution.

-io

{main|thread|direct}
Select synchronous, asynchronous or direct asynchronous I/O. Asynchronous and
direct asynchronous I/O requires a parallel licence of PERMAS. Direct asynchronous
I/O is recommended for high performance SSD devices.

-version

version
Use a different PERMAS version than the standard version. Each name of a PERMAS version subdirectory or its related symbolic link in the PERMAS root directory
is valid.

-module

module name
Select a special linked PERMAS module.
Use the permas executable permas_<module>
If a user supplied program is involved, e.g. <file>.f, use a different module specification file named permexrc_<module> for linking.

General

For an overview and the basic structure of an UCI file please see the introduction.

2.1.1 Syntax Rules

Structure of command syntax

command := key [param]∗0 [assignment]∗0

key:

Command keyword
Starts a command definition. Uppercase letters are mandatory whereas the
lower case letters may be omitted (short form).

assignment:= param = list
Param is a parameter of type name
list:=

tuple [tuple]∗0
A list contains a sequence of tuples, separated by blanks. Lists are separated
by a colon. one tuple of a list may contain items of different types, but each tuple
in a list must have the same number of items and corresponding tuples in a list
must be of the same type.

tuple:=

item[,item]∗0
Tuples contain a certain number of items, separated by commas

text (text)
Specifies the basic input entity. The syntactical abbreviations are given in brackets.

item:=

Square brackets ( [ ] ) enclose optional input. Subscripts and superscripts at the closing bracket
indicate the possible number of repetitions of the enclosed content. For example:
[cont] cont may appear once
[cont]∗ cont may appear as often as needed

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

2-1

2 User Control Interface (UCI)
[cont]m
n cont has to appear between n and m times
Braces ( {} ) contain syntax elements where one element has to be selected. If the selection
is optional, the braces are enclosed by square brackets. The default syntax element, if any, is
underlined.

UCI

The command input can be written in free format input lines with a maximum length of 256
characters . One or more blanks serve as separators between different parameters. A command always ends at the logical end of line. The logical end of line is either defined by the
physical end of line or from the comment sign (!) or by the command separator (;).
The comment sign starts documentation text which is of no further relevance. Several commands may be written onto one line, using the command separator.
(e.g. HELP NAME=TASK ; TASK ; EXEC ; STATIC ; . . .).
The logical end of line may be delayed, using the continuation character (&). This allows to
write a command onto several lines. The continuation character must be specified as the last
character on the command line.
Some UCI commands allow the input of %-Format Enriched Text (%-Text), i.e. text where the
%-character* allows the specification of some self-expanding context-sensitive format fields, like
e.g. ’the current situation’s name is %(sit)’.
Moreover those % fields may be formatted additionally according to the [s]printf syntax rules,
e.g. SET CASNAME = ’/home/%(user)/%(proj)_T=%12.6(nltime)_with_PERMAS%(vers).cas’.
See appendix H for a table of self-expanding %-fields.
A syntax error in the command input leads to an error message, nevertheless, the command
input may be continued in any way.

* Note, that – in order to prevent a native % from being mis-interpreted as a format specifier – each single % has

to be masked by a double %% (exactly like the [s]printf syntax rules).

2.1 General
The command description is partitioned into the following parts:
1. Syntax description
The syntax description contains all parameters of a command and the sequence of their
specification. If abbreviations are possible, the short form of the command is written in
capital letters.
2. Parameter description
The parameter description explains the possible settings of each parameter of a command.

UCI

3. Remarks (optional)
Contains some hints which should be watched, when applying the command.
4. Description (optional)
If necessary, the command is explained in more detail in an extended description.
5. Examples (optional)
For more complex commands, an example may follow to illustrate the application.

2.1.2 Important Files
Default file extensions
In order to save some effort in file definitions and to make batch jobs more convenient, some
default filenames are supported. The defaults are connected to the project specification and
differ just in the second part of the filename:

Naming rule : < project > < extension >

The project specification consists of up to 40 characters and serves as the leading name part.
In the following table, the default extensions are compiled.

The only file with a fixed naming rule is the PERMAS default definition file. The activation of the

data files

: The connection of the files and the data input is initiated only once if no explicit data input files have been defined so far with the first TASK definition.
Additionally some UCI sections will do the same actions when they are entered (see chapter 2.5 for more details). All files with default extensions are
read consecutively.

LOG, PRO file: Activation depends on the selected amount of output.
RES file

: Activation for all printed results, echo of data files and general model information.

The default (project) files must always be located in the working directory if they shall be taken
into account.
Similar, the standard PERMAS output files (PRO-,RES-file) are also located in the working directory. The only exception are the database files, which may be directed to different locations.
The meaning of the working directory is machine dependent, reference is made to the installation manuals.

PERMAS default definition file
The Default Definition File serves to define important parameters for the system startup. It is
an ASCII file which contains commands in free format. It may be modified through editing the
file or in an interactive way through the DEFAULT command. There are several possibilities to
redefine the default settings. The search rule of the files is as following :
1. The local default definition file.
Is located in the working directory of the user and is valid for all PERMAS runs in this

2-4

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

2.1 General
environment. However, if the changes of some parameters refer just to one project, it is
recommended to use the default command on UCI level instead of a modified version of
the defaults file in order to avoid confusion for later PERMAS runs.

3. The system default definition file.
Is located in the PERMAS directory and represents the default settings submitted by
INTES, which may be adapted to reflect general settings of one site.
Only the first default definition file in the search path is interpreted by PERMAS. The possible
locations of the default definition files are highly machine dependent. Depending on the file
system of the appropriate machine, some locations of the default definition file may be not
existent. Reference is made to the installation manuals for a detailed description.

Filename Conventions
User defined filenames have to be written in the convention which is valid for the appropriate
machine. They may be given with the complete directory path. Nevertheless the path definition
may be defined separately. Then the final filename is build through a concatenation of the
pathname and the filename. This may be advantageous if several files are located in the same
directory.

filnam = [path]fnam

There is nearly no restriction concerning the character set for a filename (i. e. the name
parts). The only character which is not allowed to be a part of the filename is the comment
sign which always defines the logical end of line. A filename must always be the last parameter
of a command, because the end of line mark (or the comment sign) will define the end of the
filename. It may not be continued upon several input lines using the continuation character.
The command separator (;) is also a part of the filename. Therefore it is not possible to write
another command on the same physical line.
The user is responsible for the required read / write permissions and the existence of the
specified directories (reading/writing) and files (reading). Missing directories will not be created
by PERMAS.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

2-5

UCI

2. The personal default definition file.
It is located in the users home directory and allows to modify the settings due to the
special needs of a certain user. If the changes are not permanent, it is recommended
to use the default command instead of a modified version of the defaults file in order to
avoid confusion for later PERMAS runs.

2 User Control Interface (UCI)
2.1.3

Keys

The treatment of keys is partitioned into two parts.
1. Global keys
2. Local keys

UCI

Global Keys are available within the whole system. They are of interest within (nearly) all
sections. They are treated within a centralized switch handler and may be set/shown through
the global SET/SHOW commands.
Local Keys are of interest only within a special environment (one or a few sections are affected).
Typical examples are system initialization parameters. These keys are defined in the PERMAS
Default Definition File. They may be changed by the same syntax convention as they are
defined (If they are changeable). Only the default keys which are of interest for the section are
available as parameters of the DEFAULT command of the section. The only exception of this
rule is the startup section, which knows all default keys in order to initialize the system.

2.1.4

Task Definition

The execution of a task is split into two phases, namely the test phase and the work phase.
During the test phase, all possible tests are performed to ensure that no mandatory input is
missing and the control flow contains no contradictions. However, no data objects belonging to
computational requests are affected during the test phase. Nevertheless, requests performing
consolidation steps are always executed in order to be able to do as much checks as possible.
A command specified within a task with an erroneous syntax will not be introduced in the task.
Therefore it may be corrected immediately without exiting the task (if the definition is done
interactively).
If errors are found during the test phase, the execution of the requests is skipped. The test
phase may also be activated separately. This allows the checking of several tasks one after
another. Since PERMAS allows to examine various variants of a model, the consolidation
process of the data is split into two phases.
1. Situation independent data
They are consolidated once, if the input process is finished. The consolidation is either
invoked through a task definition or by entering specific sections (see chapter 2.5). After
the consolidation process, the last component defined in the input data is active. This
component is also the currently active configuration. However, no situation is active at all.
2. Situation dependent data
The consolidation is done as soon as the task is defined which has to be executed for
the chosen situation. Therefore all variants of a model may be validated subsequently by
defining and storing the desired tasks.

2-6

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

2.1 General
Requests coming from Input Doors (e.g. NASTRAN) are translated into PERMAS commands
by the corresponding task translators. They form separate tasks, as soon as the task translator
is activated.
Some general rules must be obeyed when defining a task.

• A task definition requires the successful consolidation of a situation. If there are several
situations, the situation to be examined actually should be activated before defining the
task.
• If no situation is active when entering the task mode (e.g. for default input files) the first
situation defined in the model description will be activated.
• Material properties which are required for subsequent computational tasks must be
present for all referenced materials of the actual system variant in order to allow an efficient scanning process of the task.
• For more detail see page 2-55 ff.

2.1.5 Handling of Configurations, Components and Variants
After processing and consolidation of the input data, a working environment has to be defined in
order to specify the components to be treated by following computational requests and to define
the variants of the model to be examined. This environment has to be selected before defining
a computational task. There is a strong hierarchy in activating the computational environment.
1. Activate the configuration by specifying the top component
2. Activate the variants of the model by defining the situation
3. Activate a special (sub-) component to restrict some actions to this component.
These activations may be done using the -ACTivate- command (see page 2-60).
Nevertheless, if the structure consists of just one component, no configuration has to be selected. If no situation was selected explicitly, the first situation defined in the input data will be
activated by the system (see task definition, page 2-55 ff.).
All computational requests handled by the -EXEC- section (see page 2-103 ff.) work within the
components of the active configuration. The loading, system or constraint variants to be examined for this configuration are selected by the active situation which to be defined previously
through the appropriate variants.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

2-7

UCI

• The task description has to be initiated in the top component of a configuration, i.e. the
TASK [BEGIN] command must be specified while the top component is active. For substructure models, this top component has to be selected explicitly before defining the task.
It is not possible to change the configuration after the TASK [BEGIN] has been initiated.

2 User Control Interface (UCI)

Handling of variants

UCI

An arbitrary combination of loading, constraint and system variants of the model may be examined by defining the corresponding situations. New situations may be defined at any stage of
the computations and input data of the appropriate variants may be read in as often as needed,
with the only restriction, that the input of data is no more possible after the successful consolidation process of the variant. The exception of this rule are material data which may be
completed (i.e. additional material properties may be added) after the consolidation process
has been performed. However a reference to a new material must be done within another
system variant.
For each of these situations a new (computational) task may be defined. Only the data blocks
and modules which are subject to changes will be rebuild for the different situations. Nevertheless, each result will be computed only once within one situation. Each of these data modules
is only accessible within the corresponding situation.
In table T2-1 the data modules to be rebuilt for a new situation are summarized for the change
of a single variant. The result of any other combination of variants may be derived from these
basic changes.

Remarks:
1. Data Blocks serve to store the input data of one variant of a type they are named due to
the input variants. Each data block is independent from any other.
2. Data Modules are build due to the data dependency of the input variants as stored in the
data blocks. They are situation dependent and have no reference of their names to the
input variants.

Remarks:
1. The (temporary) allocation of additional memory may be performed during the coarsening
phase of the graph, depending on switch XMALOC.
2. The MESHOPT options HFSMFLC or HFSMLND are highly recommended if substructure

3. By MESHOPT option HFSMLND, the reordering is realized by (temporary) allocation of
additional memory outside of the PERMAS core memory.
4. If an external node sequence is provided via $NODESEQ, there is no need to switch off
the mesh optimization. MESHOPT = OFF is only of interest for a model check, where no
resource estimation is needed. Otherwise, a dramatical performance decrease will occur.
5. The mesh condensation may lead to better reordering results for models dominated by
higher order elements for the reordering option HFSMFLC and HFSMLND.

which is the default in PERMAS:


 strain tensor is defined as
ǫG = 12 F T F − I

UCI

ǫG_lin = 12 H T + H
with H = F − I.

P3 strain
N

and theP
logarithmic strain

are both described by the principal stretches λi and the principal stretch directions in the

Defines the record length for memory and backing
storage allocation. This parameter should not be
changed by a user without special advice (if the
pagesize is redefined, DMS settings will be reinitialized, too).
An input as real value (recommended) specifies
the pagesize in MiByte or KiByte, respectively. Typical values are 1.0 or 2.0 MiB (1024.0 or 2048.0
KiB, usually multiples of 16.0 KiB). Small real values (≤ 32.0) are interpreted as MiB, larger real values (> 32.0) are interpreted as KiB. E.g. 1.0 and
1024.0 both specify a 1.0 MiB = 1024.0 KiB page
size.
If given as integer (deprecated), the value is interpreted in integer words (note that this may lead to
different record sizes with M and L flavours).

4. VERIFICATION = MODEL requests output of an extended model and related results in
the EXPORT section.
• The exported model is not identical with the input, since it may contain internally

• A detailed description of available verification items can be found in chapter 6.1.2.

UCI
STARTUP

• Shape optimization using design element interpolation generates a parametric representation of the element coordinates involved. To check the parametric representation an item ’Design Element Verification’ is used which is a displacement vector
from the original coordinate position to parametric coordinate position. This result is
intended to check the accuracy of the parametric model in any postprocessor with
displacement support (setting magnification factor to 1.0). Please refer to Example
OP7 of [um550] on page 14-94 ff.
• Finite Element to design element assignment can be verified by item ’Elem to Design
Elem Relation’. The design element number is assigned to each finite element. This
result can be processed by postprocessor as element result. If the external design
element number exceeds a specific number ( 16777216 on 32 bit computer ) internal
design element numbering is used.
5. The default stiffness properties for the WLD spotweld model are specified by WLDSTIFFREF as a tuple of values:

mscale, nstiff, tstiff, rstiff, rotstiff

mscale Scale parameter for minimum mesh size of calibration function
nstiff

Normal stiffness

tstiff

Translational shear stiffness

rstiff

Rotational shear stiffness

rotstiff Rotational in-plane stiffness
If WLDSTIFFREF is omitted, the stiffness of each $MPC WLDSURFACE connection
property has to be specified explicitly. If specified, the STIFF field quantities of the GEODAT assignment may be omitted for the corresponding spring elements.
6. WLDMESHREF allows to define explicitly the calibration mesh size for the WLD connection. To be adapted if the system of units is being changed (see also DEAFULT SET
WLDSTIFFREF). Used to check current mesh sizes against calibrated ones. If omitted,
the averaged local mesh size is used.

7. A reduction of the nodal point partitioning value NPART is required for node-node partitioned matrices, which is for example required by the FIRST interface. This is mandatory
for the full 64 bit version of PERMAS (s64).

13. If the estimated number of parts exceeds the maximum (mxpart = VPARTLIM), then all

nof el

elements to be grouped in a part is then minelpp = mxpart
14. By default the NLMATERIAL command scans the $NLLOAD input for characteristic times
to adapt the automatic time step settings. Characteristic times are either times where
a load scaling function has a minimum/maximum or the sampling times of tabular load
scaling functions. If a smooth loading history is defined by interpolation between a large
number of individual load patterns (e.g. temperature results of a transient heat transfer analysis), this may lead to an unnecessary high number of load increments. Set
NLLOADCHECK = OFF in this special case.
15. In order to find extrema of the load scaling functions the analysis time interval is split into
smaller intervals. The number of these intervals can be adapted via the NLLOADCHECKX
switch. If the number of extrema of a single load scaling function in the interval [tstart , tend ]
is higher than NLLOADCHECKX only NLLOADCHECKX extrema will be detected and
the remaining will be ignored. In this case NLLOADCHECKX should be increased. A
reasonable choice for NLLOADCHECKX is given by 10 ∗ (tend − tstart ) /∆text,min , where
∆text,min is the minimum distance between two extrema.
16. Regarding the extrapolation of secondary results in a NLMATERIAL analysis (EXSLEN /
EXSNEN), an element is regarded as linear if it features a linear material definition and
is geometrically linear. An element is geometrically linear either due to the analysis type
(NLGEOM = NO) or because the element type generally does not feature geometrically
nonlinear behavior, please see page 5-16ff. of [um550].
17. MATIPOL: The standard linear interpolation of tabular material input data has been the
default algorithm up to PERMAS V16. Especially for material nonlinear analyses, this
may lead to worse (or no) convergence compared to the new algorithm.
18. The limiting value of damper elements MXSMWDAMP will also be used in the MLDR
algorithm for an auto-raise of the elements to the top component. That is, for a larger
number of elements than the limit, the element nodes have to be selected manually, if
they are desired to be in the top component. Be careful, this may cause longer simulation
times.

PRESET

Preset standard settings

TOLBASE = tolbase

Description:
The command initializes standard settings according to the choice of the base value.
A consistent choice for the system of units for all input data is still under user’s responsibility.
Parameter

Type

Explanation

TOLBASE

R

Multiplicator for initialization of length tolerance settings, see remark 1.

Remarks:
1. The command will re-initialize the length dependent SET parameters
TOLNOD, TOLSYS, MPCDISTOL, MPCOUTTOL,
CADISTOL, CAOUTTOL, CAGEOUPTOL, CATOLSLIP,
PFDISTOL, PFOUTTOL, PTDISTOL and PTOUTTOL
with their default values multiplied by the given tolbase factor. The default values are
documented with the SET parameters above.
For example, tolbase = 1.0E-2 will re-initialize TOLNOD to 1.0E-5 (original default:
TOLNOD = 0.001), CADISTOL to 0.1 (original default: CADISTOL = 10.0), etc.
2. Resetting length dependent tolerances may be useful if a geometrically small model is
discretized in SI units (e.g. ’millimeter sized model in meter units’). In such cases the
original defaults for the above listed tolerance parameters may be too large. Consider
using PRESET TOLBASE = 1.0E-3 (or 1.0E-2) in such cases.
3. If a particular tolerance setting shall be changed, the corresponding SET command must
be performed after the PRESET command.

Transp. commands: available
PERMAS allows to read input from different sources. The input section serves to define an
input file different from the standard input which is defined as <project>.<defext> (machine
dependent), where def ext is the default file extension (i.e. myproject.dat).
If the input is distributed upon several files, all input files should be read in before leaving the
input section because subsequent sections may activate the consolidation process of the input
data. In this case, an explicit RETURN (see page 2-24 ff.) command is recommended to leave
the input section. All sections allowing for the task mode (grouping commands) will initiate
the input of default files if they are entered. Subsequently the consolidation process of data is
invoked. The following sections require the existence of input data:
• EXEC
• PRINT
• EXPORT
• SELECT

2. The SITUATION parameter serves for an explicit definition of the situation name, regardless of the situation name defined in the input file. For the time being, only the Abaqus
