2-402

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

2.9 The EXPORT section

MATRIX

2. In addition to the matrices, a condensed model is being created for the external dofs(/modes)
of the component. This option is recommended in order to have a minimum disc space
requirement, both for the matrix file, as well as for the analysis results.
3. Allows to postprocess results also in the mathematical subcomponent model. A reduced
backtransformation is possible by the result variant parameters $PARAMETER (see page
3-1057 ff.) with options RFILTER/REFILTER. In case of a dynamic condensation, a condensed model is being created for the external modes of the component.
4. In addition to the matrices, a condensed model is being created for the external dofs and
the local dofs of the component. The option allows to hide the physical model but for
optimum performance, the ORIG option is recommended.

6. The data objects are written according to the parameters given in the OPEN command
(OPEN (see page 2-403 ff.)), or the default settings of the OPEN command are used.
Only PERMAS Format is supported for this functionality.
7. The requested data object must exist.
8. Degree of freedom information refers to possibly rotated node basis. (Component system
if no rotated basis).
9. The backtransformation matrix may be very huge, depending on the number of local and
external dofs. Hence, it may be more efficient to re-compute the matrix in subsequent
runs.
10. For fscoupled vibration analysis, please perform a structural weight analysis before invoking the matrix model command.
11. Following parameter can be set for a modified selection of data
• DRYCOND PRESSURE
• LOAD MATRIX
For a detailed description see EXPORT PARAM (see page 2-405 ff.) command.
12. For the selected elements, an output of plot elements is being performed in the artificial
model. If the NSET parameter is used, an element is only output, if all element nodes are
a part of the node set.
Example:
Please refer to Example DEVX1V4 of [um550] on page 8-25 ff.

has to be chosen using the EXPORT CURRENT (see page 2-365 ff.) command.

Send units definition to postprocessing file (see remark 10).

1. A duplicate node may be removed if all dofs are being declared as external, i.e. no local
results exist. The CCNODES option helps to reduce the size of the result output of a
combined model.
2. CRULE sets the preference for keeping identifiers in a combined model (ITEM TOPO
COMBINE). The applicability of a rule is postprocessor dependent. Please have a look in
the interface description for further information.
3. The sets are created by the PRETEST (see page 2-315 ff.) command.

off during the export with the EXPORT MATRIX (see page 2-399 ff.) command.
• The Craig Bampton matrix for the pressure dofs will not be written on the matrix file.
• The CBSOLV parameter and the local dofs of the doftype pressure is also not written
to the post file for the ARTIFICIAL method of the matrix model export.
5. The export of load matrices (BQM, BQH ...) can be switched off during the export with
the EXPORT MATRIX (see page 2-399 ff.) command.
6. Number of digits for float values of model data on PERMAS export files POST or DATO.
The default value is the value of the DEFAULT SET MODEL_DIGITS switch.
7. Number of digits for float values of results on PERMAS export file POST.
8. Reduce the amount of data for the pressure result. FLUID DOFS = ALL writes values for
all degrees of fredom of the pressure result.
9. Reduce the amount of data for displacement, velocity and acceleration results. MECHANICAL DOFS = ALL writes values for all degrees of fredom of the displacement, velocity
and acceleration results, if possible for the selected post processor format.
10. Send the units to postprocessing file. Currently only used for the I-DEAS MASTER_SERIES
file. The given units are the units of the model. It is no conversion of any data performed!

PARAM

Parameter

Value

Explanation

DEFO

DEFO

Use old fashioned MEDINA DEFO/DEFOK data structure for displacement, velocity and acceleration results. This includes the rotational data in any case, also for models with solid elements only.
(Data element DEFO with CAE-Key 231 and 7 values per node and
data element DEFOK with CAE-Key 232 and 13 values per node for
complex results.)
Use new MEDINA DEFOT/DEFOTK data structure for displacement,
velocity and acceleration results, if the model contains only translational degrees of fredom, or if only translational results are requested. (Data element DEFOT with CAE-Key 233 and 4 values per
node and data element DEFOTK with CAE-Key 237 and 7 values per
node for complex results. This is introduced in Medina Version 7.1.)
Use old fashioned MEDINA NPST data structure for nodal point
stress and strain. This includes the principal stresses, strains and
its direction cosine values (data element NPST with CAE-Key 500
and 20 values per node).
Use new MEDINA NPST data structure for nodal point stress and
strain without additional principal values. (Data element NPSTS with
CAE-Key 501 and 7 values per node. This is introduced in Medina
Version 8.2.)
Write additional Label data for a better Description of result data and
the situation name as Load Case Title (this is introduced in Medina
Version 6.3.5).
No additional Label data for result data.
Use old fashioned MEDINA SET data structure (data element SET
with CAE-Key 100 and 40 character for the set label).
Use new MEDINA SET data structure. (Data element GENSET with
CAE-Key 99 and an unlimited length for the set label. This is introduced in Medina Version 8.1.)
Write both definitions on the MEDINA model file.

Remarks:

3.1 Basic Concepts

3 Data Input (DAT)
3.1

Basic Concepts

The input to finite element systems may contain a large amount of data. To handle those data
in a user convenient and clearly structured manner the PERMAS data input was developed
following some fundamental concepts:

• Block structure
Data are input in blocks, i.e. a header line describing data type, input options etc., and
lines with input data. Data blocks are assigned to components, variants etc. by enclosing
them with bracket lines. The sequence the data blocks are input is of no importance for
the computation.
• Separation of material data
Input data for PERMAS are split up into component-dependent data, i.e. mesh definition,
constraints, loads etc., and component-independent material data. Materials are defined
by data blocks describing all needed material properties, and are referenced by their
names within component-dependent input.
• Identifiers
Node identifiers, element identifiers etc. can be chosen in an arbitrary manner but have to
be unique within one component. Performance and internal data structure do not depend
on the numbers used as identifiers.
• Set concept
Sets are used to group together elements or nodes. Sets are identified by names, and in
most cases where properties, loads etc. are assigned a set name instead of the identifier
of a single element or node may be used.
• Data input convention
In contrast to earlier versions of PERMAS the zero/overwrite convention is no longer
valid. All necessary data have to be input with the only exception that in some cases
trailing zeroes may be omitted. Overwriting of input data by new input is never possible.

3.1.1 Partition of Data Input
The data input to PERMAS consists of text lines in a sequential file which are arranged in data
blocks, enclosed by brackets of different level. High level brackets $ENTER ... $EXIT enclose
component-dependent data for one component as well as component-independent data, e.g.
material data. Medium level brackets $name ... $END name enclose data blocks which e.g.
belong to the same variant of one component. Data blocks itself consist of a data block header

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-1

DAT

• Uniform syntax
Input lines for all kind of data and, as far as possible, UCI commands follow the same
syntax rules.

3 Data Input (DAT)
line and any number of data lines. Data blocks are bounded by a new data block header line
or by bracket lines. Lines to close brackets ($EXIT, $END) are always optional. The input is
closed by a delimiter line $FIN.
The partitioning of input data is shown in the following simple example:

DAT

3.1.2 Lines and Items
Physical Lines are text lines in the input file (formatted records), and may contain up to 256
characters . Physical lines are counted during the input, therefore the line number in the input
echo print always refer to physical lines. Empty lines, i.e. lines which contain only blanks, are
skipped but nevertheless counted.
Logical Lines consist of one or more physical lines, the first of which is the starting line, the
remaining lines are continuation lines. Logical lines are handled internally as one input entity,
but nevertheless splitting of items is not allowed, i.e. each item must start and end on the same
physical line. Comments are not part of logical lines.

Header Lines contain a dollar sign ($) as first non-blank character. They are used as data block
header lines, bracket header or delimiter lines and for control purposes. Header lines (except
$ECHO) may have any number of continuation lines. The general syntax of header lines is
given by


$key

parameter





assignment

∗

where key contains the header key.
Data Lines contain as first non-blank character neither a dollar sign ($) nor an ampersand (&)
nor an exclamation mark (!). They are used to input data within data blocks and may contain
any number of continuation lines. The general syntax of data lines is given by:



id



Each logical line contains one or more token. A Token is the basic input entity. Each token
consists of one or more characters. A token may be an item or a one-character symbol, and
may be bounded by blanks or one-character symbols. No token, except text in quotation marks,
can contain any blanks.

because some output formats etc. assume integers to have not more than nine digits.

Floating Point Numbers have a mantissa with a mandatory decimal point and an optional sign.
They may also have an exponent starting with character E or D , followed by a signed or
unsigned integer number.

Text is enclosed in matching quotation marks, i.e. a pair of single (’), double (") or back quotes
(‘), and may contain any other character available including non-matching quotation marks (e.g.
"hugo’s text") and/or those characters which are used as one-character symbols otherwise.
The type of quote is not significant, e.g. ’text’ = "text" = ‘text‘. Also a quoted upper case
text is identical to the name token without quotes, e.g. name = Name = NAME = ’NAME’ but ’NAME’
6= ’Name’ 6= ’name’ 6= name
Name or text tokens may be split using an ampersand (&) as concatenation symbol, e.g.
’Text-1’ & ’, ’ & ’Text-2’ will result in a single text token with value ’Text-1, Text-2’.
Therefore, name or text tokens may be split over several physical lines using an ampersand (&)
as trailing symbol before starting a continuation line with the next part of the name/text token
(note that a concatenating ampersand can not be used as first token of the continuation line,
because this would collide with the continuation line starter, which is an ampersand symbol,
too).

DAT

$BASVAR

3.1.3 Notation for Syntax Definition
Keywords etc. the user has to input as given in the syntax description are printed in CAPITALS.
If trailing characters may be omitted they are printed in small letters.
Syntactical abbreviations, e.g. list, are printed in small letters.
Names of items the user has to substitute by his input data are printed in italic.
Square brackets ( [ ] ) enclose optional input. Subscripts and superscripts at the closing bracket
signify the possible number of repetitions of the enclosed content:
cont may appear but only once.
cont may appear as often as needed.
cont has to appear at least n-times while the maximum number is m.

Braces ( { } ) contain arrays of elements where one element has to be selected. If the content
of the braces is optional (braces enclosed in square brackets) the default element, if any, is
underlined.

3 Data Input (DAT)
3.1.4

Data Generation

The general idea of the input data generation is to define input variables which can be accessed
in generation loops. Input variables, defined by $DEFVAR commands, are identified by names
varnam and may have a finite number of values, defined by a list, or an infinite number of
values, defined by a generation rule. Each input variable has a data type which may be integer,
real, double precision or name, and each value of that input variable is of that type.
Input variables with fixed integer indices (e.g. SITNAM(3)) may be used as constant items
anywhere in the current input stream whereas input variables with index expression may be
used only within a data generation loop. Each data generation loop consists of a $LOOP
command, any number of input lines, and a $ENDLOOP command. On the $LOOP line there
is the definition of the loop variable by
lpvar = iS , iE

DAT

with the name of the loop variable lpvar, the start value iS which must be greater than zero,
and the end value iE which must be greater than or equal iS . The generation loop starts with
lpvar = iS , and after each loop lpvar is incremented by one, therefore the loop is executed
(iE − iS + 1)-times.
Within a loop, input variables may be used to replace any integer, real, double precision or
name item. The input variable is inserted as varnam(ind) where ind is an index expression of
the form
[c1 ∗] v1 [± [ci ∗] vi ] [± c0 ]

where ci are integer constants and vi are loop variables. The value varnam(ind) replaces then
the original value in the data line.
Any number of input variables may defined, but the definition may not be done within a loop,
and each input variable referenced must be defined before.
Loops may be defined within an outer loop; up to 25 loop levels are supported.
Example:
$DEFVAR
$DEFVAR
$DEFVAR

LPATNUM
ITEMID
TEMPVAL

TYPE = INTEGER
TYPE = INTEGER
TYPE = REAL

LIST = 101 102 105 106 110
GEN = 1,1
GEN = 0.0,50.0

!
$STRUCTURE
$NSET NAME = RES_NODES
$LOOP I = 1,5
$LOOP J = 1,5
$LOOP K = 1,10
ITEMID(100*I + 10*J + K - 110)
$ENDLOOP
$ENDLOOP
$ENDLOOP
$END STRUCTURE
!
$LOADING
$LOOP I = 1,5
$DISLOADN TEMP LPAT = LPATNUM(I)
NODE_SET TEMPVAL(2*I-1)

Remarks:
1. The name of a component must be unique.
2. Each component has a discretization type. Components with different discretization types
may not be mixed in one configuration.
3. A component may contain degrees of freedom of different types.

$ENTER COMPONENT

3 Data Input (DAT)

4. If a new component is defined, list(doftype) must contain all degree of freedom types used
in the new component with the exception of MATH, which is always added automatically.
If parameter DOFTYPE is omitted, the default is DISP and MATH.
5. If the component name is already existing and parameter DOFTYPE is used, list(doftype)
must contain all degree of freedom types except MATH of the existing component.

Model
Data

6. Parameter DOFTYPE on $ENTER COMPONENT line determines the default degree of
freedom type within current component definition brackets for all data block header lines
where a degree of freedom type can be selected. If a list of degree of freedom types is
given, the first one is used as default, else the default is always DISP, even if the current
component has no displacement degrees of freedom.
7. Component definition bracket is closed by an (optional) $EXIT COMPONENT line or by
any other high level bracket line.
8. The new component may be established as a copy of another (parent) component with all
its variants† . This parent component must not be consolidated previously. The complete
$STRUCTURE block and all existing variants are included. New variants may be defined,
and within the $STRUCTURE block utilities may be added, i.e. the following data blocks
are available:
$CONTLOCK
$DSVSET
$ESET
$ESETBIN
$GSYS
$IMPORT
$LNSET
$NSET
$NSETBIN
$NTRSYS
$RSYS
$RSYSAX

Element set definition
Element set bin definition
Global system definition
Import of data objects from file
Line set definition
Node set definition
Node set bin definition
Node transformation definition
Reference system definition
Axisymmetric reference system definition
Surface set definition

For all sets however, the addition must be performed after the consolidation of the component. It is not possible to add these items directly. Of course, overwriting or changing
of already defined data is not possible.

†

If the new or parent component contains a $CONTLOCK statement then contact definitions and load variants are
not copied !

Remarks:
1. Situations are defined within the top component of a configuration. A single component
is always the top component.
2. The situation name is mandatory and must be unique within one configuration. If a data
line is present and the component name is missing, then the data line specifications hold
for the current component.
3. If for a situation a variant is not assigned explicitly but needed, the default variant (DFLTCNST, DFLTSYST, DFLTLOAD, DFLTMOD or DFLTRES) is used. Default variants must not
be specified explicitly. If only default variants are used the data line of the situation definition may be omitted.
4. Up to now, structure block variants should be used only for the generalized dynamic
condensation as presented in examples DEVX8V1 to DEVX8V3, the Mixed Boundary
Craig-Bampton Method.
5. Situation definition is closed by an (optional) $END SITUATION line or by a new component input medium level bracket line or by any high level bracket line.
6. If parameter PARENT is specified, the data block defines the child situation name of parent situation parent. Child situations make use of results of the corresponding parent
situation (e.g. modal methods need the eigenmodes of the system) and have i.g. the
same system and constraint variants as the parent situation. For exceptions see remark
8.
Child situations may be connected to other situations, but situations where connections
are specified must be non-child situations, therefore parameter CONNECTED is not available if parameter PARENT is specified.
7. The following variants may be selected within definition of a (parent) situation without
parameter CONNECTED:
• Constraint, system, loading and result variants of top or single component.
• Constraint variants for all subcomponents of the configuration.
System variants of subcomponents are selected by a $SUBVAR data block within system variant definition, see page 3-556, loading variants by a $SUBVAR data block within
loading variant definition, see page 3-876, and modification variants by a $SUBVAR data
block within modification variant definition, see page 3-996.

3-18

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

3.2 Model Data

$SITUATION

8. The following variants may be selected within definition of a child situation:

Constraint variants may not be specified within a child situation definition since they are
already defined by corresponding parent situation. System variants for child situations
containing modal transient or modal frequency response analyses may only be specified
if the system variant of the parent situation is inserted into the system variant of the child
situation, see $INSERT VARIANT, page 3-525. Loading variants of subcomponents are
selected by a $SUBVAR data block within loading variant definition, see page 3-876.
9. If parameter CONNECTED is specified:
• System and modification variants for top or single components of situations controlling design optimization
All situations connected to one specific design optimization must contain the same system variant or a different system variant where the common system variant is inserted,
see $INSERT VARIANT, page 3-525. Collector situations (see remark 10) may not be
connected.
10. If parameter ASSEMBLY is specified, all referred situations must have:
• the same system variant
• the same result variant
as the collector situation. The collector situation itself does not store results, but distributes the results back to the referred situations. It must have a different loading variant
as the referred situations. The definition is currently usable for modal frequency response
analyses only and cannot be used in combination with optimization.
Please refer to Example DRA3V2 of [um550] on page 9-78 ff.
Example:
$SITUATION

NAME=MAXLOAD

! using default variants

! substructure model with constraints in top and subcomponent
$SITUATION NAME=STATIC
COMP_01
CONSTRAINTS=SYMMETRIC
LOADING=CASE_01
SUB_COMP CONSTRAINTS=C_VAR_SYM
$END SITUATION
! modal response analysis, optional component name omitted
$SITUATION NAME=MOD_TRANS PARENT=MODES
LOADING=SYMMETRIC
! assembled situation with 10 dynamic load cases (i.e. situations)
$SITUATION NAME=ASS_FREQ PARENT=MODES
&
ASSEMBLY= LC1 LC2 LC3 LC4 LC5 LC6 LC7 LC8 LC9 LC10
CAR_BODY LOADING=DUMMY
$END

Remarks:

DAT
Structure

1. ALLOCATE data blocks are used to input user-specified data for further access.
2. User-specified data may be allocated to nodes or elements.
3. User-specified data must be unique, i.e. for one name datnam and one node or element
only one tuple of data may be specified.
4. Empty node or element sets are not allowed.
5. User-specified data are stored internally in composed tables with names NY<datnam>.UDAT
for nodes and EY<datnam>.UDAT for elements. To assure uniqueness, datnam must not
have more than five characters.
6. If DSTYPE = SCALAR (default) is specified, a set of ncol scalar values is allocated.
7. If DSTYPE = VECTOR is specified, one or more vectors are allocated, and the number
of columns ncol must be a multiple of three.
8. If the input for one data object is splitted into more than one $ALLOCATE data block, then
the column titles, if any, must be specified in the first one.
9. Each data line may have up to ncol data. Trailing zeroes may be omitted.
10. The floating point data are stored internally in actual precision in any case.
Example:
$ALLOCATE

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-29

$BASVAR

3 Data Input (DAT)

2. A basic variable is a scalar value which is assumed to be non-deterministic. They are
used to describe uncertain properties of a model.
3. Each basic variable is associated with a uniquely defined name. If the name is not defined
by input, it is generated internally.
4. The type of a basic variable defines the type of uncertain entities the basic variable may
be applied on. In pure reliability analysis, the following types are available:

DAT
Structure

• Design parameter: The basic variable is used as design variable influencing properties of the FE-model. The corresponding design variable defined by $DELEMENT
(see page 3-58 ff.) or $DSVNODE (see page 3-90 ff.) must have the same identifier (bsvid = dsvid). Mean values of basic variables are used as initial values of the
design variables, input of initial values of design variables by $DSVVAL (see page
3-401 ff.) is not possible. Furthermore, design variables representing basic variables
must not be made dependent by linking, see $DSVLINK (see page 3-87 ff.).
• Load factor: The basic variable is used as multiplier for a load pattern to define
a stochastic load. The link between basic variable and load pattern is defined by
$COMBINE LOADS (see page 3-562 ff.) in the corresponding loading variant.
• Parameter of another basic variable: Each parameter of a probability distribution
function may be a non-deterministic value itself, described by a basic variable. A
basic variable used as parameter of another basic variable must be included in
the definition of the probability distribution function of the other basic variable, see
$PDFUNCTION (see page 3-208 ff.), replacing function parameters. A basic variable
depending on parameters replaced by basic variables may not be used as parameter
of another basic variable itself.
• State function parameter: The basic variable is used as direct parameter of the limit
state function. It must be included in the z-vector, see $ZVECTOR (see page 3-1110
ff.).
In combined optimization and reliability analysis, the following type is available in addition:
• Stochastic properties of a deterministic design variable: A basic variable is established as stochastic design parameter where its mean value is given by a corresponding (deterministic) design variable with the same identifier (bsvid = dsvid). The
initial value of the design variable is given by the mean value in the corresponding
probability distribution function and must not be specified by $DSVVAL (see page
3-401 ff.).
The probability distribution function itself (see $PDFUNCTION (see page 3-208 ff.))
must be specified by statistical values (DATA = MOMENTS).
5. The probability distribution function associated with a basic variable must be defined by
$PDFUNCTION (see page 3-208 ff.).
Example:

Remarks:

DAT
Structure

1. Contact regions may be locked according to the contact results of a referenced situation.
The locking is done by an implicit generation of multipoint constraints on all contact nodes
that match a corresponding locking condition:
• For Node-To-Node or Surface-To-Node contacts the DOFs of the 2nd contact partner
will be defined as dependents of the DOFs from the 1st contact partner.
• For Node-To-Ground or Surface-To-Ground contacts the DOFs of the 1st contact
partner will be defined as suppressed or dependent according to their local ROTB
system.
• Surface-To-Surface coupling works perfectly well for contact analysis, but may cause
cyclic MPC dependencies if both sides request mutual locks to opposing patches.
Therefore Surface-To-Surface contacts are not recommended to be used together
with contact locking, i.e. those contacts should be downgraded to a unique SurfaceTo-Node contact definition.
2. The contact locking request is part of the component definition, and is valid for all situations of this component.
3. Contact labels cadef refer to $CONTACT definitions in the constraint variant of the referenced situation refsit in referenced component refcomp. Pretension label ptdef refer to
$PRETENSION definitions with GUIDING=CONTACT in the structure block of the referenced component refcomp.
4. Contact locking requests must be unique, e.g. for contact label cadef only one specification (only one data line) is possible. Moreover pretension labels must be unique with
respect to contact label. In case a pretension label matches a contact label the pretension
definition must be distinguished with a PRETEN_ prefix, e.g. PRETEN_MIX for pretension definition MIX (the PRETEN_ prefix can be used in any case, so it is good practice
to use it even if both name spaces are separate).
5. With the CASFILE option a consolidated contact situation together with a matching contact status file is sufficient as reference, i.e. at least a TASK STORE of e.g. STATIC [TO
PRECHECK] is needed in the reference situation, but there is no need for an actual static
analysis as the referred ’results’ are read from the given contact status file. The contact
names/ids and nodal point IDs in the file must match the contact names/ids and nodes in
the reference situation, i.e. the file must match the reference contact topology exactly (a
variant’s template is not sufficient). However, the cas-file may contain pure normal contact

3-34

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

3.2 Model Data

$CONTLOCK

status values for frictional contacts in the reference situation or vice versa.
This is not supported in combination with limit conditions MAXGAP and MAXSLIP (see
remark 13). Also in combination with FRICTION=MATRICES the user must ensure that
the corresponding caso-file was written from a reference situation with $VELOSTATE and
that no anisotropic friction is involved.
6. If contact locking is requested and no specific contact or pretension labels are specified
at all, i.e. there is only one data block $CONTLOCK, and this data block contains only
the first data line, then all contacts and pretensions (with GUIDING=CONTACT) of the
referenced situation are taken into account. The same is true if there is a second data
line but without contact label, only with parameter NORMAL and/or FRICTION.
7. If any contact is specified, then only the specified contacts are taken into account.

• If NORMAL = FREE is specified, then the displacements in the normal direction
are always uncoupled.
• If NORMAL = LOCK_IF_ACTIVE (default) is specified, then the displacements in
the normal direction are coupled if the contact is active.
• For NORMAL = LOCK is specified, then the displacements in the normal direction
are always coupled (independent of contact status).
9. Any NORMAL condition (apart from NORMAL=FREE) may be extended by an additional
limit condition with a threshold value that must be matched before a corresponding LOCK
is actually established, see remark 13 below.
10. In the tangential plane, coupling is possible only if the current dof type establishes at least
3 DOFs per node (i.e. DOFTYPE=DISP) and if friction was taken into account by the
referred $CONTACT definition. Then the coupling is controlled by parameter FRICTION:
• If FRICTION = FREE (default) is specified, then the displacements in the tangential plane are always uncoupled.
• If FRICTION = LOCK_IF_ACTIVE is specified, then the displacements in the tangential plane are coupled if the contact is active (see ROTB restrictions below).
• If FRICTION = LOCK_IF_STICK is specified, then the displacements in the tangential plane are coupled only if the contact is in stick (see ROTB restrictions below).
• If FRICTION = LOCK is specified, then the displacements in the tangential plane
are coupled in any case (independent of contact status, see restrictions below).
• For FRICTION = MATRICES the displacements in the tangential plane are uncoupled (like FRICTION=FREE), but will lead to additional damping matrices needed for
some special dynamic analysis (e.g. brake-squeal analysis).
11. FRICTION = MATRICES is only allowed for DOFTYPE=DISP and in combination with
NORMAL = LOCK_IF_ACTIVE (default).
12. Any FRICTION condition (apart from FRICTION=FREE) may be extended by an additional limit condition with a threshold value that must be matched before a corresponding
LOCK is actually established, see remark 13 below.

Also note that the frictional conditions (MINSHEAR, MINFRICF, MAXSLIP) may be used
only if friction was taken into account and that limit values < 0.0 (for MINPRESS, MINFORCE, MAXGAP) are meaningfull only if the referred contact enforces active normal
state by a corresponding LOCK, FIXED or FORCE parameter (see $CONTACT LOAD for
details). Moreover, MAXGAP condition is usually only meaningfull together with NORMAL/FRICTION=LOCK.
14. If a colon separated list of nodes is appended to the lock condition line then the given
condition applies only to those contact nodes that are part of the extra list (instead of just
all nodes of the corresponding contact definition). Node set names refer to the current
component (nodal point identifiers as well as local ROTB systems of those nodes must
match in current and reference component).

PreTen_BOLT NORMAL=LOCK
$CONTLOCK

1. $COOR is a name alias to $NODE[COOR] which may replace $COOR in future PERMAS

4. Inaccurate nodal point coordinates may be trimmed by TRIMCOOR.
5. Trailing zeros in list of coordinates may be omitted.

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-59

DAT
Structure

3.2 Model Data

$DELEMENT

3 Data Input (DAT)

3. The specification of design variables belonging to a design element in list(dsvid . . .) on
the data line depends on the kind of optimization:

DAT
Structure

• Design variables used for sizing must always be specified. They are valid for the
whole design element, and describe property modifications for the corresponding
elements, see $DVGPAR and $DVMPAR. If the specification of design variables is
done by a set dsvset, the set must exist (must not be empty).
• Design variables used for shape optimization are not specified within the design
element. Instead they are connected to the design nodes, see $DSVNODE and
describe node coordinate modifications, see $DVCOOR.
• Design variables used for topology optimization must be specified by list(dsvid . . .)
or set dsvset. If ASSIGN = ELEMENT is specified, they are assigned to elements
one by one. For ASSIGN = DIRECT the (one and only one) design variable is valid
for the whole design element, and is assigned to all corresponding elements. The
design variables describe element filling ratios, see $DVTPAR. If design variable set
dsvset is empty (not otherwise defined), then it is established internally, see remark
9.
4. For pure sizing or topology optimization, the list of design nodes list(dnid) may be omitted.
For shape optimization, it must be specified in any case.
5. Design variables used for shape optimization are assigned to each related design element.
6. Design variable identifiers must be unique within the configuration.
7. Any element may be assigned to only one design element.
8. For sizing problems, the design element and all elements assigned to it must have the
same type of Geometrical Data Record.
9. Design variables may be specified by a set dsvset. For sizing the set must exist. For
topology optimization with ASSIGN = ELEMENT the set may be empty (not otherwise
defined), and the corresponding design variables are generated internally, one design
variable for each element.
10. If ASSIGN = ELEMENT is specified (available for topology optimization only), the design
variables are assigned to the connected elements one by one, i.e. the number of design
variables equals the number of connected elements. The sequence of elements is according to ascending element identifiers, the corresponding sequence of assigned design
variables is the sequence of appearance in list(dsvid) or the sequence within set dsvset.
A unambiguous assignment may be achieved by an ordered design variable set.
11. If ELEMENTS = AUTO is specified, then the geometry of the design element defines the
finite elements to be assigned, i.e. all finite elements in the neighborhood of the design
element with types corresponding to the type of the design element are assigned to that
design element automatically. The list of element identifiers on input line must be omitted.
The element types corresponding to the type of a design element are listed for each
design element type in the design element atlas, see page 5-1 ff.. The design element
search volume for automatic element assignement can be verified by EXPORT ITEM
TOPO DESEARCHVOL.

3-60

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

3.2 Model Data

$DELEMENT

12. The maximum allowable distance of the center of gravity of finite elements to be assigned automatically to a design element. Parameter MAXDIST must be input for oneand twodimensional design elements if ELEMENTS = AUTO is specified. Meaningful values depend on the geometry of the model and on the selected unit of length.
13. Parameter OUTTOL is used to control the assignment of finite elements near to the
boundary of design elements. If ELEMENTS = AUTO is specified, a finite element near
to the boundary is assigned, if the distance of the center of gravity from the boundary is
less than OUTTOL ∗LE where LE is a typical length of the design element. If not input,
the default value defined by global system key OUTTOL is used.

Example:
Please refer to examples OP1, OP3, OP10 and OP12.
$DELEMENT TYPE = DBEAM
101 2 3 : 2001 2002

2003

L_EDGE

! to beam elements in list

! assign design variables 78 to 80
! to shell elements in SET_145

$DELEMENT TYPE = DHEXE8
605 TOPO1 : SET_99

! topology optimization; create design
! variable set TOPO1 from ESET SET_99

Design Element Definition
Definition of design elements of type DBEAD for optimal bead pattern design.
$DELEMENT

TYPE = DBEAD

Explanation
Design element identifier.
Element identifier.
Element set name.
Identifier of design nodes.
Node set name.

Remarks:
1. Design elements may be defined only in single or top components. Their identifiers must
be unique within the component.
2. If a design element of type DBEAD is defined, the general purpose design element types
described on page 3-58 ff. may only be used to define sizing design variables.
3. The finite elements assigned to the design element define the (arbitrarily shaped) area
for bead pattern design. Only 2D-elements may be assigned to design elements of type
DBEAD. Nodes that are solely connected to assigned finite elements are inside the
design element, those that are solely connected to unassigned finite elements are outside
the design element and those that are connected to assigned as well as to unassigned
finite elements are the boundary of the design element.
4. If nodes inside the design element coincide with nodes of a substructure, they get boundary of the design element, too.
5. Nodes outside or on the boundary of the design element must not be specified as design
nodes.

3-62

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

3.2 Model Data

$DELEMENT DBEAD

6. Design nodes are connected to design variables by $DSVNODE (see page 3-90 ff.) data
blocks and their coordinate modifications are defined by $DVCOOR (see page 3-403 ff.)
definitions. This way design variables are implicitly connected to the design element.
7. The implicit connection of a design variable to a design element of type DBEAD must be
unique, i.e. a design variable must not be connected to any other design element (see
also $DSVNODE, remark 4).

9. For any other node inside the design element which is not specified as design node a
internal bead design variable is generated according to the closest located design node
assigned to a design variable. This reference design node / design variable definition is
also used to generate the corresponding
• design node coordinate modification data $DVCOOR (i.e. bead draw vector),
• design variable initial value $DSVVAL (usually zero),
• design variable limit $DSVLIMIT (i.e. bead height),
• design variable modification limit $DSVMLIM.
If more than one reference design node / design variable definition is specified by the user,
it is in his responsibility to define appropriate data listed above for each of them (usually
the same for all).
10. With addidtional $DERESTRAINT (see page 3-77 ff.) and $DESYMM (see page 3-84 ff.)
specifications the generation of bead design variables and therefore the resulting bead
patterns may be forced to fulfill symmetries, certain pattern orientations or boundary conditions. With a $DSVFILT (see page 3-987 ff.) TYPE = BEAD definition bead properties
like minimum bead width and maximum bead ratio may be controlled.
11. Finite elements may be assigned to a design element of type DSHAPE even if it is also
assigned to other design elements of same or other type (except DFREE), in particular
sizing and shape design variables may affect the same finite elements simultaneously.
12. If a node is located inside more than one design element of type DBEAD, DSHAPE
(see page 3-68) or DNODE (see page 3-66) it is subject to the superimposed coordinate
modifications evoked by each of these design elements (or rather of the design variables
connected to them).
Example:
! assign design node 592 to ESET geo1_mat1
$DELEMENT TYPE = DBEAD
101 : geo1_mat1 : 592

For a typical application of design element type DBEAD see OP5V1 of [um550].

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-63

DAT
Structure

8. The coordinate modifications of higher order finite element midnodes inside the design
element that are not specified as design nodes are linearly interpolated with respect to
the corresponding corner nodes.

unique, i.e. a design variable must not be connected to any other design element (see
also $DSVNODE, remark 4).
10. The coordinate modifications of higher order finite element midnodes inside the design
element that are not specified as design nodes are linearly interpolated with respect to
the corresponding corner nodes.
11. The finite elements assigned to the design element define the area for mesh relaxation
after modification of design node coordinates.
12. Finite elements may be assigned to a design element of type DFREE even if it is also
assigned to other design elements of same or other type (but not DSHAPE, DBEAD and
DNODE, see above), in particular sizing and shape design variables may affect the same
finite elements simultaneously.
Example:
Please refer to example OP19 of [um550].
$DELEMENT TYPE = DFREE
1 : DELEM_1
& : SHAPE

Design element identifier.

Element set name.
Identifier of design nodes.
Node set name.

Remarks:
1. Design elements may be defined only in single or top components. Their identifiers must
be unique within the component.
2. If a design element of type DSHAPE is defined the general purpose design element types
described on 3-58 ff. may only be used to define sizing design variables.
3. The finite elements assigned to the design element define the (arbitrarily shaped) area
for shape deformation. Nodes that are solely connected to assigned finite elements are
inside the design element, those that are solely connected to unassigned finite elements
are outside the design element and those that are connected to assigned as well as to
unassigned finite elements are the boundary of the design element.
4. If nodes inside the design element coincide with nodes of a substructure, they get boundary of the design element, too.
5. Nodes outside or on the boundary of the design element must not be specified as design
nodes.

3-68

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

3.2 Model Data

$DELEMENT DSHAPE

6. Design nodes are usually connected to design variables by $DSVNODE (see page 3-90
ff.) data blocks and their coordinate modifications are defined by $DVCOOR (see page
3-403 ff.) definitions. This way design variables are implicitly connected to the design
element. Notice: Design nodes without connection to a design variable will have no
coordinate modification!
7. The implicit connection of a design variable to a design element of type DSHAPE must
be unique, i.e. a design variable must not be connected to any other design element (see
also $DSVNODE, remark 4).

9. Any other node inside the design element which is not specified as design node is subject
to a coordinate modification that is smoothly interpolated between those of the design
nodes and the zero values at the boundary of the design element. The interpolant has
the fundamental properties of:
• C2-continuity inside the design element
• C0-continuity at the boundary of the design element
• minimizing the mean squared curvature of the complete shape deformation
• being of global nature, i.e. every design node coordinate modification affects every
interpolated coordinate modification
10. With addidtional $DERESTRAINT (see page 3-77 ff.) and $DESYMM (see page 3-84
ff.) specifications the fundamental properties listed above may be modified by symmetries, constant or linear interpolation restraints and additional or higher order boundary
conditions.
11. Finite elements may be assigned to a design element of type DSHAPE even if it is also
assigned to other design elements of same or other type (except DFREE), in particular
sizing and shape design variables may affect the same finite elements simultanously.
12. If a node is located inside more than one design element of type DSHAPE, DBEAD (see
3-62) or DNODE (see 3-66) it is subject to the superimposed coordinate modifications
evoked by each of these design elements (or rather of the design variables connected to
them).
Example:
Please refer to examples OP11, OP15, OP16 and OP17 of [um550].

2. The reference system used for restraint directions in TYPE = CONST and TYPE = LINEAR
may be also be a cyclic or spherical system. Nevertheless, in any case the axes of the
corresponding cartesian system at the origin are used to define the restraint direction.
3. Up to three restraints of TYPE = CONST or TYPE = LINEAR may be defined. They must
share the same reference system with different axes for each restraint. They may also be
combined with a $DESYMM specification as long as this combination keeps unambigous
and consistent.

i.e. the sub-range of its hull which is connected to finite elements outside the design
element. Further ranges of the hull or higher continuity conditions may be applied with a
restraint definition of TYPE = BOUND.

5. Frozen regions can be defined to enforce accretion of material within topology optimization. The usage of this restraint is restricted to design elements of type DTOPO (see
page 3-71) and applies only for default parameter TOPOVAR = MAPPED or NODAL, see

6. Layer restraints serve to define equality or inequality constraints on functions of topo
design variables in different layers, i.e. by multiple definition of DTOPO design elements
to the same finite element set. Hence all design elements referred by the specified design
element set must be of type DTOPO and must be defined for the same element set (see
page 3-71). The number of items in the design element set must match the number of
arguments of the specified function.

Remarks:

1. Design element symmetry specifications are possible only in single or top components,
and are only available for design element type DSHAPE (see page 3-68), DBEAD (see
page 3-62) and DTOPO (see page 3-71).
2. The reference system used for symmetry specification may be also be a cyclic or spherical
system. Nevertheless, in any case the axes of the corresponding cartesian system at the
origin are used to define symmetry.
3. The axes-definition in the data line have the following meaning depending on symmetry
type:
• PLANAR: axes define symmetry plane through origin.
• AXI: axis defines rotation axis.
• CYCLIC: first axis defines rotational axis, second axis defines starting point for first
sector (counted counterclockwise).
4. SECTSYM = YES within a cyclic symmetry definition additionally enforces planar symmetry with respect to the angle bisectors.
5. Design element symmetry definitions may be combined with each other. All definitions for
one design element must share the same reference system. Up to three planar symmetries with orthogonal symmetry planes may be defined. Cyclic and axial symmetry may
be combined with a planar symmetry, where the symmetry plane must be orthogonal to
the rotation axis.

$DSVSET

Remarks:
1. Design variable set names are unique within one component and must not begin with
DFLT.
2. Design variable sets defined with $DSVSET must be defined within one data block. Extension of existing sets by $DSVSET is not possible.
3. In one set any item may appear only once; any further appearance in the list will be
ignored.
4. If RULE = ALL is specified the set contains all existing design variables. No data line is
allowed.

DAT
Structure

5. If RULE = RANGE is specified the set contains all existing design variables with identifiers
dsvid1 ≤ dsvid ≤ dsvid2 . For multiple selections, no check is performed for overlapping
definitions. Each data item occurs only once in a set.
6. If RULE = BOOLEAN is specified, the defined set is the result of a logical operation on
two other sets. The following operations are available:
AND
OR
XOR
AND NOT

All design variables which are included in set dsvset1 as well as
in set dsvset2 .
All design variables which are included in set dsvset1 or in set
dsvset2 .
All design variables which are included in set dsvset1 or in set
dsvset2 but not in both.
All design variables which are included in set dsvset1 but not in
set dsvset2 .

7. If the sequence of set items is important an ordered set can be obtained by specifying on
header line SEQUENCE = ORDERED. The set items are then ordered in the sequence
of their appearance in the set definition. Nevertheless duplicated items are ignored.
8. Sets used to define an ordered set must be ordered sets itself.
9. Ordered sets are only possible if RULE = ITEM is specified.
10. Set definition by using set names may not be recursive.

Remarks:
1. Global element system definitions which are inputted by $ELSYS within the $STRUCTURE
bracket, are inserted into the geometrical data records of the referenced elements in all
system variants, see $GEODAT.

DAT
Structure

2. The definition of local element systems is possible only if the geometrical data record of
each referenced element contains the field PREF, REFSYS or REFSYSX resp., or for
gasket elements, see remark 3. With the exception of POINT and RSYS, the specification made on header line must match the field in the geometrical data record of each
referenced element. For that, and for the rules to establish the local element system see
element description.
3. For gasket elements, the definition of element systems with option POINTS or RSYS is
optional, and must be done within the $STRUCTURE bracket. We remark that the z’ axis
(3) of the element system must coincide with the through-the-thickness direction.
4. Local element systems which may be defined via REFSYS or REFSYSX resp. can be established by three points (or two points resp.), see pictures below, using the specification
POINTS, or can be derived from a reference system, see remark 6, if RSYS is specified.
5. Beam element systems are established using a reference point PREF. This reference
point may be determined with reference to a system defined by three points, using the
specification POINTS, see picture below, or to a reference system, see remark 6, if RSYS
is specified. In any case, the direction from the center of gravity of the first beam section
to the reference point is given by the direction of the first coordinate axis of the reference
system (local cartesian system for cylindrical or spherical reference system).
6. If RSYS is specified on header line, the given reference system rsys is used to establish the local element system. Reference systems are defined by data blocks $RSYS or
$RSYSAX resp. for axisymmetric structures. RSYS = 0 means component system.
For cylindrical or spherical reference systems the local cartesian system for the orientation of the local element system is generated using the generation rules defined on page
1-11.
If parameter AXES is omitted, the local element system coincides with the local cartesian
system, else idof x specifies the axis of the local cartesian system which is used as x-axis
of the element system, and idof y specifies the axis of the local cartesian system which
is used as y-axis of the element system. Following values may be used:
1
(-1) : Positive (negative) x-axis of reference system (r-axis for axisymmetric structures).
2
(-2) : Positive (negative) y-axis of reference system (z-axis for axisymmetric structures).

1. External degrees of freedom form a separate degree of freedom family. Within the current (sub-)component they cannot be suppressed or prescribed nor used as dependent
degrees of freedom in MPC’s.

Remarks:
1. Reference to a global system is allowed only on basic or single component level.
2. The $GSYS data block defines position and orientation of the component with respect to
an assumed global system, i.e. the component system used for the input of the component coincides with the system defined on data line.
3. The system definition itself refer to the assumed global system, i.e. the coordinates of
points used for system specification refer always to the assumed global reference system,
and determine position and orientation of the input component system with respect to the
assumed global reference system.
4. During the consolidation process, all corresponding data of the component are transformed to a new component system which coincides with the assumed global coordinate
system. After that, e.g. for model output, all component data refer to that new component
system.
5. Only one global system reference is possible within a component.
6. If the relation between global and component system is a pure translation, then it is possible to specify TRKIND = TRANS, and only the origin of the system must be input. For
axisymmetric discretization, only a translation along the zC -axis is possible.
7. If TRKIND = COMPLETE is specified, i.e. the component system may be rotated with
respect to the global system, then the following restrictions exist:
• If a node carries dofs of type DISP or POTE, and the dofs are not in the same degree
of freedom family, a rotated basis must be assigned to the nodal point. Example: dof
1 is dependent, dof 2 and 3 are local.

• All nodes with prescribed degrees of freedom must have rotated bases in any case.
• All nodes of elements referring directly to nodal point degrees of freedom (e.g. elements with GEDA field DOF like X1STIFF3, X1DAMP3 etc.) must have rotated

Remarks:
1. Import of data objects by file may be defined only in the structure bracket of a component.
All data objects on the specified files must belong to the actual component, and are
assigned to the specified situation. If the situation is omitted, the import is performed for

in addition.

DAT
Structure

3. For all sources with the exception of PERMAS itself the corresponding degree of freedom
type of the data objects must be specified. For default see $ENTER COMPONENT line,

coupled degrees of freedom (e.g. PRES and DISP) must be specified.

Remarks:
1. Lines are not supported for discretization type axisymetric
2. Lines may be defined in any component, its identifiers must be unique within the component. Each data block contains the complete definition of one line.
3. A line is a non-interrupted sequence of straight or curved parts, connected at corner
nodes. It starts at the first node, and first and last node may be the same.
4. Lines may be defined as part of the finite element idealization (specification of ELEMENTS) or by a pure geometrical definition (specification of GEO), see remark 9.
5. If ELEMENTS is specified, the line consists of the edges of the corresponding finite elements. For solid, membrane and shell elements, edges must be selected by edge identifier edgid, see element description.
6. For solid elements the element edge itself is used, for shell, membrane or beam elements
the lines defined by the element nodes are used ignoring node offsets, element thickness
etc..
7. If ELEMENTS or GEO is specified, the first node of a line may be defined explicitly by
nid1 which must be a corner node. To get a unique definition, the second corner node
nid2 must be input in addition.
8. If the first node of a line is not explicitly defined, it is determined according to following
rules:
• If ELEMENTS is specified, the edge of the first element is the first part of the line,
and the line starts at the first corner node of the edge.
• If GEO is specified, the line starts at the first node of the first geometry element.
9. If GEO is specified, the line is defined by interpolation of specified nodes. To do that, the
following geometry elements are available:

Linear multipoint constraints establish a linear relation between guiding (ug ) and dependent
(ud ) degrees of freedom:
ud

Multipoint constraint conditions can be defined in PERMAS within two different input brackets.
Definitions in the $STRUCTURE bracket are valid for all situations, whereas definitions in the
$CONSTRAINTS bracket are valid for specific situations only.
Multipoint constraint conditions must be defined for each degree of freedom type separately,
indicated by the DOFTYPE parameter. PERMAS automatically uses the multipoint constraints
corresponding to the degree of freedom type of the current analysis. Other definitions are

1. Label (integer, name or text string) of MPC definitions must be unique within one component.
2. MPC labels may be also given as quoted text – e.g. to enclose mixed case or non-alphanumeric letters (note that ’MyName’ is different from ’MYNAME’, but the latter text is equal
to the unquoted name token MYNAME).
3. The dependent degrees of freedom will be introduced at the dependent nodes if not yet
existent. For example, DPDOFS = 4 will create degree of freedom 4 at a node, even if
(solid) elements connected to this node introduce only degrees of freedom 1, 2 and 3.
4. Dependent degrees of freedom form an own family of physical degrees of freedom, therefore they cannot be declared as suppressed, prescribed or external. Of course a degree
of freedom may appear only once as dependent degree of freedom, but can be used as
guiding degree of freedom in other MPC conditions.
5. MPC conditions may be hierarchical, but not recursive.
6. The verification items MPC DEFinition, MPC GEOmetry and MPC SYStem can be
requested by the user with the UCI-switch DEFAULT SET VERIFICATION.
An export of internally resolved MPC definitions, e.g. one $MPC ISURFACE → multiple
$MPC IQUAD4 definitions, is also available.

Local Coupling System
Constraint conditions are enforced at dependent degrees of freedom with respect to a local
coupling coordinate system. In general, the coupling system coincides with the (possibly) rotated basis, defined by $ROTB, at each dependent node. An explicit system specification is
available for some MPC types by the parameter DPSYS, e.g. $MPC ISURFACE.

Neighborhood Detection
Several MPC types use neighborhood search algorithms to identify corresponding guidingdependent partners. Of special interest is the $MPC ISURFACE definition, where different
search algorithms are available, depending on the parameter DPSYS.
• If DPSYS = NORMAL is specified, then the same surface based neighborhood search
as for contact definitions is used.
• If DPSYS 6= NORMAL is specified, then a patch based neighborhood search by an
OCTREE-method is used.
The neighborhood detection is controlled by the headerline parameters DISTOL and OUTTOL.
The default search tolerances can be modified by the UCI commands SET MPCDISTOL and
MPCOUTTOL. Figure F3-2 shows the meaning of the tolerance settings.

3.2 Model Data

$MPC ILINE

The degree of freedom identifier rdof may not be part of the activated degrees of freedom
at the dependent node to prevent undesired movement constraints. Typically rdof = 9 offers a secure separation. The movement actuation urdof must be given by a $PRESCRIBE
/ $PREVAL definition for rdof of the dependent node.
7. Application areas of MPC ILINE are butt joints of shell elements or coupling of line elements.

9. If a dependent node is not located on the guiding line, for translational degrees of freedom the eccentricity of the node is taken into account by establishing a rigid lever arm
connecting dependent node and projected point in order to preserve overall balance of
external loads and reactions. The rigid lever arm correction requires a dependent DOF
mask of 1,2,3,4,5,6, otherwise it will be omitted.
10. To control neighborhood relation determination between points and element lines, two parameters are available: DISTOL and OUTTOL. A point may be aligned to an element line
if its distance from the line is less than DISTOL ∗LE and its distance from the boundary of
the element is less than OUTTOL ∗LE where LE is a typical element length. If not input,
the default values defined by global system keys DISTOL and OUTTOL are used. See
also general description on page 3-129.
11. A table with statistical information on the neighborhood calculation of MPC ILINE connections is printed in the result file.
12. Rotated node bases are taken into account automatically. The interpolation is always
true for the displacement components transformed into the (possibly rotated) bases at
the nodes with dependent degree(s) of freedom.

Please refer to Example LS10 of [um550] on page 2-117 ff.

degrees of freedom at nodes. Rotated node bases are taken into account automatically.
3. With DPSYS = rsys an explicit permanent local coupling coordinate system may be defined (rsys=0 for component system), i.e. its coupling directions are not influenced by any
change of nodal point positions.

5. If DPSYS = MATRIX is specified, then the coupling system is specified explicitly by its
base matrix.
6. If RELDOF is specified, then the additional degree of freedom identifier rdof is introduced
for each dependent node controlling the relative movement between dependent and guiding nodes in principal direction. This is realized by an additional part urel of an extended
constraint equation based on the first unit vector e1 of the local coupling system:
ud = Ag ug + urel ,

urel := urdof · e1 .

The degree of freedom identifier rdof may not be part of the activated degrees of freedom
at the dependent node to prevent undesired movement constraints. Typically rdof = 9 offers a secure separation. The movement actuation urdof must be given by a $PRESCRIBE
/ $PREVAL definition for rdof of the dependent node.
7. Application areas of MPC ILIN2 and ILIN3 are butt joints of shell elements or coupling of
line elements.
8. The coordinates of the guiding nodes define an isoparametrically curved line as interpolation element. The interpolation uses the normal projection of the dependent nodes onto
the interpolation element.
9. If a dependent node is not located on the guiding line, for translational degrees of freedom the eccentricity of the node is taken into account by establishing a rigid lever arm
connecting dependent node and projected point in order to preserve overall balance of
external loads and reactions. The rigid lever arm correction requires a dependent dof
mask of 1,2,3,4,5,6, otherwise it will be omitted.
10. Rotated node bases are taken into account automatically. The interpolation is always
true for the displacement components transformed into the (possibly rotated) bases at
the nodes with dependent degree(s) of freedom.

7. For all nodes with dependent degrees of freedom, interpolation relations are determined
from guiding surface or surface set. The interpolation uses the normal projection of the
dependent nodes onto the interpolation (guiding) surface. If dependent nodes are not
located on the interpolation surface, for translational degrees of freedom node eccentricity
is taken into account by establishing a rigid lever arm connecting dependent node and
projected point in order to preserve overall balance of external loads and reactions.
8. If, for mechanical problems, the number of dependent dofs is chosen higher than the
number of dofs at the guiding nodes, the kinematic motion of the guiding nodes (volume
element(s)) is coupled with the dependent nodes (usually 6 degrees of freedom of the
shell element node) in the following way:
• The translational degrees of freedom are interpolated due to the shape function of
the guiding region.
• The rotational degrees of freedom of the dependent (shell) element nodes are interpolated by the translations of the guiding region.
See also page 3-160.
9. To control neighborhood relation determination between points and element surfaces, two
parameters are available: DISTOL and OUTTOL. A point may be aligned to an element
surface if its distance from the surface is less than DISTOL and its distance from the
boundary of the element is less than OUTTOL. If not input, the default values defined by
global system keys MPCDISTOL and MPCOUTTOL are used. See also figure F3-2
10. A table with statistical information on the neighborhood calculation of MPC ISURFACE
connections is printed in the result file.
11. For each node with dependent degrees of freedom a local coupling coordinate system
xC is used to establish interpolation relations from guiding surface or surface set.
If dependent nodes are not located on the interpolation surface, for translational degrees
of freedom node eccentricity is taken into account by establishing a rigid lever arm connecting dependent node and interpolation point in order to preserve overall balance of
external loads and reactions.

12. If DPSYS = NORMAL is specified, the calculation of the coupling coordinate system uses
the same generation rules and methods as in $CONTACT SURFACE with CONTSYS =
NORMAL allowing combined/mixed definitions.
The origin of the local coupling coordinate system is located at the position of the dependent node. The local surface normal direction at the position of the projection of this node
on the guiding surface geometry is used as first system axis xC . For the second and third
system axes fixing the tangential plane of the coupling, see remark 13.

Figure F3-3: Coupling coordinate system

The coupling normal axis xC is derived from the surface normal nS at each dependent
node’s nadir point N automatically (N is determined by the normal projection of the node
onto the guiding surface geometry). ‡ By the variable plane > 0 a reference plane
is selected from two of the three coordinate axes of the reference system rsys. For a
cylindrical or spherical reference system the reference plane is built by a local cartesian
system at the surface point according to the rules given on page 1-11. Parallel to this
reference plane an intersection plane is established cutting the surface at the point in
question, thus leading to a tangent line. The tangential vector ts is given by the vector
product nR × nS . The yC axis of the local coupling coordinate system is then calculated
by a rotation of ts about nS by angle γ. The third axis zC then completes this right-hand
system.

‡

See the $SURFACE input on on page 3-258pp for how the surface normal nS is defined.

2. If DPSYS = ROTB is specified, the coupling is done for the (possibly rotated) dependent
degrees of freedom at nodes. Rotated node bases are taken into account automatically.

$MPC ITRIAx

4. Together with DPSYS = rsys the AXES parameter may be used to specify two orthogonal directions defining xC - and yC -axes of the coupling coordinate system.

5. If DPSYS = MATRIX is specified, then the coupling system is specified explicitly by its
base matrix.
6. If RELDOF is specified, then the additional degree of freedom identifier rdof is introduced
for each dependent node controlling the relative movement between dependent and guiding nodes in principal direction. This is realized by an additional part urel of an extended
constraint equation based on the first unit vector e1 of the local coupling system:
ud = Ag ug + urel ,

urel := urdof · e1 .

The degree of freedom identifier rdof may not be part of the activated degrees of freedom
at the dependent node to prevent undesired movement constraints. Typically rdof = 9 offers a secure separation. The movement actuation urdof must be given by a $PRESCRIBE
/ $PREVAL definition for rdof of the dependent node.
7. The coordinates of the guiding nodes define an isoparametrically curved quadrilateral
surface as interpolation element. The interpolation uses the normal projection of the
dependent nodes onto the interpolation surface. If dependent nodes are not located on
the interpolation surface, for translational degrees of freedom node eccentricity is taken
into account by establishing a rigid lever arm connecting dependent node and projected
point in order to preserve overall balance of external loads and reactions.
8. If, for mechanical problems, the number of dependent dofs is chosen higher than the
number of dofs at the guiding nodes, the kinematic motion of the guiding nodes (volume
element(s)) is coupled with the dependent nodes (usually 6 degrees of freedom of the
shell element node) in the following way:
• The translational degrees of freedom are interpolated due to the shape function of
the guiding region.
• The rotational degrees of freedom of the dependent (shell) element nodes are interpolated by the translations of the guiding region.
See also page 3-167.

Remarks:
1. Please refer to the global MPC remarks which are valid for all MPC types.
2. The constraint conditions are always established between pairs of corresponding nodes.
3. If node sets are ordered, then node pairs are formed according to the sequence of nodes
in the sets. If node sets are not ordered, then node pairs are formed by assigning to each
node of the first set that node from the second set with the smallest distance. In any case,
both sets must contain the same number of nodes.
4. For MPC JOIN defined by node sets containing more than one node, the coupled node
pairs are listed in the result file.

Remarks:

$MPC NODE

3 Data Input (DAT)

The degree of freedom identifier rdof may not be part of the activated degrees of freedom
at the dependent node to prevent undesired movement constraints. Typically rdof = 9 offers a secure separation. The movement actuation urdof must be given by a $PRESCRIBE
/ $PREVAL definition for rdof of the dependent node.
7. Each guiding node has always up to three potential degrees of freedom and the dependent degrees of freedom are constrained to the translational movement (or temperatures
etc.) of the guiding node.
Degrees of freedom at the guiding node which are not coupled to the structure have to be
suppressed or prescribed.

DAT
Structure

8. If DPITYP = NODE is specified, then the constraint conditions are established between
pairs of corresponding nodes. If the node sets are ordered, then node pairs are formed
according to the sequence of nodes in the sets. If node sets are not ordered, then node
pairs are formed by assigning to each node of the first set that node from the second
set with the smallest distance. In any case, both sets must contain the same number of
nodes.
9. If DPITYP = GROUND is specified, then homogeneous constraint conditions are established at the (dependent) nodes, i.e. declaring a prescribed/suppressed behavior which
requires at least one unconstrained degree of freedom. Thus the definition of DPDOFS =
1,2,3 is not supported.
10. If DPITYP = NODESAME is specified, then gid / gidset must consist of exactly one
guiding node.

Remarks:
1. Please refer to the global MPC remarks which are valid for all MPC types.
2. Rigid body movements are restricted to displacement degrees of freedom.
3. The total number of guiding degrees of freedom must equal six. They must be capable to
describe any kinematic motion of the defined rigid region.
4. If gdof is omitted, all six degrees of freedom of the corresponding node gid are assumed
to be guiding degrees of freedom, defining the rigid body movement entirely.
5. Degrees of freedom at the guiding nodes which are not coupled to the structure have to
be suppressed or prescribed.

Structure

freedom.

1. Please refer to the global MPC remarks which are valid for all MPC types.
2. If RELDOF is specified, then the additional degree of freedom identifier rdof is introduced
for each dependent node controlling the relative movement between dependent and guiding nodes in principal direction. This is realized by an additional part urel of an extended
constraint equation based on the initial position vectors xi :
ud = Ag ug + urel ,

urel := urdof ·

xd − xg
.
|xd − xg |

The degree of freedom identifier rdof may not be part of the activated degrees of freedom
at the dependent node to prevent undesired movement constraints. Typically rdof = 9 offers a secure separation. The movement actuation urdof must be given by a $PRESCRIBE
/ $PREVAL definition for rdof of the dependent node.
3. MPC RIGID is restricted to displacement or temperature degrees of freedom.
4. The node set for the guiding node must consist of only a single node.
5. If displacement degrees of freedom are constrained:
• The guiding node has always six potential degrees of freedom, describing the possible kinematic motion of a rigid region. Degrees of freedom at the guiding node which
are not coupled to the structure have to be suppressed or prescribed.
• Rotated node bases are taken into account automatically, i.e. the rigid body movement is transformed to the (possibly rotated) bases at the nodes with dependent
degree(s) of freedom.
6. If temperature degrees of freedom are constrained:
• The guiding node has always two potential degrees of freedom. Degrees of freedom
at the guiding node which are not coupled to the structure (e.g. ∆T at solids) have
to be suppressed or prescribed.
• The constraints for T and ∆T are separated; there is no coupling between them.

Remarks:
1. Please refer to the global MPC remarks which are valid for all MPC types.
2. Weighted averaged connections are restricted to displacement degrees of freedom.
3. Weld connections are generated in the following way:

found. NCPNT connection points of a circle with radius cradius around the projection point are coupled using a WLSCON connection, see $MPC WLSCON. The
corresponding finite elements in the domain are a part of the weld connection (see
also figure F3-5).
• Nodes where the surface normal differs from the normal at the projection point by
more than angmax specified by parameter MAXANGLE are not taken into account.
• If the distance between the node and its projection point exceeds the absolute distance dstmax specified by MAXDIST, no MPC will be generated.
• If the radius cradius is equal zero, a point to point connection is established.

$MPC WLSCON

Weighted Averaged Connection
The displacements associated with the dependent degrees of freedom ddof at node did are
constrained to a rigid body movement defined by the averaged, weighted displacements of the
guiding degrees of freedom gdof at nodes gid or gidset, respectively.
If the constraint is defined for temperature degrees of freedom, then the dependent temperature
is defined by the averaged, weighted temperature at the guiding nodes.

$MPC WLSCON

did

Identifier of node with dependent degree(s) of freedom.
Name of set of node with dependent degrees of freedom (see remark 3
on page 3-188).

Remarks:
1. Please refer to the global MPC remarks which are valid for all MPC types.
2. Weighted averaged connections are restricted to displacement or temperature degrees
of freedom.
3. The node set for the dependent node must consist of only a single node.

DAT
Structure

4. If displacement degrees of freedom are constrained:
• The sum of all guiding degrees of freedom must be capable to describe an arbitrary
kinematic motion of a rigid body, i.e. at the dependent point all six degrees of freedom must be provisionally supported by the WLSCON – even if not all of them are
taken as dependent DOFs !
• The displacements at the guiding degrees of freedom are weighted by factor w and
all guiding contributions are averaged by least square method to define the motion
of a rigid body. The dependent degrees of freedom are constrained to that rigid body
motion.
• If gdof is omitted, all translational or all translational and rotational degrees of freedom of the corresponding node gid are assumed to be guiding degrees of freedom.
See also switch MPCWLSGDOF, SET/SHOW see page 2-41
• Degrees of freedom at the guiding nodes which are not coupled to the structure have
to be suppressed or prescribed.
• It is not recommended to use rotational degrees of freedom as guiding degrees of
freedom except if necessary regarding paragraph one (e.g. if the guiding nodes are
collinear).
• Rotated node bases are taken into account automatically, i.e. the displacements of
the guiding nodes with (possibly rotated) local bases are transformed to the component system before calculating the rigid body movement.
5. If temperature degrees of freedom are constrained:
• If gdof is omitted, always two degrees of freedom of the corresponding node gid are
assumed to be guiding degrees of freedom.
• Degrees of freedom at the guiding nodes which are not coupled to the structure (e.g.
∆T at solids) have to be suppressed or prescribed.
• The constraints for T and ∆T are separated; there is no coupling between them.
6. If w is omitted, w = 1.0 is assumed.
7. See also default switch WLSSCALE, DEFAULT see page 2-81

1. Node set names are unique within one component and must not begin with DFLT.
2. Node sets defined with $NSET must be defined within one data block. Extension of
existing sets by $NSET is not possible.
3. Node sets defined with $NSET may not be extended by implicit set generation of $COOR
data blocks.
4. In one set any item may appear only once; any further appearance in the list will be
ignored.
5. If RULE = ALL is specified the set contains all existing nodes. No data line is allowed.
6. If RULE = RANGE is specified the set contains all existing nodes with identifiers
nid1 ≤ nid ≤ nid2 . For multiple selections, no check is performed for overlapping definitions. Each data item occurs only once in a set.
7. If RULE = BOOLEAN is specified, the defined set is the result of a logical operation on
two other sets. The following operations are available:
AND
OR
XOR
AND NOT

All nodes which are included in set nset1 as well as in set nset2 .
All nodes which are included in set nset1 or in set nset2 .
All nodes which are included in set nset1 or in set nset2 but not in both.
All nodes which are included in set nset1 but not in set nset2 .

8. If the sequence of set items is important an ordered set can be obtained by specifying on
header line SEQUENCE = ORDERED. The set items are then ordered in the sequence
of their appearance in the set definition. Nevertheless duplicated items are ignored.
9. Sets used to define an ordered set must be ordered sets itself.
10. Ordered sets are only possible if RULE = ITEM is specified.
11. Set definition by using set names may not be recursive.
12. Default set names NODEDISP, NODETEMP, NODEPRES and NODEPOTE (see remark
10 of $COOR description) may not be used as names for other node sets. Furthermore
they cannot be used for the definition of new node sets.

2. One node transformation is entirely defined within one data block, which must contain all

Remarks:

a situation is being created to compute free eigenmodes for this component. This is done
if the definition of external modes does not refer to an explicitly defined situation (see

also Data Object Labels).
Modes which would yield a singular stiffness are removed to avoid additional rigid body
modes.
DYNCOND = MBCBDIAG is well suited for matrix export, as it yields smaller matrices.
The final results are the same as for DYNCOND = MBCB. See example DEVX8V2.

for the current component.

’name’

: Standard color name, e.g. name = red, green, blue, orange, gold, yellow,
cyan, magenta, brown, etc.

’#RRGGBB’ : Standard 8-bit RGB color definition, specified by 3∗2 hexadecimal digits for
red, green and blue intensity in 256 steps each (00-FF).

’##AdRdGdBdxxRaGaBaSsRsGsBsyyReGeBe’: αRGB-ambient-specular-emissive definition,
i.e. a double hash ## followed by 4 sequences of 4∗2 hexadecimal digits.
The 1st sequence contains the standard 8-bit αRGB color definition (see
above). The following 3 sequences contain the RGB definition for the ambient
(RaGaBa), specular (RsGsBs) and emissive (ReGeBe) portions (with specular
shininess in Ss and the extra digits xx=00 and yy=04 for internal use).
