Remarks:
1. At least one fatigue load definition is required for a fatigue / durability analysis.
2. One fatigue analysis refers to one specified fatigue load definition. An arbitrary number
of fatigue loads may be defined, but only one may be defined without an explicit FLDEF
label, i.e. the FLDEF labels for various fatigue load definitions must be disjoint.
If no explicit FLDEF is given, the default name FLDEF = DFLT_FLDEF is used.
3. Defining fatigue load collections is only possible within the result variant of a single or top
component. It is applicable for all analyses with primary load pattern results, i.e. UCI
commands STATIC or INERTIA (without a nonlinear load history from $NLLOAD).
4. Each data line defines one load contribution of the load collective. A load contribution is
the combination of a min / max scaled load pattern lpat with a number of repetition cycles
ncyc.
5. Scaling factors sl and su define the lower / upper load scaling per cycle. For, e.g. fully
reversed load cycles, sl may be set to the value of −su .

6. A load collective may consist of an arbitrary number of load contributions. Also the same
lpat may be used for several load contributions with varying scaling and / or cycle parameters. Defining the very same lpat, sl , su combination several times will simply result in
one load contribution with the sum of all corresponding cycle values.
7. The input type FLDEF yields a damage result by superimposing previously generated
fatigue results without the additional cost of performing a rainflow analysis. E.g. this
allows to define a load collective based on damage results from time history data.

3 Data Input (DAT)

4. If both values tS , tE are omitted, the stress results of the complete time history of the
analysis will be used. If, otherwise, only tS is defined, the stress history starting at tS
will be used. If additionally tE is defined, all stress results of the time interval [tS , tE ] are
used. The usage of a stress history ending at tE may be specified by omitting a lower
bound,i.e. by using the dash symbol for tS . Multiple sections / intervals of the timehistory
may be referenced, but is must be ensured that they do not overlap except for isolated
points. At these points the arithmetic mean value of the scaling parameters are used.
5. Two mechanism are available to use a combination of stresses during a fatigue analysis.
(a) A result combination rule may be referenced in the definition of the fatigue load. In
this case, the result combination rule $COMBINE RESULTS, is applied during the
fatigue analysis on-the-fly, i.e. this option uses minimal extra DMS space but does
not allow to export the combined stresses.

Results

(b) An alternative is to use an in situ result combination via COMBINE. In this case, a
combination rule must not be referenced in the fatigue load definition.

Remarks:
1. Definition of excitation frequencies for frequency response analysis is only possible within
a result variant of a single or top component.
2. The DOFTYPE must match the type of the performed analysis. For fluid-structure coupled
models this will be DISP for pure mechanical, PRES for pure acoustic and MATH for FS
coupled analysis.
3. Each data block defines one list of primary frequencies and, optionally, refinement rule
and bounds for that list.
4. Each frequency value list is determined in three steps:
• Definition of a list of primary frequencies by input or by selection of result frequencies.
• Optional elimination of frequency values outside of corresponding boundaries.
• Optional refinement of that list of primary frequencies. Values generated outside of
corresponding boundaries are omitted.
5. All frequency values of all lists defined in one result variant are collected and sorted in
ascending order. Duplicated or very close frequencies are eliminated.

in the (close) environment of each primary frequency, i.e. in addition to each primary
frequency fi in respective list 2 ndf frequency values
fi ± i df ; i = 1, . . . , ndf
are generated.
• If GEOM is specified, the intervals between successive primary frequencies of respective list are subdivided symmetrically in geometrical progressions with common
ratio s, leading to 2ns − 1 additional frequency values per interval, becoming closer
and closer with approach to the primary frequencies, i.e. within each interval fi , fi+1
of the sorted primary frequencies the values

$NLRESULTS

Remarks:
1. Requesting nonlinear result steps is only possible within the loading variant of single or
top components. It is applicable for nonlinear static and temperature analysis (UCI commands NLMATERIAL, NLTEMP and DIRECT NLTEMP) and for stepwise linear contact
analysis with a $NLLOAD load history (UCI command STATIC).
2. The degree of freedom type must correspond to the analysis performed, i.e. DISP for
mechanical and TEMP for thermal analyses.

4. For nonlinear static and temperature analysis, the final result step is always stored. If
STEPS = ALL is specified, results are calculated and stored for all steps in question
(number and length of those steps are defined via the UCI-command and automatic
step length adaption). If STEPS = INTERVAL is specified, results are calculated and
stored for all steps in question (number and length of those steps are defined via the
UCI-command and automatic step length adaption) inside the declared time interval. If
there are no result step definitions in the result variant, only the results of the final state
are stored.
5. If STEPS = PERIOD is specified for a DIRECT NLTIME analysis results are calculated
and stored after each period of time. It should not be mixed up with the result request
command STEPS = ALL . STEPS = PERIOD is ignored for all other analysis types.
6. For a stepwise linear contact analysis (UCI command STATIC) no automatic time stepping
is available. Therefore the result steps also define the time discretization of the loading
process, i.e. evaluation times and result steps are identical and all result steps are stored.
A set of default result steps is derived from the sampling times used for the $NLLOAD load
history definition, i.e. if STEPS = ALL is specified (or if $NLRESULTS is omitted) results
are calculated and stored for all sampling times given by $NLLOAD plus any additional
result steps given herein (a $NLLOAD GENERAL without explicit bounds or sampling
times will introduce time steps t = 0.0 and t = 1.0). Hence – for the stepwise linear contact
analysis – $NLRESULTS may just be used to specify additional evaluation points.
If STEPS = ALL is omitted, but at least one result step is given, then the highest result
step specified also sets the maximum time value for the evaluation of the loading process
(taking precedence over the maximum sampling time from $NLLOAD).
7. If STEPS = EQUI is specified, a list of points is generated according to
r1 , r1 + ∆r, . . . , r1 + i ∆r, . . . , r1 + n ∆r ;

r1 + n ∆r ≤ r2

8. If STEPS = LIST is specified, a list of points is expected, ordered according to ascending
magnitude.
9. If STEPS = INTERVAL is specified results are calculated and stored for all steps which
are lying inside the given lower ts and upper te bound. It should not be mixed up with the
result request command STEPS = ALL .

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-1053

DAT
Results

3. Each data block defines a list of points during the loading process. All lists defined within
one result variant are collected, sorted, and define the steps where results are calculated
and stored during the loading process.

$NLRESULTS

3 Data Input (DAT)

10. The specified result times might contradict with other time stepping information from
NLMATERIAL (TSTART, TINCI, TEND, TMIN), $TIMESTEPS and the load history check
(default switch NLLOADCHECK). Contradictions are resolved according to the following
priority list (from high to low priority):
(a) TSTART, TEND, TMIN: No time steps outside the interval [TSTART, TEND]. No time
increments smaller than TMIN.
(b) NLRESULTS
(c) TIMESTEPS
(d) NLLOADCHECK

Remarks:

only. They may refer to result items in any component of a configuration.

from each corresponding result item selection, and transfer the data in that order as independent variables to function fun. The function value is then available as xy data sets
over the sample counter.

specified result item is controlled by skey.

in the data object, starting with the first one. This selection is available up to now only
for complex eigenvalue extraction by $RSLITEM CFREQ (see page 3-1081 ff.) or by
$RSLITEM CAMPBELL (see page 3-1075 ff.).

Remarks:

DAT
Results

1. Definition of rotational speed values for analyses of rotating systems is only possible
within a result variant of a single or top component.
2. Each data block defines one list of primary rotational speeds and, optionally, refinement
rule and bounds for that list.
3. Each rotational speed value list is determined in three steps:
• Definition of a list of primary rotational speeds by input or by selection of result values
(eigenfrequecies).
• Optional elimination of rotational speed values outside of corresponding boundaries.
• Optional refinement of that list of primary rotational speeds. Values generated outside of corresponding boundaries are omitted.
4. All rotational speed values of all lists defined in one result variant are collected and sorted
in ascending order. Duplicated or very close rotational speeds are eliminated.
5. Lists of primary rotational speed values may be generated.
• If PRIMARY = EQUI is specified, a list of equidistant rotational speeds is generated:
f1 , f1 + ∆f, . . . , f1 + i ∆f, . . . , f1 + n ∆f ;

f1 + n ∆f ≤ f2

• If PRIMARY = LOG is specified, a list of rotational speeds with logarithmic intervals
is generated:
fi = f1 exp((i − 1) α) ; i = 1, . . . , nl + 1

with

α=

1
f2
ln
nl f1

6. Each list of primary rotational speed values may be refined separately.
• If CLUSTER is specified, rotational speed values with equidistant intervals are generated in the (close) environment of each primary rotational speed, i.e. in addition to
each primary rotational speed fi in respective list 2 ndf rotational speed values
fi ± i df ; i = 1, . . . , ndf
are generated.

• If GEOM is specified, the intervals between successive primary rotational speeds of
respective list are subdivided symmetrically in geometrical progressions with common ratio s, leading to 2ns − 1 additional rotational speed values per interval, becoming closer and closer with approach to the primary rotational speeds, i.e. within
each interval fi , fi+1 of the sorted primary rotational speeds the values

7. Rotational speeds may have negative values if they are specified by list with PRIMARY
= LIST or generated with equidistant intervals by PRIMARY = EQUI. In addition, for
negative rotational speeds neither bounds nor refinements are allowed. Furthermore,
negative rotational speeds are not allowed if FRICTION = MATRICES is specified in the
$CONTLOCK data block (see page 3-32), e.g. for brake squeal analysis.
8. The unit of input values is defined by parameter XTYPE; the default is input of frequency
values in cycles per unit time (i.g. cycles per second). Of course, the selected type of
input values is valid for bound and cluster definition values too.
Example:

3-1069

$RSLITEM

3 Data Input (DAT)

Remarks:
1. Result item selections may be defined for any component of a configuration with the
exception of global results which are related to configuration and therefore restricted to
single or top components. They are referenced by its identifier rstid or its name rstname.
2. Up to now, result item selections are available for sampling (UCI-command SAMPLING),
optimization (UCI-command OPTIM and TOPO) and reliability analysis (UCI-commands
MCS RELIABILITY ANalysis, RELIABILITY ANalysis and OPTREL), and must be specified in the result variants belonging to the situations for sampling or reliability analysis.
3. Result item selection identifiers and names must be unique within the result variant.

DAT
Results

4. Global results are valid for the whole configuration and the specified situation. Therefore,
only one global result item selection is possible for one result value (eg. one eigenfrequency etc.) and one situation.
5. Component results are extracted for the current component, i.e. for each element or node
resp. belonging to the component, and the specified situation. Only one component result
item selection is possible for one result value (eg. displacement or stress component),
one component and one situation.
6. Design model results are extracted for the whole design model, i.e. for all elements or
nodes assigned to any design element, and the specified situation. Only one design
model result item selection is possible for one result value and one situation.
7. Design element results are extracted for only one design element and one situation, i.e.
the specified result item selection is valid for all elements or nodes assigned to the design
element deid.
8. Set results are extracted for all elements or nodes resp. belonging to the specified element set eset or node set nset and one situation.
9. Direct results are valid for one specific result value at one node nid or element eid and
one situation.
10. Result item selections may be valid for all or restricted to one particular load pattern, time
step etc. according to column specification. Default, if applicable, is LPAT = ALL , i.e.
valid for all load pattern of a (static) situation. Which column specification parameter is
applicable depends on the analysis type of the corresponding situation.
11. Result values at specified nodes and elements are selected by local identifier lid, which
is the degree of freedom identifier for node related data and the component identifier for
element related data. The local identifier must not be omitted.

TYPE = COMPONENT

SITUATION = STATIC

LPAT = ALL

Depending on element type, there are different stress formats available to define element stress
results:
I

All elements with uniaxial stress state, i.e. 3D and axisymmetric flange elements.

II

All 3D elements where averaged nodal point stresses are available, i.e. all 3D
solids and membranes with the exception of shear panel SHEAR4. Stress components refer to component system.

III

Homogeneous shell elements with stress output at lower and upper surface. For
Tresca equivalent stress only plane shear stress is taken into accoint, i.e. it does
not necessarily deliver the actual maximum shear stress. Principal stresses are
only available for real arithmetic and belong to the plane stress state at surface.

IV

Axisymmetric solids. Stress components refer to component system.

V

Beam elements with standard cross-sections. Only normal stresses are taken
into account, shear stress contributions are ignored completely.

V 19.00.287

3.2 Model Data

$TIMESTEPS

Remarks:
1. Requesting time steps is only possible within the result variant of single or top components. It is applicable for linear and nonlinear analysis (UCI commands STATIC,
NLMATERIAL, NLTEMP and DIRECT NLTEMP).
2. Each data block defines a pair of time/time increments/time gate/solution method during the loading process. All lists defined within one result variant are collected, sorted,
and define the times/time step increment/time gate/solution method during the loading
process.

4. If no time gate tG is specified, the given time increment ∆t is used once at time t. Afterwards the automatic time incrementation is applied if no other user time requests exist.
5. The global solution method given in the UCI command by NLSOLV = xxxx can be overwritten by the definition of the name in NLSOLV = NR/MNR/SNM/QNM/THOMAS. The
solution method declared here is used from time t as long as no other solution method is
defined. The solution method is never automatically switched back to the given solution
method in the UCI command.
6. The maximum number of pairs for time/time increments within one result variant is restricted to 250.
7. For contradictions between the requested time steps and other time stepping information
see $NLRESULTS.
8. If KIND = ABS is specified, then the points during the loading process are defined as
actual values of the process itself, i.e. the input values must satisfy 0 ≤ r ≤ T EN D where
0 represents the beginning and TEND the end of the loading process as declared in the
UCI command.
It must not be mixed up with KIND = RATIO in the same result variant.
9. If KIND = RATIO is specified, then the points during the loading process are defined as
fraction of the loading process itself, i.e. the input values must satisfy 0 ≤ r ≤ 1 where 0
represents the beginning and 1 the end of the loading process.
For a stepwise linear contact analysis (UCI command STATIC) KIND = RATIO is not
applicable, since all result steps must be specified explicitly with absolute ’process time’
values according to the $NLLOAD load history.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-1103

DAT
Results

3. If a time gate tG is specified, the given time increment ∆t is used and held constant for
all following time steps from time t as long as the time is less or equal the time gate.

Remarks:
1. Z-vectors are defined in the result variant of single or top components only. Their identifier
must be unique within the actual variant.
2. Each element of each z-vector must be referenced at least once by a failure function
definition, see $FAILFUNCTION data block.
3. Z-vectors contain the state variables of reliability analyses. State variables may be result
items of the finite element analysis or basic variables used as state function parameters
directly.
4. The length of a z-vector is defined implicitly by the highest index zvindmax . Within the
z-vector, all elements 1 ≤ zvind ≤ zvindmax must be defined.
5. Two or more z-vector elements may refer to the same result item or basic variable.
6. Each z-vector must contain at least one result item.
7. Result items to be inserted into z-vectors are defined within a $RSLITEM data block
and accessed by its identifier rstid or name rstname. If result items are calculated in
subcomponents, the name name of the subcomponent must be specified in addition.
8. All result items to be inserted into one z-vector must belong to the same load pattern. If
the load is a stochastic one, then the referred load pattern must be the combined load
pattern describing the stochastic load.
9. Basic variables to be inserted into z-vectors must be declared as state function parameters at their definition, see $BASVAR data block.
10. Each data line inserts at least element zvind of the z-vector. If a result item contains more
than one value (e.g. displacements of a node set), than by nof val the number of result
values may be specified which are inserted consecutively into the z-vector, starting at
index zvind. The selection of result values to be inserted out of all result values available
for the specified result item is controlled by skey.

3.3 Function Data

$FUNCTION CHAIN

Remarks:
1. One data line defines an assembled function
zν = cν fun ν (. . . , xi , . . . )

where the first tuple defines the top level primary function call c0 fun 0 (. . . , zi , . . . ), followed
by a list of tuples defining the primary function calls which are used in the sequence of
occurrence as variables of the top level primary function. Primary functions with the
exception of the top level primary function may be replaced by a constant value c. For
only one independent variable the function reduces to
fun(x) = c0 fun 0 (c1 fun 1 (x))
2. Only one data line per data block is allowed.
3. The parameter NVAR is used to specify the number of independent variables of the assembled function, not the number of independent variables of the top level primary function. If parameter NVAR is not specified then nof var = 1 is assumed.
4. Functions used to define assembled functions must be primary functions, i.e. they may
be defined as library, tabular or user-supplied functions, and must not be assembled
functions by itself.
5. Definitions of assembled functions may not be recursive.
6. First derivatives are available for all assembled functions, if the derivatives exist for all
corresponding primary functions. Second derivative is available in addition for assembled
functions with only one independent variable.
7. Arguments of trigonometric functions are expected to be in radians.
8. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.
9. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component, and
are valid and accessible for all components.

Example:
f502 (x1 , x2 , x3 , x4 , x5 ) = 3.75 · f109 (z1 , z2 , z3 )
= 3.75 · (4.22 + z1 + z2 + z3 )
z1 = f101 (x1 , x2 ) = 1.0 + x1 2 + x1 x2
z2 = f101 (x3 , x5 ) = 1.0 + x3 2 + x3 x5
z3 = 2.0 · f102 (x4 ) = 2.0 · (3.3 + 27.2 · x4 )

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-1113

12. Given three points P0 , P1 and P2 the two orthogonal unit-length direction vectors D1 , D2 ∈
R3 are computed as:
D1 =

P1 − P0
kP1 − P0 k

and

D2 = N × D1

where N is the unit length normal vector
N =

(P1 − P0 ) × (P2 − P0 )
k(P1 − P0 ) × (P2 − P0 )k

of the plane spanned by P0 , P1 and P2 .

Explanation
Name of function. Has no functionality in Permas, for readability only.
Independent variables of the function. Up to 100 variables
are possible.
Formula expression. The valid list of mathematical functions
and syntax is listed below.

The formula syntax follows the general known math notation (e.g. f (x, y) = (x+y)ˆ2.0). First the
user must enter the name of the function (e.g. f ), followed by the list of variables of the function
in brackets (e.g. (x, y)). After the equality sign =, a formula expression may be defined, using
the mathematical operations and constants defined in the tables below, numbers and previously
defined variables. In addition, brackets () may be used. All numbers may be integer or floating
point numbers (1, 2., 3.0, −3.62E − 5 etc.).
For all formula functions, first and second derivatives are available. All formula functions are
threadsafe and may be used in a parallel environment. Performance wise, formula functions
are slower compared to standard library functions. So if the function evaluation is critical for
performance, standard library functions should be used.

Remarks:
1. By $FUNCTION FOURIERSRS a Fourier transformation is done for an existing tabular
function fun, defined for a period T .
2. Since the Fourier transform of a real function is a complex one, two new tabular functions fun 1 and fun 2 are generated. If DATTYPE = RI (default) is specified, function fun 1
contains the real part and function fun 2 the imaginary part of the Fourier transform, for
DATTYPE = AP function fun 1 contains the amplitude and function fun 2 the phase in degrees. The values of the new tabular functions are the coefficients ck of a complex Fourier
series of order K which may be written as real series for DATTYPE = RI by
x(t) =

K
X

k=0

k=0

ℜ(ck )

Phase angle

3. According to parameter METHOD, a discrete Fourier transformation (DFT) or a fast
Fourier transformation (FFT) is performed. If not specified, the method is selected internally.
4. The function to be transformed must be a tabular function in the time domain, i.e. the
independent variable is assumed to represent the time. It is given by N0 + 1 tuples
(x(tn ), tn ), n = 0, 1, . . . , N0 ; extrapolation is not taken into account. The period of the
function is defined as difference between first and last time value:

$FUNCTION FOURIERSRS

5. For Fourier transformation, the function in the time domain must be given at N equidistant
time steps, i.e.
x(tk ), tk = k∆t; k = 0, 1, 2, . . . , N − 1

with

∆t =

T
N

• If fast Fourier transformation is requested, N must be a power of 2. Therefore N is
determined according to
N = 2M

with

2M −1 < (N0 − 1) ≤ 2M ,

M integer

• If the function values are not equidistant or if N is not equal N0 − 1, the function is
evaluated at N equidistant points to prepare the input for Fourier transformation.
6. The order of the generated Fourier series can be specified by parameter LIMIT, directly
by mf or by upper frequency limit f req. The highest possible order, however is given by
N/2 corresponding to a frequency of N/(2T ).
7. If a threshold is defined, all terms of the Fourier series with amplitudes less than the
threshold value are removed from the generated function.
8. Tabular functions generated by Fourier transformation may be used as primary functions
for the definition of assembled functions.
9. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.
10. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component, and
are valid and accessible for all components.
Example:
$FUNCTION FOURIERSRS LABEL = 2101,2102

Remarks:
1. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.
2. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component and
are valid and accessible for all components.
3. Only one data line per data block is allowed.
4. At least one function coefficient must be different from zero.
5. Since in some cases input values are considered as integer values, floating point as well
as integer values are accepted on the data line.
6. The maximum number of coefficients for library functions is restricted to 2000.
7. Trailing zeros in list of coefficients may be omitted. Exception: function type TRINOMIAL.
8. First derivatives are available for all library functions, second derivatives only for library
functions with one independent variable and for polynomials of type WSUMLIN, WSUMQUARE,
SUMSQDIFF, FRACLINXY and TRINOMIAL.
9. Arguments of trigonometric functions are expected to be in radians.
10. Results of inverse trigonometric functions are in radians.
11. For function type POWERLIN the argument x must be greater than zero.
12. If for function type POWEREXPCOS the exponent c2 and the factor c1 are both different
from zero, then the argument x must be greater than zero.
13. For function type FRACPOLYPOLY the number of coefficients must be always greater
than 2, and the denominator must be always nonzero.
14. Since for functions type WSUMLIN and WSUMQUARE the number of coefficients determine the number of independent variables, at least 2 coefficients must be specified.

$FUNCTION LIB

15. For function type FRACLINQUAD the number of coefficients must be always greater than
3, and the denominator must be always nonzero.
16. For function type VARIANCE the number of independent variables is given by n, and at
least one of the coefficients a and b must be unequal zero.
17. For function type SUMSQDIFF the number of coefficients must be always be odd and
greater than 2, and all di must be non-zero.

18. For function type TRINOMIAL the number of coefficients must always match the corresponding maximum polynomial degree specified in the first coefficient. It is not possible to
omit coefficients, e.g. for a maximum polynomial degree of 2 there must be 10 polynomial
coefficients otherwise an error will be returned. The maximum polynomial degree is 20,
resulting in 1772 coefficients.
19. The zero function does always return zero. Sometimes it is useful to exchange a function
for zero for testing purposes for example.

Remarks:
1. Function labels must be unique within the whole data base.
2. Functions may be defined within the $ENTER FUNCTION, the $STRUCTURE as well as
any variant bracket. Nevertheless, they never belong to any variant or component, and
are valid and accessible for all components.
3. At least two function values have to be input.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-1151

$FUNCTION TABLE

3 Data Input (DAT)

4. The pairs fun(xi ) : xi have to be given in ascending order of the independent variable x
for functions with JUMPS = YES. For functions with JUMPS = NO, the pairs may be given
in arbitrary order.
5. If JUMPS = YES is specified, jumps, that means two data pairs with the same argument
(xi+1 = xi ) are allowed, but not at the end points. The function value at jump points is the
average value, i.e. fun(x) = 0.5 (fun(xi ) + fun(xi+1 )).
If a jump is defined by three data pairs with the same argument (xi−1 = xi = xi+1 ), then
the function value at jump point is given by the middle one, i.e. fun(x) = fun(xi ).
If JUMPS = YES is specified, parameters XGEN or GRID cannot be used.

Function
Data

6. If parameter XGEN is specified, the values of the function are input for equidistant values
of the independent variable x. The equidistant values are generated automatically, where
the first value is xA and the increment per step is ∆x. If n function values are input the
last one belongs to x = xA + (n − 1)∆x.
7. If parameter GRID is specified, the values of the function are input for a regular grid
in up to three dimensions. The number of points nxj for each dimension (i.e. independent variable) must be input, and for each dimension one data line with coordinate
values in ascending order is expected. At least two values are expected for each independent variable in question. The function values itself are input on nx2 ∗ nx3 data lines,
and each line contains all function values belonging to one pair x2 , x3 , i.e. nx1 values
fun(x1,i , x2,j , x3,k ), i = 1, nx1 . The data lines with function values must be given in ascending order of x3 , and for equal values x3 in ascending order of x2 .
For grids with two or only one dimension this scheme is reduced accordingly. Generation
(parameter XGEN) or jumps (JUMP = YES) are not available for grids.
8. Linear interpolation is used for calculation of function values within the defined range
of the tabular function with one independent variable. For functions with two or three
independent variables, bilinear and trilinear interpolation is used, respectively.
9. First and second derivatives are available for all tabular functions without jumps, if not
JUMP = YES is specified. Due to linear interpolation the second derivative of tabular
functions with one independent variable is always zero, except for option
INTERPOLATE = SMOOTH, see remark 10.
10. Interpolation of function values may be improved if INTERPOLATE = SMOOTH is selected. This option is only available if JUMPS = NO is selected and the function values
dependent on one independent variable only. In this case the second derivative is nonzero and the first derivative is improved. This option can be used in a TIMEHISTORY simulation, where some nodes have a predescribed displacement given by a tabular function.
If consistent mass is used, an additional force term f = −Mü can be taken into account
because of the non-zero second derivative.
11. Sometimes data is given in a log-log or lin-log diagram. In this case, a line in the diagram is actually a power function (log-log) or an exponential function (lin-log). If the
data is supposed to be interpolated as in the diagram the option SCALE = LOGLOG or
SCALE = LINLOG must be selected. This option is only available if JUMPS = YES is
selected and the function values dependent on one independent variable only. No derivatives are available.

3-1152

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

$FUNCTION TABLE

12. The parameter EXTRA defines the extrapolation rule which has to be used if function
values are needed outside of the definition region, i.e. if x < xmin or if x > xmax , where
xmin is the first (lowest) value of the independent variable and xmax the last (highest)
value.
If no extrapolation rule is selected, then the value of the function outside of the definition
region is zero.
If constant extrapolation is selected, then the value of the function outside of the definition
region is equal to the function value at the first point for x < xmin or at the last point for
x > xmax , respectively.
If linear extrapolation is selected, then the function value outside of the definition region
is determined by a linear extrapolation using the first two points for x < xmin or the last
two points for x > xmax , respectively.
13. Tabular functions may be used as primary functions for the definition of assembled functions.
Example:
Please refer to examples DRA1 and DRA14 of [um550]. See also DRA6V1 for an example of
the JUMPS option, DRX3 for an example of the SCALE option and LS18 for the GRID option.

6. Only one data line per data block is allowed.

12. For THREADSAFE = YES the user supplied function must be thread-safe and so it must
not have any internal state. In the simplest case, the output parameters of the subroutine
depend only on input parameters, and constant data is specified within the subroutine.

block $PARAMETER, page 3-549, it is possible to access internally provided functions
as user supplied function. If the function identifier fun lies within the range defined by
those two parameters, subroutine FNUSRF (if not replaced by the user) calls a subroutine
FNUSRFXX with the same list of parameters. If subroutine FNUSRFXX is not replaced, it
calls an internally provided function for the calculation of cutting forces of machine tools.
A call to subroutine FNUSRFXX is possible only within an active situation.
14. If a user defined function has a name or text as label, then the name of the user defined
function can be accessed in the Fortran subroutine by

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of heat conductivity behavior by an $CONDUCTIVITY data block is
allowed within the definition of one material.

Homogen.
Material

2. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167.
3. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic behavior for 1-D, 2-D and 3-D elements. Nevertheless in any case all heat conductivity
matrices which can be derived from input data are build up.
4. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1173, is
recommended.
5. If the material is not isotropic the orientation of the material axes has to be defined by a
material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527.
6. The general three dimensional heat conductivity matrix λ is defined by

8. Temperature-dependent heat conductivity is available only in single or top components.
9. If a linear analysis is performed, temperature-dependent material data are evaluated at
the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER COMPTEMP.
10. Material porosity is the fraction of the volume of voids over the total volume, 0.0 ≤ p < 1.0.
11. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
12. Temperature- and/or porosity-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
are used outside the table definition range.
13. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of creep behavior by a $CREEP data block is allowed within the definition of one material.
2. Creep behavior as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in
single or top components.
3. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
only isotropic material is actually supported for nonlinear material behavior.
4. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
can be found in the element description.
5. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1184, is
recommended.
6. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
7. For isotropic material the creep behavior is defined by
εcr = f(σef f , T, t)

$DAMPING

Remarks:

2. Structural damping is understood as a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not depend
on the degree of anisotropy of the material.
3. Structural damping within material description yields complex elemental stiffness matrices
of the form
K̄ E = (1 + igE (f ))K E
with the (optional) frequency-dependent elemental damping factor gE (f ).
4. Elemental structural damping may be used for direct or modal frequency response analysis and any other analysis in frequency domain. For use in time domain, e.g. for transient
response analysis, it is converted to equivalent viscous damping by
Dg,E =

gE (fE )
KE
2πfE

The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by parameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.
5. Material porosity is the fraction of the volume of voids over the total volume, 0.0 ≤ p < 1.0.
6. Frequency- and/or porosity dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
are used outside the table definition range.
7. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
8. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
Example:
$MATERIAL NAME=STA_325
$DAMPING
0.02
$END MATERIAL
$MATERIAL NAME=A2390
$DAMPING INPUT=TABLE
0.02 : 0.0
0.03 : 10.0
0.05 : 20.0
$END MATERIAL

DEP=FREQ

11. The coefficient of mutual influence which characterizes shearing strain in the ij-plane
caused by normal stress in the i-direction is defined by
ηij,i =

γij
εi

for σi = σ and all other stresses are zero.
12. The Chentsov coefficient which characterizes shearing strain in the ij-plane due to shearing stress in the kl-plane is defined by
µij,kl =

γij
γkl

for σi = σ and all other stresses are zero.
13. Temperature-dependent elastic material behavior is available in all kinds of components.
The corresponding constant element temperature state is defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP, see page 3-440, and system variant parameter
COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.
14. Material porosity is the fraction of the volume of voids over the total volume, 0.0 ≤ p < 1.0.
15. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
16. Temperature- and/or porosity-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
are used outside the table definition range.
17. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

18. The linear elastic behavior of isotropic material may be described by a user supplied function, i.e. by a FORTRAN subroutine. The subroutine call is given by

CALL MUELAS (MATNAM,NOFDEP,ZVEC,NODATA,IDRREQ,DATA,DERIV,IRC)

Homogen.
Material

Input:
MATNAM
NOFDEP
ZVEC

Character∗(∗)
Integer
Real(∗)

NODATA
IDRREQ

Integer
Integer(∗)

Ouput:
DATA
DERIV
IRC

Real(∗)
Real(∗)
Integer

Material name
Number of actual dependencies
Array with state variables. Values for all dependencies
defined by input for actual material property, sorted according to internal sequence of dependencies (see below).
Number of expected data
(1) Derivative request etc.
0 No derivatives requested
1 Derivatives requested, must be returned
(2) Seletion at jumps
0 or 1 Right-hand side of a jump
-1 Left-hand side of a jump
(3) External element identifier
Array with NODATA material data
Array with NODATA∗NOFDEP derivatives.
Return code
0 Material data returned
-1 Error(s) occurred
-200 Material data not available

Meaning and number of material data correspond to input described for tabular function
(of course without values of independent variables), depending on material property type
and degree of anisotropy.
The sequence of state variables and, correspondingly, the sequence of material data
derivatives is determined by the internal sequence of independent variables, which for
stress - plastic strain relation is given by

19. For THREADSAFE = YES the user supplied function must be thread-safe and so it must
not have any internal state. In the simplest case, the output parameters of the subroutine
depend only on input parameters and constant data specified within the subroutine.

3-1229

$HARDENING

3 Data Input (DAT)

Remarks:
1. The hardening type ratio defined by a $HARDENING data block is used if plastic deformation behavior as defined by a $PLASTIC data block is taken into account.

Homogen.
Material

2. Only one definition of the hardening type ratio is allowed within the definition of one material.
3. If not defined, pure isotropic hardening is assumed.
4. Hardening as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single or
top components.
5. Hardening type ratio is understood as a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not depend on the degree of anisotropy of the material.
6. The hardening type ratio m with 0.0 ≤ m ≤ 1.0 describes the relation of isotropic hardening to total hardening by
isotropic hardening
m=
total hardening
and, consequently, for the relation of kinematic hardening to total hardening it follows
1.0 − m =

kinematic hardening
total hardening

m = 0.0 means pure kinematic, m = 1.0 pure isotropic hardening.
7. If linear kinematic hardening is applied (i.e. m < 1.0 and no $NLKINHARD specified) the
yield curve in the $PLASTIC data block should be linear, see its remark 18.
8. The hardening type ratio may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis with nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DISLOAD
etc), then the temperatures to evaluate temperature-dependent material data are taken
from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element temperature state is
defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP and system variant
parameter COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.
9. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is
used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside
the table definition range.
10. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

$HEATCAP

3 Data Input (DAT)

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of heat capacity by a $HEATCAP data block is allowed within the
definition of one material.

Homogen.
Material

2. Heat capacity is understood as a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not depend on
the degree of anisotropy of the material.
3. Temperature-dependent heat capacity is available only in single or top components.
4. If a linear analysis is performed, temperature-dependent material data are evaluated at
the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER COMPTEMP.
5. Material porosity is the fraction of the volume of voids over the total volume, 0.0 ≤ p < 1.0.
6. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
7. Temperature- and/or porosity-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
are used outside the table definition range.
8. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
Example:
$MATERIAL NAME=STA202
$HEATCAP
0.2E-3
$END MATERIAL
$MATERIAL NAME=A2390
$HEATCAP INPUT=TABLE
0.2E-3 :
0.0
0.3E-3 : 10.0
0.5E-3 : 100.0
$END MATERIAL

4 values on one logical line.

Item(s)

f name
mname

name
name
R>0
R>0

Name of fiber material.
Name of matrix material.
Volume fraction of fiber material2, 0.0 < vf < 1.0.
Length to diameter ratio of fibers, ldr > 0.0.

Remarks:
1. Data block $HOMOGENIZE allows for establishing material property data of a homogeneous material by Mōri-Tanaka type mean-field homogenization.

2. The volume fraction of the fiber(inclusion) material can be input elementwise with $ELSTATE VOLFFRA
on page 3-445. In this case, the value in the material block will be ignored for the corrisponding elements.
3. If FIBER_MATRIX is specified as homogenization type, then the material consists of unidirectionally spheroidal or spherical (depends on ldr) inclusions and an isotropic matrix
material. The homogenized material is therefore (transversely) isotropic (depends on
value of ldr), where the orientation of the inclusions coincides with the first material direction. If it is defined as orthotropic and the corresponding fiber orientation distribution

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-1235

$HOMOGENIZE

3 Data Input (DAT)

is given with the structure tensors (see $ELSTATE STCTENS on page 3-437), then a
second level homogenization will be performed to mix the transversely isotropic material
properties in different directions into an orthotropic one.
• The homogenized material must be declared as transversely isotropic or orthotropic,
see 3-1167.

Homogen.
Material

• For fibers (inclusions) as well as for the matrix an isotropic material must be input.
• Actually, only elasticity and density data may be established by homogenization. To
do so, fiber as well as matrix material must contain the corresponding property with
constant data. Any dependency is not allowed.
• With the exception of plasticity data and yield limit with CRITERION = GENANISO
for TYPE = TRANS, no other properties may be input for that material up to now.
• If plasticity data are not specified for the main material but are given for fiber (inclusion) or matrix material, then dummy data are generated internally for plasticity and
yield limit to assure a formal correct processing on element level.
• For orthotropic material the input of the structure tensor of fiber orientation distribution per element by a $ELSTATE STCTENS data block (see page 3-437) is necessary. Only (transverse) isotropy can be considered if it is not given, despite of
TYPE = ORTHO.
• If the length to diameter ratio of fiber ldr is given as 1.0, any anisotropy will vanish, it
results in an isotropic material stiffness despite of input by TYPE on the $MATERIAL
line, see page 3-1167.
4. If any property of a material used for homogenization (i,e, fiber (inclusion) or matrix materials) is given by a user supplied function, then this function must be thread-safe.
5. Since the homogenized material is always considered as anisotropic, the orientation of
the material axes has to be defined by a material reference system or element structure
tensor within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527 or $ELSTATE STCTENS
on page 3-437.

Following material stiffness data are derived:
C
Stiffness matrix of general 3-D case, dimension 6x6.
Example:
Please refer to examples MNL17V1 of [um550].
$MATERIAL NAME=MATX
TYPE=TRANS
$HOMOGENIZE FIBER_MATRIX
FIBER_MATERIAL
MATRIX_MATERIAL
$END MATERIAL

$HYPERELASTIC

Remarks:

2. Hyperelastic behavior as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only
in single or top components.
3. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
currently only isotropic material is supported for this nonlinear material.
4. The $HYPERELASTIC data block describes the complete elastic behavior of the material,
so elastic data must not be specified by an $ELASTIC data block. Furthermore, the
material properties for nonlinear material behavior specified by data blocks $CREEP,
$HARDENING, $NLELASTIC, $NLKINHARD, $PLASTIC, $VISCOELASTIC and $YIELD
are meaningless and must not be specified.
5. Parameter SPTYPE specifies the type of strain energy potential form.
6. If INPUT = FITTING is specified, then the hyperelastic property data are derived from
measured stress over strain data, which must be input in a $MEASUREMENT data block
(see page 3-1244 ff.) with data type STRESS_STRAIN. The requested type of strain
energy potential form generated by fitting must be given by parameter SPTYPE.
7. Measured stress over strain data used for fitting may not be temperature-dependent.
8. The range of measured stress over strain data may be limited by parameter RANGE, i.e.
only stress data within the range eps1 ≤ ε ≤ eps2 are taken into account for fitting.
9. The polynomial strain energy potential is defined in terms of the invariants of the right
Cauchy-Green tensor C = FT F, where F is the deformation gradient. In order to split
the strain energy potential into an isochoric and a volumetric part the Jacobi determinant
J = detF, the isochoric deformation gradient F̄ = J −1/3 F and the isochoric right CauchyGreen tensor C̄ = F̄T F̄ are introduced. The isochoric invariants are defined as I¯1 = trC̄
¯2 − tr(C̄2 )). The strain energy potential reads

Here Jel is the elastic Jacobi determinant which is defined in terms of the total Jacobi
determinant via Jel = J/(1 + ǫth )3 and ǫth is the thermal strain. The Cij parameters
describe the shear behavior of the material while the Di parameters describe its compressibility. Note that the small strain shear and bulk modulus for the material are given
as µ0 = 2 (C10 + C01 ) and k0 = 2/D1 .
10. The reduced polynomial strain energy potential is equivalent to the polynomial strain energy potential with Cij = 0 if j 6= 0 such that the potential does not depend on the second
invariant I¯2 , see remark 9.
11. The Neo-Hookean strain energy potential is equivalent to the reduced polynomial strain
energy potential with n = 1, see remark 10. Hence, it does not depend on the second
invariant I¯2 .

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of nonlinear elastic material behavior by a $NLELASTIC data block is
allowed within the definition of one material.
2. To complete the description of elastic behavior, the corresponding linearized elastic behavior for vanishing elastic strains must be input by $ELASTIC (see page 3-1202 ff.).
3. Nonlinear Elastic behavior as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available
only in single or top components.
4. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
only isotropic material is actually supported for nonlinear material behavior.
5. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
can be found in the element description.
6. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1250, is
recommended.
7. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.

$NLELASTIC

3 Data Input (DAT)

10. For constant temperature the stress should be a preferably smooth and monotonically
increasing function of the strain. Hence, scattered raw data from measurements must not
be input directly but smoothed like exemplified for $PLASTIC (see page 3-1268 ff.) on
page 3-1268.

Homogen.
Material

11. The nonlinear elastic behavior may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis with
nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DISLOAD etc, see page 3-581 ff.), then the temperatures to evaluate temperature-dependent
material data are taken from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element
temperature state is defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP,
see page 3-440, and system variant parameter COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.
12. If the nonlinear elastic behavior is temperature-dependent, the linearized elastic behavior
defined by $ELASTIC must be temperature-dependent too.
13. Input may be done as tabular function. Linear interpolation is used within the table to
determine function values, and boundary values are used outside the table definition
range.
14. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
15. The nonlinear elastic behavior may be described by a user supplied function, i.e. by a
FORTRAN subroutine. The subroutine call is given by

3.4 Material Data

$NLKINHARD

1. Nonlinear kinematic hardening defined by a $NLKINHARD data block is applied if plastic
deformation behavior (see $PLASTIC (see page 3-1268 ff.)) and kinematic hardening
(see $HARDENING (see page 3-1232 ff.)) are taken into account. If the yield curve defined in the $PLASTIC data block is linear, linear kinematic hardening should be applied,
i.e. the $NLKINHARD data block should be skipped.
2. Only one definition of the nonlinear kinematic hardening is allowed within the definition of
one material.
3. Nonlinear kinematic hardening as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single or top components.
4. The description of nonlinear kinematic hardening is extracted from the plasticity data (see
$PLASTIC (see page 3-1268 ff.)) using the maximum plastic strain εpl,max . If plasticity
data are given as tabular function, εpl,max should coincide with the maximum plastic strain
of that table, if plasticity data are given by user supplied function, εpl,max should be the
maximum expected plastic strain.
If plasticity data depend on temperature, the nonlinear kinematic hardening must depend
on temperature, too.

Homogen.
Material

Remarks:

5. The nonlinear kinematic hardening may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis
with nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks
$DISLOAD etc, see page 3-581 ff.), then the temperatures to evaluate temperaturedependent material data are taken from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element temperature state is defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE
TEMP (see page 3-438 ff.), and system variant parameter COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.
6. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is
used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside
the table definition range.
7. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

list(x)
z

R
R

List of data describing stress - plastic strain relation.
Value of independent variable.

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of stress - plastic strain behavior by a $PLASTIC data block is allowed
within the definition of one material.
2. To complete the plastic deformation behavior description of the material, yield behavior
(data block $YIELD, see page 3-1305 ff.) must and hardening (data block $HARDENING,
see page 3-1229 ff.) may be defined in addition. If hardening type is not defined explicitly,
then pure isotropic hardening is assumed. For transversly isotropic material, Poisson’s
ratio for plastic deformation may be input by data block $PLSPOISSON, see page 3-1277
ff..
3. Plasticity as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single or
top components.
4. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
only isotropic or transversely isotropic material is actually supported for nonlinear plastic
material behavior.
5. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
can be found in the element description.
6. If the effective stress depends on the plastic strain, then the dependency on εpl ≥ 0.0
must always be specified. For pressure modified v.Mises or cast iron yield condition (see
$YIELD (see page 3-1308 ff.)) and isotropic material, the dependency εpl ≤ 0.0 may
be different, and must be specified in addition with a jump at εpl = 0.0. Note that the
compression yield stress must be greater than the tension yield stress for any state, i.e.
|σef f (−εpl , T )| > σef f (εpl , T ) for each effective plastic strain εpl ≥ 0.0 and temperature T .
7. If for transversely isotropic material the dependencies for positive and negative plastic
strain are different, all functions describing the transversely isotropic plasticity must be
input with jumps as requested in remark 6.

14. The stress must be given as engineering stress, i.e. the ratio of the applied force to the
original (undeformed) cross section area. The strain must be given as engineering strain,
i.e. the ratio of the length change to the original length.

16. If strain-dependency is omitted (INPUT = DATA specified or only temperature-dependent
tabular input) then the material behaves perfectly plastic.
17. The stress value for εpl = 0.0 is equal to the initial yield stress σy of the material, and must
be input in any case.
18. If linear kinematic hardening is applied (see $HARDENING (see page 3-1232 ff.)) the
stress vs. plastic strain relation should be linear. The yield stress and hardening modulus
should represent the material behavior in an average sense within the expected range of
plastic strain.

3-1268

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

$PLASTIC

19. The stress - plastic strain relation may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis
with nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks
$DISLOAD etc, see page 3-581 ff.), then the temperatures to evaluate temperaturedependent material data are taken from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element temperature state is defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP, see page 3-440, and system variant parameter COMPTEMP, see page
3-549.
20. Strain- and temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are
used outside the table definition range.
21. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
22. The stress - plastic strain relation of isotropic material may be described by a user supplied function, i.e. by a FORTRAN subroutine. The subroutine call is given by

CALL MUPLAS (MATNAM,NOFDEP,ZVEC,NODATA,IDRREQ,DATA,DERIV,IRC)

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of Poisson’s ratios for plastic deformation by a $PLSPOISSON data
block is allowed within the definition of one material. Up to now it is applicable only for
transversely isotropic material.

Homogen.
Material

2. If Poisson’s ratios for plastic deformation are input, plastic deformation behavior description (data block $PLASTIC, see page 3-1265 ff.) must be specified in any case.
3. Plasticity as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single or
top components.
4. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
only transversely isotropic material is actually supported for plastic deformation behavior.
5. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
can be found in the element description.
6. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1280, is
recommended.
7. If the material is not isotropic, the orientation of the material axes has to be defined by a
material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527.
8. Poisson’s ratio for transverse plastic strain in j-direction when stressed in i-direction is
defined by
εjj,pl
νij,pl = −
εii,pl
where εii,pl is the plastic strain in i-direction etc.
9. The coefficient which characterizes plastic shear strain in the ij-plane due to shearing
stress in the kl-plane is defined by
µij,kl,pl =

εij,pl
γij,pl
=
γkl,pl
εkl,pl

where γij,pl is the plastic shear strain in the ij-plane etc.
10. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
11. Poisson’s ratios for plastic deformation behavior may be temperature-dependent. If in
a static analysis with nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DISLOAD etc, see page 3-581 ff.), then the temperatures to evaluate
temperature-dependent material data are taken from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element temperature state is defined within the system variant by data
blocks $ELSTATE TEMP, see page 3-440, and system variant parameter COMPTEMP,
see page 3-549.

2. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167.
3. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic behavior for 1-D, 2-D and 3-D elements. Nevertheless in any case all thermal
expansion matrices which can be derived from input data are build up.
4. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1293, is
recommended.
5. If the material is not isotropic the orientation of the material axes has to be defined by a
material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527.

$THERMEXP

with T0 as the (element) temperature where the thermal strain is zero. The element
temperatures T0 are defined within the loading variant for each loading case with thermal
loads by $REFVAL TEMP data blocks, see page 3-872, and loading variant parameter
REFTEMP, see page 3-852.
Loading variant parameter REFTEMP must not be mixed up with parameter REFTEMP
on header line.

9. Material porosity is the fraction of the volume of voids over the total volume, 0.0 ≤ p < 1.0.
10. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
11. Temperature- and/or porosity-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear
interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values
are used outside the table definition range.
12. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
13. The thermal expansion behavior of isotropic material may be described by a user supplied function, i.e. by a FORTRAN subroutine. The subroutine call is given by

εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )

3 Data Input (DAT)

Viscoelasticity
Definition of viscoelastic material behavior.

$VISCOELASTIC

Homogen.
Material



GENERAL



Data line:
1 value on one logical line.

τ

Item(s)

Type

Explanation

τ

R

Time constant, see remark 2

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of viscoelastic material behavior by an $VISCOELASTIC data block is
allowed within the definition of one material.
2. Viscoelastic behavior is specified by a scalar time constant τ . The viscous damping part
of viscoelastic elements is then given by τ k where k is the corresponding elastic stiffness
matrix. For isotropic material, the damping constant is given by D = τ E where E is
Young’s modulus.
3. Viscoelastic behavior constant is always a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not
depend on the degree of anisotropy of the material.
Example:
Please refer to examples DRA20 and DRA20V1 of [um550].

0.033514

Remarks:
1. Viscoplasticity as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single
or top components.

Homogen.
Material

2. To define the complete viscoplastic behavior, plasticity data (see $PLASTIC (see page
3-1268 ff.)) must be specified in addition.
3. Viscoplastic behavior is described by a power–law viscoplastic model
"

− 1.

where the strictly positive material constants µ and ε are the viscosity and rate–sensitivity
parameters and σ and σef f are the effective and yield stress (σef f = f (εpl , T )), respectively.
4. The viscoplastic properties may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis with
nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DISLOAD etc, see page 3-581 ff.), then the temperatures to evaluate temperature-dependent
material data are taken from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element
temperature state is defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP
(see page 3-438 ff.), and system variant parameter COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.
5. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is
used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside
the table definition range.
6. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

Value of independent variable.

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of yield behavior by a $YIELD data block is allowed within the definition
of one material.
2. The definition of yield limit by a $YIELD data block is necessary if plastic deformation
behavior as defined by a $PLASTIC data block (see page 3-1265 ff.) is taken into account.
3. Yield behavior as well as each other nonlinear material behavior is available only in single
or top components.
4. Number and meaning of the values on the data lines depend on the degree of anisotropy
of the material which is defined on the $MATERIAL line, see page 3-1167. Nevertheless,
only isotropic material is actually supported for nonlinear material behavior.
5. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic material for different element families. Nevertheless in any case all material data
which can be derived from input data are build up. Input options for each element type
can be found in the element description.
6. For isotropic material the default material property type GENERAL, see page 3-1309, is
recommended.
7. If the material is not isotropic the orientation of the material axes has to be defined by a
material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on page 3-527.

3-1306

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

3.4 Material Data

$YIELD

9. If Drucker-Prager (CRITERION = DPAS) or Mohr-Coulomb (CRITERION = MCAS) yield
condition with associated flow rule is selected, the yield limit is defined by two values, the
cohesion c and the angle of interior friction ϕ. For a non-associated flow rule (CRITERION
= DPNA or CRITERION = MCNA specified) an additional value is needed, the dilatancy
angle ϕP .
10. If general anisotropic (CRITERION = GENANISO) yield condition is selected, the yield
stresses for each stress component are taken from the stress - plastic strain relation
of the material, see $PLASTIC data block, page 3-1265 ff., therefore no data lines are
needed, and parameter INPUT and DEP are ignored. Different yield limits for tension and
compression are taken into account.
11. The yield limits may be temperature-dependent. If in a static analysis with nonlinear material behavior the load contains element temperatures (data blocks $DISLOAD etc, see
page 3-581 ff.), then the temperatures to evaluate temperature-dependent material data
are taken from the element loads, else the corresponding constant element temperature
state is defined within the system variant by data blocks $ELSTATE TEMP, see page
3-440, and system variant parameter COMPTEMP, see page 3-549.
12. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is
used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside
the table definition range.
13. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
14. Temperature-dependent data may be described by a user supplied function, i.e. by a
FORTRAN subroutine. The subroutine call is given by
CALL MUYIEL (MATNAM,NOFDEP,ZVEC,NODATA,IDRREQ,DATA,DERIV,IRC)

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-1307

Homogen.
Material

8. If v.Mises (CRITERION = VMISES), Tresca (CRITERION = TRESCA), pressure modified
v.Mises (CRITERION = PMVMISES) or cast iron (CRITERION = CASTIRON) yield condition is selected, the yield limit equals the yield stress already defined in the stress plastic strain relation of the material, see $PLASTIC data block, page 3-1265 ff. . Therefore no data lines are needed, and parameter INPUT and DEP are ignored. The flow rule
is always associated, i.e. the flow direction is normal to the yield surface.

$DAMPING

3 Data Input (DAT)

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of structural damping by a $DAMPING data block is allowed within the
definition of one material.
2. Structural damping is understood as a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not depend
on the degree of anisotropy of the material.
3. Structural damping within material description yields complex elemental stiffness matrices
of the form
K̄ E = (1 + igE (f ))K E
with the (optional) frequency-dependent elemental damping factor gE (f ).

Sandwich
Material

4. Elemental structural damping may be used for direct or modal frequency response analysis and any other analysis in frquency domain. For use in time domain, e.g. for transient
response analysis, it is converted to equivalent viscous damping by
Dg,E =

gE (fE )
KE
2πfE

The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by parameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.
5. Frequency-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is used
within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside the
table definition range.
6. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
Example:
$SANDWICH NAME=STA_325
$DAMPING
0.02
$END SANDWICH
$SANDWICH NAME=A2390
$DAMPING INPUT=TABLE
0.02 : 0.0
0.03 : 10.0
0.05 : 20.0
$END SANDWICH

6. If data are temperature-dependent, total thermal expansion coefficients are expected describing thermal expansion from reference temperature Tref , which is defined by parameter REFTEMP on header line, to actual temperature T . The thermal strain is than calculated according to

on header line.

Remarks:
1. Material names must be unique. No default exists.
As sole exception, PERMAS accepts repeated input of identical material definitions. That
is, material name and material properties must be identical in this case.
2. There are two ways available to describe a laminated material
• If DESTYPE = PLY is specified, the laminate is defined by the complete description
of each ply, see data block $PLY, page 3-1353 ff.. The properties of the laminate
are derived internally according to an extension of classical laminate theory.Material
damping, however, may be input for the laminate.
• If DESTYPE = MATRIX is specified, integrated values are expected describing the
laminate properties. Consequently, ply-dependent results, e.g. stresses within one
ply, are not available.
• A mixture of PLY and MATRIX description for one material is not possible.
3. Laminates are always handled as anisotropic with monoclinic behavior (see page 8-1),
even if the material itself is isotropic. Therefore a material reference system must be
defined for all elements with laminated material by a $MATREF data block, see page
3-527 ff..

$DAMPING

Remarks:

2. If description type PLY is specified, damping input for the laminate, if any, is used. If not
specified, damping is derived from the description of the ply materials.
3. Structural damping is understood as a scalar quantity. Nevertheless since laminated
material is always handled as anisotropic, the orientation of the material axes has to be
defined by a material reference system within system variant input, see $MATREF on
page 3-527.
4. Structural damping within material description yields complex elemental stiffness matrices
of the form
K̄ E = (1 + igE (f ))K E
with the (optional) frequency-dependent elemental damping factor gE (f ).
5. Elemental structural damping may be used for direct or modal frequency response analysis and any other analysis in frquency domain. For use in time domain, e.g. for transient
response analysis, it is converted to equivalent viscous damping by
Dg,E =

gE (fE )
KE
2πfE

The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by parameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.
6. Frequency-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is used
within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside the
table definition range.
7. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
Example:
$LAMINATE NAME=LAM_432 DESTYPE=MATRIX
$DAMPING
0.02
$END LAMINATE
$LAMINATE NAME=A2390 DESTYPE=MATRIX
$DAMPING INPUT=TABLE DEP=FREQ
0.02 : 0.0
0.03 : 10.0
0.05 : 20.0
$END LAMINATE

3-1353

$PLY

3 Data Input (DAT)

Remarks:
1. Description of laminate materials by plies is possible only within $LAMINATE brackets
where description type PLY is specified.

Laminated
Material

2. Each data line describes one ply of the laminate, starting at lower surface. According
to the specified treatment as shell, membrane or shear-carrying core, the referenced
material must be capable to deliver the material stiffness matrix for plane stress analysis
Q and/or the transverse shear stiffness matrix C ts , see page 3-1203.
3. If ASYM is specified, the laminate is assumed to be asymmetric, and each ply has to be
described.
4. If SYM or ANTI is specified, a symmetric or antisymmetric resp. laminate is assumed,
and only the lower half of the laminate has to be described whereas parameter NPLY
must contain the total number of plies. For an even number of plies nof ply/2 data lines
are expected, for a symmetric laminate with an odd number of plies (nof ply + 1)/2 data
lines, including the description of the middle ply.
5. The resulting laminated material contains all material properties which are defined for
each homogeneous material referenced in the ply description. Dependency of ply material on temperature or frequency is not yet supported.
6. The thickness of the laminate is the sum of all ply thicknesses, and must be greater than
zero. Single plies with thickness = 0 may be used to evaluate interlaminar shear stresses.
7. The stiffness of each ply may be reduced to membrane or transverse shear stiffness only.
The complete laminate, however, must be able to carry all kind of loads.
Example:
$PLY ASYM
CFRP_1
CFRP_1
CFRP_2

NPLY=3
2.0
0.0
3.0 90.0
1.0
0.0

$PLY SYM
EPE_10
FOAM_2

NPLY=3
1.0
6.0

4. If data are temperature-dependent, total thermal expansion coefficients are expected describing thermal expansion from reference temperature Tref , which is defined by parameter REFTEMP on header line, to actual temperature T . The thermal strain is than calculated according to
εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )

with T0 as the (element) temperature where the thermal strain is zero. The element
temperatures T0 are defined within the loading variant for each loading case with thermal
loads by $REFVAL TEMP data blocks, see page 3-872, and loading variant parameter
REFTEMP, see page 3-852.
Loading variant parameter REFTEMP must not be mixed up with parameter REFTEMP
on header line.

T . Linear interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary
values are used outside the table definition range.
6. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

Remarks:
1. Material names must be unique. No default exists.
As sole exception, PERMAS accepts repeated input of identical material definitions. That
is, material name and material properties must be identical in this case.
2. For definition of degree of anisotropy types see material description, page 8-1.
3. The degree of anisotropy is a basic property of the material to be defined. Therefore all
subsequent data blocks must contain data lines according to the degree of anisotropy
selected.
4. Since for gasket elements the material reference system is derived from the element system, the element system must be defined by an $ELSYS data block in the $STRUCTURE
bracket, see page 3-97, the material reference system itself, however, must not be specified.
5. The material 1-direction coincides always with the e3 -direction (through-the-thickness direction) of the element system.
6. Material definition bracket is closed by an (optional) $END GASKET line or by a new
material definition bracket line or by any high level bracket line.

$DAMPING

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of structural damping by a $DAMPING data block is allowed within the
definition of one material.

3. Structural damping within material description yields complex elemental stiffness matrices
of the form
K̄ E = (1 + igE (f ))K E
with the (optional) frequency-dependent elemental damping factor gE (f ).
4. Elemental structural damping may be used for direct or modal frequency response analysis and any other analysis in frquency domain. For use in time domain, e.g. for transient
response analysis, it is converted to equivalent viscous damping by
Dg,E =

gE (fE )
KE
2πfE

The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by parameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.
5. Frequency-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is used
within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside the
table definition range.
6. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
Example:
$GASKET NAME=STA_325
$DAMPING
0.02
$END GASKET
$GASKET NAME=A2390
$DAMPING INPUT=TABLE
0.02 : 0.0
0.03 : 10.0
0.05 : 20.0
$END GASKET
