3.4 Material Data

$GSKLOAD

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of loading behavior by an $GSKLOAD data block is allowed within the
definition of one material.

3. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic behavior. For gasket material, however, only transversely isotropic material is
available.
4. The material system axes are defined by the element geometry, i.e. the first material
direction is given by the normal to the mean plane of the element. Therefore, a material
reference system must not be defined.
5. The sequence of dependencies specified by parameter DEP on the header line determines the sequence of independent variable values on data lines.
6. Loading behavior of gasket elements is valid only for deformation in the first material
direction (the normal to the mean plane of the element), therefore it is a scalar function.
It is described as pressure on the gasket material for the loading process, depending on
deformation and, optionally, on temperature. The relation is given by
pL = f(dn , T )
where
pL

If loading and unloading behavior are different, the corresponding unloading behavior
must be defined within a $GSKUNLOAD data block, see pages 3-1377 ff. . Furthermore,
the corresponding elastic behavior for the remaining material directions must be defined
within a $ELASTIC data block, see pages 3-1369 ff. .
7. If by parameter FACTOR a scaling factor is specified, then the pressure input values pL
are scaled by factor fs .
8. Reaching the maximum deformation (dn )max , no further compression of the gasket material is possible; internally it is handled as a closed contact, see figure F3-42. If, however,
MAXDEFX is not specified, the maximal given deformation value is used.

3.4 Material Data

$HEATCAP

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of heat capacity by a $HEATCAP data block is allowed within the
definition of one material.

3. Temperature-dependent heat capacity is available only in single or top components.
4. If a linear analysis is performed, temperature-dependent material data are evaluated at
the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER COMPTEMP.
5. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions. Linear interpolation is
used within the table to determine function values, and boundary values are used outside
the table definition range.
6. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

$GASKET NAME=STA202 TYPE=TRANS
$HEATCAP
0.2E-3
$END GASKET

$HEATCAP INPUT=TABLE DEP=TEMP

$END GASKET

$THERMEXP

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of thermal expansion behavior by an $THERMEXP data block is allowed within the definition of one material.

3. Different material property types mattype allow for user convenient description of anisotropic behavior. For gasket material, however, only transversely isotropic material is
available.
4. The material system axes are defined by the element geometry, i.e. the first material
direction is given by the normal to the mean plane of the element. Therefore, a material
reference system must not be defined.
5. The general three dimensional thermal expansion matrix α for transversely isotropic material is defined by

6. If data are temperature-dependent, total thermal expansion coefficients are expected describing thermal expansion from reference temperature Tref , which is defined by parameter REFTEMP on header line, to actual temperature T . The thermal strain is than calculated according to
εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )

with T0 as the (element) temperature where the thermal strain is zero. The element
temperatures T0 are defined within the loading variant for each loading case with thermal
loads by $REFVAL TEMP data blocks, see page 3-872, and loading variant parameter
REFTEMP, see page 3-852.
Loading variant parameter REFTEMP must not be mixed up with parameter REFTEMP
on header line.

7. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions of the actual temperature
T . Linear interpolation is used within the table to determine function values, and boundary
values are used outside the table definition range.
8. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

Type

Explanation

R

Fluid material compressibility, see remark 2.

Remarks:
1. Only one definition of fluid compressibility by an $COMPRESS data block is allowed within
the definition of one material.
2. Fluid compressibility is always a scalar quantity. It is the reciprocal of the bulk modulus
K, which is related to the speed of sound c by
K = ρf c2
For an incompressible fluid, the velocity of sound and the bulk modulus are infinite, thus
the compressibility K1 is zero.
Example:
$FLUID NAME = AIR_0
$COMPRESS
7.37E-6
$END FLUID

pressure ṗ according to
u̇n = sc p + sk ṗ
3. Local fluid boundary absorption in a frequency response analysis with pure harmonic

Zn (Ω) = ZR (Ω) + i ZI (Ω) =

Remarks:

2. Structural damping is understood as a scalar quantity, therefore the input does not depend
on the degree of anisotropy of the material.
3. Structural damping within material description yields complex elemental stiffness matrices
of the form
K̄ E = (1 + igE (f ))K E
with the (optional) frequency-dependent elemental damping factor gE (f ).
4. Elemental structural damping may be used for direct or modal frequency response analysis and any other analysis in frquency domain. For use in time domain, e.g. for transient
response analysis, it is converted to equivalent viscous damping by
Dg,E =

gE (fE )
KE
2πfE

The reference frequency fE must be defined within the selected system variant by parameter RFREQE, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.

table definition range.

more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

6. Tabular values are sorted internally, therefore they may be input in any order. Jumps, i.e.
more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.
Example:
$FLFSOLID NAME=PIPE
$ELASTIC
2.1E11
0.3
$END FLFSOLID

Remarks:

Fluid

Material

3. If data are temperature-dependent, total thermal expansion coefficients are expected describing thermal expansion from reference temperature Tref , which is defined by parameter REFTEMP on header line, to actual temperature T . The thermal strain is than calculated according to
εϑ = α (T ) (T − Tref ) − α (T0 ) (T0 − Tref )

with T0 as the (element) temperature where the thermal strain is zero. The element
temperatures T0 are defined within the loading variant for each loading case with thermal
loads by $REFVAL TEMP data blocks, see page 3-872, and loading variant parameter
REFTEMP, see page 3-852.
Loading variant parameter REFTEMP must not be mixed up with parameter REFTEMP
on header line.

4. Temperature-dependent data may be input as tabular functions of the actual temperature

values are used outside the table definition range.

more than one function value for the same argument, are not allowed.

DAT
Shape

Remarks:
1. Edge labels must be unique within one geometry.
2. An edge (if not degenerated, see remark 5) is a parametric space curve C(t) ∈ R3 that is
bounded by vertex1 and vertex2 with coordinates V1 , V2 ∈ R3 and corresponding parameter values t1 6= t2 . The tangential vectors C ′ (t) establish the orientation of the edge.
3. TYPE = PARAMETRIC defines an edge with a general parametric space curve fc3d ,
optionally subject to a coordinate transformation defined by rule trule :
fc3d (t) −→ C(t) ,

t ∈ [tS , tE ]

where tS := min{t1 , t2 } and tE := max{t1 , t2 }. The parameters t1 and t2 must lie in the
possibly trimmed (see $FUNCTION CURVE3D, remark 13) definition range Ω of fc3d (t).
Additionally, for periodic curves (i.e. circles and ellipses) the range |t2 − t1 | must not
exceed the period length 2π. To form a closed edge, both vertices must be the same (and
not only have the same coordinates), but with different curve parameters. To be a valid
parametric edge, the relations
kC(t1 ) − V1 k ≤ tol1

and kC(t2 ) − V2 k ≤ tol2

must be fulfilled, where tol1 and tol2 are the corresponding vertex representation tolerances (see $VERTEX, remark 3) or the tolerance given by the global TOLGEO parameter.
4. TYPE = LINE defines an edge with a straight line between the vertices:
C(t) = V1 + t · (V2 − V1 ) ,

t ∈ [0, 1]

The vertices vertex1 and vertex2 must be different.
5. TYPE = DEGENERATE defines an edge, that degenerates to a singular vertex vertex
with coordinates V , that is
C(t) = V
for arbitrary values of t. A degenerated edge has no orientation and resides e.g. on the
apex of a cone, the pole of a sphere or any other surface singularity.

$EDGE

DAT

6. Edges referred by parametric faces have alternative representations, namely as plane
curves in parameter space of surfaces ($FACE), that may result in slightly deviating coordinates. This deviation normally must not exceed the tolerance given by the global
TOLGEO parameter. To allow for tolerant modeling for edges with known issues, an enlarged tolerance may be defined in its data line. The tolerance value for an edge should
not exceed the tolerance value of its vertices. Otherwise the smallest vertex tolerance
value will be used for the edge.

Remarks:
1. Face labels must be unique within one geometry.
2. A face is a parametric surface S(u, v) ∈ R3 that is bounded by at least one (outer) closed
loop of edges edgei with space curves Ci (t) ∈ R3 and corresponding plane curves in
(u, v)-parameter space Pi (t) ∈ R2 . The surface normal directions

3. TYPE = PARAMETRIC defines an face with a general parametric surface fsurf , optionally subject to a coordinate transformation defined by rule trule :
fsurf (u, v) −→ S(u, v) ,

(u, v) ∈ D

The domain D is bounded by at least one outer closed loop of edges edgei resp. their representation as plane curves Pi (t) with bounding parameters t̃1,i and t̃2,i , and optional further inner closed loops representing holes. They must lie entirely in the possibly trimmed
definition range (see $FUNCTION SURFACE, remark 15) definition range Ωu × Ωv of
fsurf (u, v) and may not intersect itself or each other. Non-degenerate edges may be
runned through at most two times, but then in reverse directions (e.g. seam edges of a
cylindrical surface). Degenerate edges may be runned through only one time, and must
only have non-degenerate edges as neighbours.
In the list(s) of edges the specification of fc2d,i , t̃1,i , t̃2,i is
• mandatory for a parametric or line edge (index i omitted in the following). The bounds
t̃1 and t̃2 must lie in the possibly trimmed (see $FUNCTION CURVE2D, remark 12)
definition range of fc2d (t). To be a valid parametric edge, the relations
kS(P (t̃1 )) − V1 k ≤ tol1

and kS(P (t̃2 )) − V2 k ≤ tol2

must be fulfilled, where V1 resp. V2 are the coordinates of edge vertices, and tol1
resp. tol2 are the corresponding vertex representation tolerances (see $VERTEX,
remark 3) or the tolerance given by the global TOLGEO parameter.

t ∈ [0, 1]

Remarks:
1. Shell labels must be unique within one geometry.
2. All faces of the shell must be connected, that is, starting with the first face, each must
must be visitable by crossing edges ($EDGE) adjacent to two faces.

DAT
Shape

3. The set of faces must be a manifold, that is, each edge must not be referred by more then
two faces.
4. The set of faces must be orientable, that is, it must be possible to define a common
frontside for all faces of the shell without any contradiction between to adjacent faces. For
iorient = 1 the frontside of the shell coincides with frontside (see $FACE, remark 2) of the
first face (or single face for RULE = ALL) in the dataline, otherwise this is the backside.
5. If all edges referred by faces of a shell are adjacent to exactly two faces (or two times in
opposite direction to the same face for seam edges), the shell is closed. Closed shells
may be referred by a $SOLID.
6. Faces (and also their edges and vertices) may be referred by an arbitrary number of
shells.
7. The COLOR parameter defines a default color for visualization purposes. For details on
color values please refer to remark 5 on page 3-207.

$ECHO

Echo Print Control
Controls the echo print of PERMAS data input lines.

$ECHO



OFF



HEADER


ON



 GEN 







1. $ECHO lines may appear anywhere and as often as needed in the data input stream.
2. If ECHO is set to OFF printout of lines is suppressed.
3. If ECHO is set to HEADER only header and bracket lines are printed.
4. If ECHO is set to ON all input lines are printed.
5. If ECHO is set to GEN all generated lines are printed in addition.
6. The default may be set by the default parameter ECHO (see page 2-68).
7. If an error is detected during the input the erroneous line is printed in any case. If the
erroneous line is a data line and ECHO is set to OFF, the corresponding data block header
line is printed in addition.
8. In some cases the error message may appear before the echo-print of the erroneous line.
This is not possible if ECHO is set to ON or GEN.
9. $ECHO lines cannot have any continuation lines, they are always restricted to one physical line.

$COMMENT

3 Data Input (DAT)

Short Comment
Input of a short comment on one line
$COMMENT

Parameter

text

Type

Value

Explanation

text

text

Text of short comment in quotation marks.

DAT
Misc

Remarks:
1. Each $COMMENT line defines exactly one comment which belongs to the current environment, i.e. to the current component, variant, data type, material etc..
2. Comments by $COMMENT lines are available up to now for components, variants, situations, sets, geometrical data records, materials, material properties and general functions.
3. $COMMENT lines may not appear within a $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket or within a
logical line, i.e. between a physical line and its continuation line.

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

3-1443

$DEFVAR

3 Data Input (DAT)

Remarks:
1. $DEFVAR lines may appear anywhere and as often as needed in the data input stream,
but not within a $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket and not within a logical line, e.g between a
physical line and its continuation line.
2. Input variables used within a $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket must be defined before the
$LOOP statement.
3. Input variables with fixed integer index (e.g. VARNAM(3)) may be used, after its definition,
anywhere in the current data input stream as constant items but not in the logical input
line immediately after its definition.

DAT
Misc

4. If generation is selected, the variable values of type integer, real or double precision are
generated according to
x(i) = xS + (i − 1) ∗ xI
For name and text values, an integer value is generated according to
k(i) = kS + (i − 1) ∗ kI
and appended to the constant name part cpname, i.e. the generated name/text is given
by
name(i) =< cpname >< k(i) >
without blanks etc. between name part and number. In case of text variables, cpname
must be given in quotation marks.
5. $DEFVAR lines may have any number of continuation lines.
6. If KEEP = NO is specified, input variable definitions by $DEFVAR are valid only for the
current data input stream, including, however, data files added by a $INCLUDE (see
page 3-1444 ff.)-statement.
7. If KEEP = AUTO is specified (default), the $DEFVAR definition is kept global like KEEP=YES
as long as the definition is globally unique. However, if the same name is used in other
$DEFVAR statements with a different definition then KEEP=NO is applied (but identical
duplicates are still kept globally).
8. If KEEP = YES is specified, the $DEFVAR definition is global and valid for all subsequent
PERMAS data and UCI input streams. In addition, it may be used in corresponding UCIcommands by the help of self expanding format strings like ’%(defvar[name])’ (if the
same name is used in other $DEFVAR statements with a different definition an error will
be issued).
9. Gobal $DEFVAR definitions may be included, with identical definition, in all subsequent
PERMAS data and UCI input streams.

3-1444

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

Explanation
Name of loop variable (max. 12 significant characters).
Start value of loop variable.
Last value of loop variable, iE ≥ iS .

Remarks:
1. Each $LOOP line initializes a new data generation loop with a unique loop variable lpvar.
2. Each data generation loop must be closed by a $ENDLOOP line.
3. Data generation loops may be defined within the $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket of a higher
level data generation loop; up to 25 loop levels are supported.
4. $DEFVAR lines may not appear within a $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket.
5. A loop is executed iE − iS + 1-times where the loop variable is incremented by one at

0.0

0.0

Remarks:
1. A $IF line starts an IF . . . ENDIF construct.

3. If the logical expression on the $IF line is false, all input lines between $IF- and $ENDIF

4. IF . . . ENDIF constructs must not be nested.

Equal condition
Not equal condition
Greater or equal condition
Greater condition

For name or text operands only equal or not equal conditions are available. Comparison
of names is always done in uppercase representation.

4.1 General
The element description contains for each element following parts:
• Basic information about topology, geometry and discretisation.
• Geometrical data.
• Material properties.
• Specific properties for each available degree-of-freedom type:
– Degrees of freedom and specific description.
– Element-based results, e.g. stresses.

Some parts of the element description, which are common for most or all elements of a family,
are placed in the introduction to the element family, e.g. the precise definition of local element
systems or the summary of all applicable material input options.

4.2 Flange Elements
4.2

Flange Elements

Overview on Available Flange Elements:
2 Noded Straight Flange (Rod) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

4-8

FLA3

3 Noded Straight Flange (Rod) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-15

The flange elements are displacement models that are fully compatible with the membrane elements QUAM and TRIM. Their main application is thus the modelling of enforcements (flanges,
stringers, prestressing cables) in membrane shells and in plane stress problems.
Both elements have their cross section centroids aligned along a straight axis z’, on which the
elements nodes are also located.
Flange elements can carry loads only along their axis (no bending, torsion, or shear stiffness).
If a more general load-carrying capacity is needed, beam elements must be used instead.
Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the flange
elements may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed explicitly.
When flange elements are combined with other elements it is important that elements of the
same order are coupled:
• FLA2 elements are compatible with the edges of HEXE8, PENTA6, PYRA5, QUAD4,
QUAM4, SHEAR4, TET4, TRIA3 and TRIM3.
• FLA3 elements are compatible with straight edges of HEXE20, HEXE27, PENTA15,
PENTA18, TET10, QUAM8, QUAM9 and TRIM6 if the inner node of the edge is at midpoint position.
Flange elements may have, according to their nature, only homogeneous isotropic material,
therefore a homogeneous material has to be defined with TYPE = ISO (default). The appropriate material property type is GENERAL, but SHELL and PLANE, if existent, are accepted in
addition. All applicable material input options for flange elements are summarized in the following table:

element.
Method:

Calculation in one (central) Gauss–Point. All nodal points will have
identical values.

Printed field quantities:

In the nodal points.

4.3

Membrane Elements

Overview on Available Membrane Elements:
QUAM4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Plane Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-26

QUAM8

8 Noded Quadrilateral Plane Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-34

QUAM9

9 Noded Quadrilateral Plane Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-43

SHEAR4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Plane Shear Panel Element . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-52

TRIM3

3 Noded Triangular Plane Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-57

TRIM6

6 Noded Triangular Plane Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-65

Membrane elements can carry loads only within their reference plane (no bending). Quadrilateral elements are mapped into that plane, therefore corner nodes don’t have to be exactly
coplanar. When a more general load-carrying capacity is needed, shell elements must be used
instead. Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the
membrane elements may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
explicitly.
When membrane elements are combined with flange elements it is important that elements of
the same order are coupled:
• FLA2 elements are compatible with the edges of TRIM3 and QUAM4.
• FLA3 elements are compatible with straight edges of QUAM8, QUAM9 and TRIM6, if the
inner node of the edge is at midpoint position.
The local element system for triangular elements is defined as follows:
1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.
2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.
3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.
For quadrilateral elements the local element system is defined in the following way:
1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4-21

Membrane
Elements

The membrane elements are displacement models that are, straight element edges assumed,
fully compatible with the flange elements FLA.

4 Element Atlas
2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
corner node).
3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.
4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
the reference surface.

Definition of local element systems, element corner nodes Ci and element edges Ei for

The membrane elements as currently available are implemented for plane stress analysis, the
appropriate material property type is PLANE. The material is assumed to be homogeneous,
and may be isotropic, orthotropic or anisotropic (i.e. monoclinic). Plane strain analysis is
possible by defining the material as anisotropic (TYPE = ANISO) and input of the corresponding
material stiffness matrix for plane strain, as described on page 8-13 ff..
Since, by a matter of principle, material input data from all material property types are accepted
as far as possible, beside PLANE the property types GENERAL and SHELL, if existent, may be
used in addition. All applicable material input options for membrane elements are summarized
in the following table:

QUAM4

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:
Plane first order displacement model with bilinear displacement field, carrying loads
only within its reference plane. No stiffness normal to element surface. Unless the
element is sufficiently supported by adjacent elements or constraints, it will introduce redundant degrees of freedom which must be suppressed explicitly.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at Gauss points, extrapolated to nodes.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes
Printed element stresses: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ ) at all nodes
isotropic material: referred to element system
anisotropic material: referred to material system

∇t A, B, H, E, D, J, ρ.

will be Zero, since the second derivative of the scalarpotential is Null in a (bi–) linear
element.
Method:

Membrane
Elements

identical values.

Stored in books xxxx.POTE: In the nodal points.
Printed field quantities:

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:
Plane second order isoparametric displacement model with incomplete biquadratic
displacement field and curved edges, carrying loads only within its reference plane.
No stiffness normal to element surface. Unless the element is sufficiently supported
by adjacent elements or constraints, it will introduce redundant degrees of freedom
which must be suppressed explicitly.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at Gauss points, extrapolated to nodes.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes
Printed element stresses: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ ) at all nodes
isotropic material: referred to element system
anisotropic material: referred to material system

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:
Plane first order displacement model with linear displacement field, carrying loads
only within its reference plane. No stiffness normal to element surface. Unless the
element is sufficiently supported by adjacent elements or constraints, it will introduce redundant degrees of freedom which must be suppressed explicitly.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at Gauss points, extrapolated to nodes.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes
Printed element stresses: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ ) at all nodes
isotropic material: referred to element system
anisotropic material: referred to material system
Averaged nodal stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes

4.3 Membrane Elements

TRIM3

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type POTE:
Degrees of Freedom:

(Ax , Ay , Az , φ) at each node

General Description:
Plane first order isoparametric potential model with linear potential field.

Field Quantities:
See page 1-24 for general description of available electromagnetic field quantities.
The element is capable to calculate the following field quantities :
∇t A, B, H, E, D, J, ρ.

For ELECTROstatic and STEADY ELECTRIC CURRENT problems the electric charge
will be Zero, since the second derivative of the scalarpotential is Null in a (bi–) linear
element.
Method:

Calculation in one (central) Gauss–Point. All nodal points will have
identical values.

Printed field quantities:

In the nodal points.

Stored in books xxxx.POTE: In the nodal points.

4 Noded Solid Tetrahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-142

TET10

10 Noded Solid Tetrahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-150

The solid elements can be classified with respect to their geometry or the order of their shape
functions. In terms of geometry there are four types of elements:
• The Brick elements HEXE8, HEXFO8 HEXE20 and HEXE27.
• The Wedge elements PENTA6, PENTA15 and PENTA18.
• The Tetrahedron elements TET4, and TET10.
• The Pyramid element PYRA5.
Although tetrahedron elements are sufficient to mesh any geometry, better results are obtained
when brick elements are used whenever possible, restricting the use of wedges, tetrahedrons
and pyramids to those parts of the mesh where they cannot be avoided.
In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified:
• Elements with linear shape functions: HEXE8, HEXFO8, PENTA6, TET4 and PYRA5.
• Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: HEXE20 and PENTA15.
• Elements with quadratic shape functions: HEXE27, PENTA18 and TET10.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4-73

Solid
Elements

Overview on Available Solid Elements:

4 Element Atlas
The element with the same order of shape function are fully compatible with each other whenever they match face to face. When the faces do not match completely (e.g. when two triangles
are mated with a quadrilateral), the full kinematic compatibility is lost.
All solid elements carry 3 displacement degrees of freedom per node. At times it may be physically meaningful to combine solid elements with other elements (e.g. FLA, TRIM or QUAM),
taking into account that at the connections there may be severe discontinuities resulting in
distorted stress patterns.
For the combination of solid and shell elements a volume shell transition using interpolation
regions is recommended (see page 3-150, 3-155 or 3-163 ).
For all solid elements, the positive face normal is directed outwards and does not depend on
the sequence of corner nodes of the face.

Elements

Solid elements have general linear homogeneous material, therefore the appropriate material
input type is GENERAL. The material may be isotropic or anisotropic, whereby transversely
isotropic, orthotropic, monoclinic and triclinic or general anisotropic material behavior is available. Beside GENERAL the material property types PLANE and SHELL, if existent, may be
used in addition for the definition of isotropic material. All applicable material input options for
solid elements are summarized in the following table:

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type POTE:

Degrees of Freedom:

(Ax , Ay , Az , φ) at each node

General Description:
First order electromagnetic element with trilinear potential field.

Field Quantities:
See page 1-24 for general description of available electromagnetic field quantities.
The element is capable to calculate the following field quantities :
∇t A, B, H, E, D, J, ρ.

For ELECTROstatic and STEADY ELECTRIC CURRENT problems the electric charge
will be Zero, since the second derivative of the scalarpotential is Null in a (bi–) linear
element.
Method:

Calculation in one (central) Gauss–Point. All nodal points will have
identical values.

Stored in books xxxx.POTE: In the nodal points.
Printed field quantities:

In the nodal points.

HEXE20

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:
Second order isoparametric displacement model with incomplete triquadratic displacement field (serendipity element). Not suited for contact analysis, since due to
’serendipity’ interpolation the resulting nodal forces for a constant pressure load on
an element face are positive at corner nodes but negative at midside nodes.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at Gauss points, extrapolated to nodes.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes
Printed element stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes
Averaged nodal stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes

Element Loads:
See page 3-581 for general description of input of distributed loads defined at elements by
$DISLOAD, page 3-693 for general description of distributed loads defined at structural nodes
by $DISLOADN and page 3-765 for general description of distributed loads defined at surfaces
by $DISLOADS.

(Ax , Ay , Az , φ) at each node

General Description:

PENTA6

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type POTE:

Degrees of Freedom:

(Ax , Ay , Az , φ) at each node

General Description:
First order electromagnetic element with linear-bilinear potential field.

Field Quantities:
See page 1-24 for general description of available electromagnetic field quantities.
The element is capable to calculate the following field quantities :
∇t A, B, H, E, D, J, ρ.

For ELECTROstatic and STEADY ELECTRIC CURRENT problems the electric charge
will be Zero, since the second derivative of the scalarpotential is Null in a (bi–) linear
element.
Method:

Calculation in one (central) Gauss–Point. All nodal points will have
identical values.

Stored in books xxxx.POTE: In the nodal points.
Printed field quantities:

In the nodal points.

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:
Second order isoparametric displacement model with incomplete quadratic-biquadratic
displacement field (serendipity element). Not suited for contact analysis, since due
to ’serendipity’ interpolation the resulting nodal forces for a constant pressure load
on an element face are positive at corner nodes but negative at midside nodes.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at Gauss points, extrapolated to nodes.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes
Printed element stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes
Averaged nodal stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes

Element Loads:
See page 3-581 for general description of input of distributed loads defined at elements by
$DISLOAD, page 3-693 for general description of distributed loads defined at structural nodes
by $DISLOADN and page 3-765 for general description of distributed loads defined at surfaces
by $DISLOADS.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type POTE:

Degrees of Freedom:

(Ax , Ay , Az , φ) at each node

General Description:
First order electromagnetic element with linear potential field.

Field Quantities:
See page 1-24 for general description of available electromagnetic field quantities.
The element is capable to calculate the following field quantities :
∇t A, B, H, E, D, J, ρ.

For ELECTROstatic and STEADY ELECTRIC CURRENT problems the electric charge
will be Zero, since the second derivative of the scalarpotential is Null in a (bi–) linear
element.
Method:

Calculation in one (central) Gauss–Point. All nodal points will have
identical values.

Stored in books xxxx.POTE: In the nodal points.
Printed field quantities:

In the nodal points.

4-150

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

4.4 Solid Elements

TET10

Remarks:
1. The integration scheme can be selected using the uci default key
DEFAULT SET QTETIPNT = CLASSIC (Default)
or
DEFAULT SET QTETIPNT = STANDARD
STANDARD uses only four integration points. This leads to some performance improvements, but means that the integration is exact only in the case of straight edges with each
mid node located in the center of its corner nodes.
However, for curved edges the integration is exact only with the default CLASSIC option (using ten integration points) and for parallel execution any STANDARD performance
improvements are negligible anyway.
2. The geometrical data for the element are optional.
3. The shown order of the element numbering is mandatory.

4.5 Beam Elements
4.5

Beam Elements

Overview on Available Beam Elements:
BECOS

2 Noded Straight Solid Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-172

BECOC

2 Noded Straight Thin-Walled Tube . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-178

BETAC

2 Noded Straight Tapered Thin-Walled Tube . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-184

BECOP

2 Noded Straight Thin-Walled Open Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-190

BETOP

2 Noded Straight Tapered Thin-Walled Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-196

BEAM2

2 Noded Straight General Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-202

BEAM2W

2 Noded Straight General Beam . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-209

FSCPIPE2

2 Noded Straight or Curved Fluid-Filled Pipe . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-216

Beam
Elements

The beam elements BECOS, BECOC, BETAC, BECOP and BETOP are formulated as equilibrium models, based on engineering theory of bending and St. Venant torsion. In addition, shear
effects in bending (BECOC, BETAC, BETOP) and torsion-bending (BECOP, BETOP) may be
included.
The beam elements BEAM2 and BEAM2W are Timoshenko beams with St. Venant torsion and
shear effects in bending, BEAM2W including torsion-bending in addition.
With the exception of the fluid filled pipe element FSCPIPE2, all beam elements have their
cross section centroids G aligned along a straight axis, and may have excentric nodes, i.e. offset vectors from node Pi to the corresponding centroid Gi .

Definition of local element system for beam elements
1. The z ′ -axis coincides with the beam axis (neutral axis), pointing from the center of gravity
G1 at node P1 to G2 at node P2 . For beam elements without offset the z ′ -axis is running
from node P1 to node P2 .
2. The z ′ x′ -plane is spanned by the z ′ -axis and the vector from centroid G1 to the reference
point P0 .
3. The x′ -axis, lying in the z ′ x′ -plane perpendicular to the z ′ -axis, is directed towards the
reference point P0 .
4. The y ′ -axis forms a right hand system with the z ′ - and the x′ -axis.

The beam elements with the exception of FSCPIPE2 have homogeneous material. It may be
isotropic or transversely isotropic, where Young’s modulus is used for bending and elongation,
and the shear modulus for torsion and shear deformation. The appropriate material property
type is BEAM, but GENERAL, SHELL and PLANE, if existent, are accepted in addition. All
applicable material input options are summarized in the following table:

Element Stresses
The calculation of element stresses is only possible, if information about the geometry of the
beam cross-sections is available, i.e. if standard beam cross sections are used. Only normal
stresses due to elongation and bending are taken into account, shear stresses, e.g. due to
torsional deformation, are completely ignored. For each cross section, normal stresses at four
different points are calculated, which are shown in the following pictures:

Stress Resultants

N

Normal force in direction of beam axis z ′ . Positive if beam is elongated.

Sx′

Shear force in x′ -direction, acting at shear center of cross-section. Positive at
node P1 if pointing into negative x′ -direction, and at node P2 if pointing into positive x′ -direction.

Sy ′

Shear force in y ′ -direction, acting at shear center of cross-section. Positive at
node P1 if pointing into negative y ′ -direction, and at node P2 if pointing into positive y ′ -direction.

Mx′

Bending moment about x′ -axis. Positive at node P1 if anti-parallel to x′ -axis, and
at node P2 if parallel to x′ -axis.

My′

Bending moment about y ′ -axis. Positive at node P1 if parallel to y ′ -axis, and at
node P2 if anti-parallel to y ′ -axis.
Twisting moment about z ′ -axis (beam axis). Positive at node P1 if anti-parallel to
z ′ -axis, and at node P2 if parallel to z ′ -axis.

T
B

Bimoment (only for BECOP, BETOP and BEAM2W).

pi

Pressure of inner fluid (only for FSCPIPE2).

Initial Deformations
In analogy to the stress resultants, the initial strains which can be specified for beam elements
are integrated quantities. They are able to produce virtual work on the stress resultants, and
can be understood as initial deformations referring to the local beam coordinate system:

Beam
Elements

δ

Elongation of the beam along z ′ -axis.

φx,1

Bending deformation of the beam axis at node P1 about x′ -axis.

φx,2

Bending deformation of the beam axis at node P2 about x′ -axis.

φy,1

Bending deformation of the beam axis at node P1 about y ′ -axis.

φy,2

Bending deformation of the beam axis at node P2 about y ′ -axis.

Total initial twist of the beam axis.

All initial deformations are pure elastic deformations, measured between the end cross-section
centroids G1 and G2 on the beam axis, relative to rigid body motion of the element as shown in

The initial elongation δ is positive if the beam is stretched. The initial bending deformations
φ can be interpreted as the initial slopes at the ends of a simply supported beam. They are
positive if produced by a pair of positive bending moments. The initial twist deformation θ is
the initial relative angle of twist and positive, if produced by a pair of positive twisting moments.
The sign conventions for the initial deformations thus are in agreement with those for the stress
resultants.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz ) at each node

General Description:
Equilibrium model: Tension, ETB, St.Venant torsion and shear effects in bending.
Optionally with rigid lever arms from nodal point to centroid of end cross section.

Stresses:
Method:

Direct evaluation of normal stresses at end cross section stress
points (for standard beam cross sections only, see page 4-167).

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σz ′ z ′ ,S1 , σz ′ z ′ ,S2 , σz ′ z ′ ,S3 , σz ′ z ′ ,S4 ) at both end cross sections
Printed element stresses: (σz ′ z ′ ,S1 , σz ′ z ′ ,S2 , σz ′ z ′ ,S3 , σz ′ z ′ ,S4 ) at both end cross sections
Averaged nodal stresses: Element ignored, no contribution.

Stress Resultants:
Method:

Direct evaluation of stress resultants at end cross sections, referring to local element system.

Stored in book RSFR.DISP: (N, Sx′ , Sy′ , Mx′ , My′ , T ) at both end cross sections

Beam
Elements

Printed stress resultants: (N, Sx′ , Sy′ , Mx′ , My′ , T ) at both end cross sections

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz , ϑ′ ) at each node
ϑ′ : Rate of twist along beam axis, degree of freedom
identifier 7.

General Description:
Equilibrium model: Tension, ETB, St.Venant torsion and torsion-bending interaction
(warping). No shear effects in bending. Optionally with rigid lever arms from nodal
point to centroid of end cross section.

Stresses:
Method:

Direct evaluation of normal stresses at end cross section stress
points (for standard beam cross sections only, see page 4-167).

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σz ′ z ′ ,S1 , σz ′ z ′ ,S2 , σz ′ z ′ ,S3 , σz ′ z ′ ,S4 ) at both end cross sections
Printed element stresses: (σz ′ z ′ ,S1 , σz ′ z ′ ,S2 , σz ′ z ′ ,S3 , σz ′ z ′ ,S4 ) at both end cross sections
Averaged nodal stresses: Element ignored, no contribution.

Stress Resultants:
Method:

Direct evaluation of stress resultants, including bimoment, at end
cross sections, referring to local element system.

Stored in book RSFR.DISP: (N, Sx′ , Sy′ , Mx′ , My′ , T, B) at both end cross sections

Beam
Elements

Printed stress resultants: (N, Sx′ , Sy′ , Mx′ , My′ , T, B) at both end cross sections

Definition of Element System:

beam elements is used, defined by the beam axis (neutral axis) and reference point

For curved elements (curvature 1/R > 0) it is assumed that the element lies within

reference point is inside of the curvature on the opposite side of the straight line
connecting the element nodes.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz , uf ) at each node
uf : Displacement of inner fluid along pipe axis, degree
of freedom identifier 8.

General Description:
Circular tube with constant ring cross section, filled with a compressible internal
fluid. The ends of the tube may be connected to other tubes, closed or open. Equilibrium model for tension, bending (Timoshenko beam), St.Venant torsion, transverse shear. Longitudinal stresses/strains due to internal pressure are included.
Linear interpolation for displacement of internal fluid along pipe axis. If the internal
fluid is omitted, the corresponding degree of freedom has to be suppressed.
The mass of the inner fluid is split up between the translational degree of freedom
of the fluid and the translational degrees of freedom of the structure normal to the
pipe axis. If an outer fluid is present, no degree of freedom is associated with that
fluid, but its mass is added to the translational degrees of freedom of the structure
normal to the pipe axis.

Stresses:
No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

Stress Resultants:
Method:

Direct evaluation of stress resultants, including pressure of inner
fluid, at end cross sections, referring to local element system.

Stored in book RSFR.DISP: (N, Sx′ , Sy′ , Mx′ , My′ , T, pi ) at both end cross sections
Printed stress resultants: (N, Sx′ , Sy′ , Mx′ , My′ , T, pi ) at both end cross sections

Shell Elements

Overview on Available Shell Elements:
QUAD4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-227

QUAD4S

4 Noded Quadrilateral Sandwich Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-234

4 Noded Quadrilateral Shell Element for Laminates . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-247

3 Noded Triangular Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-253

TRIA3K

3 Noded Triangular Thin Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-260

TRIA3S

3 Noded Triangular Sandwich Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-267

For the combination of solid and shell elements a volume shell transition using interpolation
regions is recommended (see page 3-150, 3-155 or 3-163 ).
The local element system for triangular elements is defined as follows:
1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.
2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.
3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.
For quadrilateral elements the local element system is defined in the following way:
1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.

3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.
4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
the reference surface.

2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
corner node).

4.6 Shell Elements
For homogeneous shell elements the material data describing elastic behavior are split into
data relating in-plane stresses and strains corresponding with tension and bending deformation,
and data which relate transverse shear stresses and strains. The material may be isotropic, orthotropic or anisotropic (i.e. monoclinic), the appropriate material property type is SHELL for
elastic material data, else PLANE. Since heat conduction perpendicular to the shell reference
plane is taken into account, the material for heat conduction may be triclinic or general anisotropic in addition, the appropriate material property type always being GENERAL. Beside SHELL
and PLANE, for isotropic material or scalar properties GENERAL may be used in addition. All
applicable material input options for homogeneous shell elements are summarized in the following table:

4 Element Atlas
For sandwich shell elements two sets of material data are necessary, one set describing the
behavior of cover plates (skins), and another describing core behavior. Therefore elastic data
are split into data relating in-plane stresses and strains corresponding with tension and bending
deformation, and data which relate core transverse shear stresses and strains. The material
may be isotropic, orthotropic or anisotropic (i.e. monoclinic), the appropriate material property
type is SHELL. Since heat conduction perpendicular to the shell reference plane is taken into
account, the material for heat conduction describes three-dimensional behavior, and may be
isotropic, orthotropic or triclinic (general anisotropic), the appropriate material property type
always being GENERAL. All applicable material input options for homogeneous shell elements
are summarized in the following table:

For shell elements with laminated material there are two different possibilities to define material
data. The first one is the description by plies, where for each ply of the laminate thickness,
orientation and reference to a homogeneous material has to be input, and the properties of the
laminate are derived internally. The second one is to describe laminate behavior by matrices
which contain quantities integrated over laminate thickness.

4-229

QUAD4

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz ) at each node

General Description:
Plane element with bilinear displacement field for membrane, linear bending moment along element edges and constant transverse shear forces. Warped elements
are handled by transformation into a plane reference configuration. Separation of
membrane and bending stiffness is possible. Suited for thin and thick shell applications. Artificial (small) stiffness for in-plane rotations. Optionally with rigid lever
arms from nodal point to corner of element middle surface.
Two additional formulations are available. Setting
DEFAULT SET LQUADSHAPE = QUAD4N
yields a formulation with modified membrane and bending stiffness whereas with
DEFAULT SET LQUADSHAPE = QUAD4R
a formulation is applied where the in-plane rotations are coupled to the membrane
displacement field.

Control of Stiffness Calculation
The parameter sep in the geometrical data input allows for separation of membrane
and bending stiffness:
sep = 0
Complete stiffness matrix is calculated (default).
sep = 1
Only bending and shear stiffness is calculated.
sep = 2
Only membrane stiffness is calculated.
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by
Kϕz ′ = (0.01 + c)KB
where KB is a mean bending stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by default
equals zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.01 means no
artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least
at one nodal point. This is no longer true if the modified formulation ’QUAD4R’ is
selected.

Elements

Calculated at center of element

maximum transverse shear stresses (σy′ z ′ , σx′ z ′ )
(σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ ) in lower surface
isotropic material: referred to element system
anisotropic material: referred to material system

SHELL3

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz ) at each node

General Description:
Plane element with linear displacement field for membrane, linear bending moment
along element edges and constant transverse shear forces. Separation of membrane and bending stiffness is possible. Suited for thin and moderate thick shell
applications. Artificial (small) stiffness for inplane rotations. Optionally with rigid
lever arms from nodal point to corner of element reference surface. Laminate middle surface and element reference surface may be separated.

Control of Stiffness Calculation
The parameter sep in the geometrical data input allows for separation of membrane
and bending stiffness:
sep = 0
Complete stiffness matrix is calculated (default).
sep = 1
Only bending and shear stiffness is calculated.
sep = 2
Only membrane stiffness is calculated.
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by
Kϕz ′ = (0.01 + c)KB
where KB is a mean bending stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by default
equals zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.01 means no
artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least at
one nodal point.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at center of element.
Available only for laminate description by plies.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ σy′ z ′ , σx′ z ′ ) in the middle surface of each ply,
referred to material system
Printed element stresses: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ σy′ z ′ , σx′ z ′ ) in the middle surface of each ply,
referred to material system

TRIA3K

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz ) at each node

General Description:
Plane element with linear displacement field for membrane, incomplete quartic displacement field for bending (Kirchhoff bending theory) and constant transverse
shear forces. Separation of membrane and bending stiffness is possible. Suited
only for thin shell applications. Artificial (small) stiffness for inplane rotations. Optionally with rigid lever arms from nodal point to corner of element middle surface.

Control of Stiffness Calculation
The parameter sep in the geometrical data input allows for separation of membrane
and bending stiffness:
sep = 0
Complete stiffness matrix is calculated (default).
sep = 1
Only bending and shear stiffness is calculated.
sep = 2
Only membrane stiffness is calculated.
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by
Kϕz ′ = (0.01 + c)KB
where KB is a mean bending stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by default
equals zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.01 means no
artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least at
one nodal point.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at center of element

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ ) in upper surface
maximum transverse shear stresses (σy′ z ′ , σx′ z ′ )
(σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ ) in lower surface
isotropic material: referred to element system
anisotropic material: referred to material system

Elements

maximum transverse shear stresses (σy′ z ′ , σx′ z ′ )
(σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σx′ y′ ) in lower surface
Von Mises equivalent stresses in upper and lower surface
isotropic material: referred to element system
anisotropic material: referred to material system

4.7 Solid Shell Elements
4.7

Solid Shell Elements

Overview on Available Solid Shell Elements:
QUAMS4

4 Node Quadrilateral Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-280

QUAMS8

8 Node Quadrilateral Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-286

QUAMS9

9 Node Quadrilateral Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-292

TRIMS3

3 Node Triangular Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-298

TRIMS6

6 Node Triangular Solid Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-304

The solid shell elements can be classified with respect to their geometry and order of their
shape functions. In terms of geometry there are two types of elements:
• The quadrilateral elements QUAMS4, QUAMS8 and QUAMS9.
• The triangular elements TRIMS3, TRIMS6.
In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified :
• Elements with linear shape functions: QUAMS4, TRIMS3.
• Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: QUAMS8.
• Elements with quadratic shape functions: QUAMS9, TRIMS6.
The element with the same order of shape function are fully compatible with each other whenever they match face to face. When the faces do not match completely (e.g. when two triangles
are mated with a quadrilateral), the full kinematic compatibility is lost.
All solid shell elements carry 7 degree of freedoms per node. Linear solid shell elements can
be combined with the linear shell elements TRIA3 and QUAD4.
For the combination of solid and shell elements a volume shell transition using interpolation
regions is recommended (see page 3-150, 3-155 or 3-163).
Lower and upper surface of solid shell elements are defined by the shell director which points
from the lower to the upper element surface. The shell director forms a right hand system
with the axes of the reference surface in the initial configuration at the nodal points. The shell
director varies over and is not necessarily perpendicular to the axes of the reference surface.
When common shell directors at the nodal points are used (DEFAULT SET CSHDIR = ON), the
shell directors of adjacent solid shell elements should have approximately the same direction.
The allowable kink angle is specified by DEFAULT SET CSHDIRKINK.

QUAMS4

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz , ∆t) at each node

General Description:
Element with straight edges, bilinear displacement field on reference surface and
linear displacement field across the thickness. Suited for thin and thick shell applications. Artificial (small) stiffness for inplane rotations.

Control of Stiffness Calculation
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by
Kϕz ′ = (0.001 + c)Krot
where Krot is a mean rotational stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by
default equal zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.001
means no artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least at
one nodal point.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at Gauss points on reference surface and at Lobatto
points through the thickness. Extrapolated to corner nodes.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx )
at all nodes with five layers through the thickness
first layer belongs to upper surface
third layer belongs to the reference surface
fifth layer belongs to lower surface
Printed element stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx )
at all nodes with five layers through the thickness
first layer belongs to upper surface
third layer belongs to the reference surface
fifth layer belongs to lower surface
Averaged nodal stresses: Element ignored, no contribution.

TRIMS3

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz , ∆t) at each node

General Description:
Element with straight edges, linear displacement field on reference surface and
across the thickness. Suited for thin and thick shell applications. Artificial (small)
stiffness for inplane rotations.

Control of Stiffness Calculation
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element, are provided with a small artificial stiffness, which is given by
Kϕz ′ = (0.001 + c)Krot
where Krot is a mean rotational stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by
default equal zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = −0.001
means no artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least at
one nodal point.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at center of reference surface and at Lobatto points
through the thickness. Submitted to corner nodes.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx )
at all nodes with five layers through the thickness
first layer belongs to upper surface
third layer belongs to the reference surface
fifth layer belongs to lower surface
Printed element stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx )
at all nodes with five layers through the thickness
first layer belongs to upper surface
third layer belongs to the reference surface
fifth layer belongs to lower surface
Averaged nodal stresses: Element ignored, no contribution.

4.8 Gasket Elements
Gasket Elements

Overview on Available Three–Dimensional Gasket Elements:
GKHEX8

8 Noded Solid Hexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-316

GKHEX20

20 Noded Solid Hexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-322

GKHEX27

27 Noded Solid Hexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-328

GKPNT6

6 Noded Solid Pentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-334

GKPNT15

15 Noded Solid Pentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-340

GKPNT18

18 Noded Solid Pentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-346

Three–dimensional Gasket Elements are used to model sealing components between structural components. The through–the–thickness behavior is uncoupled from membrane and
transverse shear behavior and is defined by a non–linear pressure/closure curve known from
test data. The nonlinearity can be elastic or plastic. Membrane and transverse shear behaviour
is linear elastic. There is no thermal expansion in through–the–thickness direction.
With the default settings (GSKSOLV = CONTACT) the gasket model corresponds to a membrane with decoupled non-linear springs.
γ

Schematic of a gasket element
The midsurface behaves like a membrane element with material parameters E and ν. Decoupled springs act in through-the-thickness direction at element edges with a nonlinear gasket
loading curve. The shear behavior of the springs corresponds to a shear modulus G with
τ = G tan γ.
Element specific results are GASKET CLOSURE and GASKET PRESSURE, which are created automatically.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4-311

Gasket
Elements

4.8

4 Element Atlas

Gasket
Elements

The Gasket elements can be classified with respect to their geometry or the order of their shape
functions. In terms of geometry there are two types of elements:
• The Brick elements GKHEX8, GKHEX20 and GKHEX27
• The Wedge elements GKPNT6, GKPNT15 and GKPNT18.
In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified:
• Elements with linear shape functions: GKHEX8 and GKPNT6.
• Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: GKHEX20 and GKPNT15.
• Elements with quadratic shape functions: GKHEX27 and GKPNT18.
Elements with the same order of shape function are fully compatible with each other whenever
they match face to face. When the faces do not match completely (e.g. when two triangles are
mated with a quadrilateral), the full kinematic compatibility is lost.
All Gasket elements carry 3 displacement degrees of freedom per node.
By default the through–the–thickness direction of the Gasket elements is orthogonal to the
midsurface between element faces 1 and 6 for the brick elements and element faces 1 and 5
for the wedge elements. For brick elements also another midsurface can be chosen by defining
an element system $ELSYS (see page 3-97 and remark 3) in the structure bracket. Then the
through–the–thickness is orthogonal to the midsurface which is orthogonal to the z’ axis of the
element system.
For all Gasket elements, the positive face normal is directed outwards and does not depend on
the sequence of corner nodes of the face.

partner.

body modes.

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Gasket
Elements

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:
Second order isoparametric displacement model with incomplete biquadratic displacement field (serendipity element). Not suited for contact analysis, since due to
’serendipity’ interpolation the resulting nodal forces for a constant pressure load on
an element face are positive at corner nodes but negative at midside nodes.

Stresses:
Method:

Calculated at Gauss points on midsurface, assigned to nodes.

Stored in book SIG.DISP: (σx′ x′ , σy′ y′ , σz ′ z ′ , σx′ y′ , σy′ z ′ , σz ′ x′ ) at all nodes
referred to element system
Printed element stresses: (σxx , σyy , σzz , σxy , σyz , σzx ) at all nodes
Averaged nodal stresses: Element ignored (no contribution)

Element Loads:
See page 3-581 for general description of input of distributed loads defined at elements by
$DISLOAD, page 3-693 for general description of distributed loads defined at structural nodes
by $DISLOADN and page 3-765 for general description of distributed loads defined at surfaces
by $DISLOADS.
Available Element Load Types:

If necessary, local element systems for spring elements are defined using three points R1 , R2
and R3 as follows:
1. The xR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .
2. The yR -axis is perpendicular to the xR -axis, pointing to the third point R3
3. The zR -axis forms a right hand system with the xR - and yR -axis.
4. The local element system (x′ , y ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (xR , yR , zR ) with
its origin at the first element node.

4.9 Spring Elements

For spring elements only stress resultants instead of stresses are available. They are calculated for both nodes, referring to the local element coordinate system (x′ y ′ z ′ ), and can be
easily interpreted as the forces acting on the element in order to produce the elastic deformations. The latter are represented by the difference of total element deformations and element
initial deformations. For SPRING1, SPRING3, NLSTIFF and NLSTIFFR elements corresponding stress resultants at both nodes are antivalent (equal magnitude, opposite direction), with
positive values at the second node for positive elastic elongations ∆ui = ui,P 2 − ui,P 1 .
In analogy to the stress resultants, the initial strains which can be specified for spring elements
are initial deformations, referring to the local element coordinate system:
δ1

Elongation along the x′ -axis.

δ2

Elongation along the y ′ -axis.

δ3

Elongation along the z ′ -axis.

δ4

Twist about the x′ -axis.

δ5

Twist about the y ′ -axis.

δ6

Twist about the z ′ -axis.

When all degrees of freedom at the first element node P1 are suppressed, a positive elongation
will move the second element node P2 in the direction of the corresponding local coordinate
axis, and a positive twist will rotate node P2 in a positive sense of rotation around the respective
local coordinate axis.

4.9 Spring Elements

NLSTIFF

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:

Fx′ = f (∆u′ )

with

∆u′ = u′P 2 − u′P 1

No stiffness with respect to transverse displacements or rotations. The nonlinear
force is split up into a linear and a nonlinear part according to
Fx′ = k ∆u′ + fnl (∆u′ )
where the constant value k is determined by the derivation of the nonlinear function
for ∆u′ = ulin
dFx′
k=
d(∆u′ ) ∆u′ =ulin
and included in the stiffness matrix, whereas the nonlinear part
fnl (∆u′ ) = Fx′ − k ∆u′
is added to the right-hand side of the dynamic equation in transient response analysis. Consequently, in statics, eigenmodes and frequency response analysis only
the linear part is taken into account.
Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the
element may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed explicitly.

Stresses:
No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

Stress Resultants:

4.9 Spring Elements

NLSTIFFR

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz ) at each node

General Description:

Mx′ = f (∆ϕ′ ),

with

∆ϕ′ = ϕ′P 2 − ϕ′P 1

Rotation is given in [rad]. No stiffness with respect to translations or rotations perpendicular to element axis. The nonlinear moment is split up into a linear and a
nonlinear part according to
Mx′ = kϕ ∆ϕ′ + fnl (∆ϕ′ )
where the constant value kϕ is determined by the derivation of the nonlinear function
for ∆ϕ′ = ϕlin
dMx′
kϕ =
d(∆ϕ′ ) ∆ϕ′ =ϕlin
and included in the stiffness matrix, whereas the nonlinear part
fnl (∆ϕ′ ) = Mx′ − kϕ ∆ϕ′
is added to the right-hand side of the dynamic equation in transient response analysis. Consequently, in statics, eigenmodes and frequency response analysis only
the linear part is taken into account.
Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the
element may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed explicitly.

Stresses:
No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

Stress Resultants:
Method:

Direct evaluation of element forces at nodes, referring to local element system.

Stored in book RSFR.DISP: (0 , 0 , 0 , Mx′ , 0 , 0) at both element nodes
Printed stress resultants: (0 , 0 , 0 , Mx′ , 0 , 0) at both element nodes

Element Loads:
No distributed loads available.

NLDAMP

Viscous Damper for Six Degrees of Freedom . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-425

X1DAMP3

Scalar Viscous Damper at One Node with Three Degrees of Freedom . . 4-428

X1DAMP6

Scalar Viscous Damper at One Node with Six Degrees of Freedom . . . 4-431

X2DAMP3

Scalar Viscous Damper at Two Nodes with Three Degrees of Freedom . 4-434

X2DAMP6

Scalar Viscous Damper at Two Nodes with Six Degrees of Freedom . . . 4-437

All available damper elements have viscous damping, i.e. their element forces depend on the
time derivative of the element deformations. Element structural damping, however, may be
represented using any type of linear ’stiffness’ element with material property $DAMPING.
If necessary, local element systems for damper elements are defined using three points R1 , R2
and R3 as follows:
1. The xR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .
2. The yR -axis is perpendicular to the xR -axis, pointing to the third point R3
3. The zR -axis forms a right hand system with the xR - and yR -axis.
4. The local element system (x′ , y ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (xR , yR , zR ) with
its origin at the first element node.

Definition of local element system for viscous damper elements

Damper
Elements

Viscous damper elements do not refer to any material property, therefore no material has to be
assigned.

Stress Resultants and Initial Deformations
For viscous damper elements only stress resultants are available. They are calculated for both
nodes, referring to the local element coordinate system (x′ y ′ z ′ ), and can be easily interpreted
as the forces acting on the element in order to produce the element deformation velocity. For
DAMP1, DAMP3, NLDAMP and NLDAMPR elements corresponding stress resultants at both
nodes are antivalent (equal magnitude, opposite direction), with positive values at the second
node for positive element deformation velocity ∆u̇i = u̇i,P 2 − u̇i,P 1 .

4.11 Damper Elements

NLDAMP

NLDAMP
Nonlinear Translational Viscous Damper
Nodes may have identical or different locations in space.

x’
P2

Damper
Elements

P1

Number of Nodes: 2
Coordinates:

Necessary for both nodes P1 and P2 , may be identical.

Discretisation:

Nonlinear force/velocity characteristic in direction of the damper axis.
No damping with respect to transverse displacements and rotations.

D. O. F. Types:

DISP

Definition of Element System:
Damper axis and local x′ -axis are always identical.
If the element nodes have different locations in space, the damper axis points from
node P1 to node P2 .
If the element nodes have identical coordinates, the local element system has to be
defined using three points, see page 4-411.

Remarks:
1. The element does not refer to any material property.
2. The nonlinear part of the element force is restricted to direct or modal transient response
analysis. For any other kind of linear analysis only the linearized element characteristic
(constant viscous damping coefficient) is taken into account.
3. Since the element has no temperature degrees of freedom, it is ignored in thermal analysis.

4.11 Damper Elements

NLDAMP

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:
Discrete equilibrium model with nonlinear force/velocity characteristic for elongation
along the spring axis:
Fx′ = f (∆u̇′ )

with

∆u̇′ = u̇′P 2 − u̇′P 1

The nonlinear force is split up into a linear and a nonlinear part according to
Fx′ = du ∆u̇′ + fnl (∆u̇′ )
where the constant value du is determined by the derivation of the nonlinear function
for ∆u̇′ = u̇lin
dFx′
du =

NLDAMPR
Nonlinear Rotational Viscous Damper
Nodes may have identical or different locations in space.

x’

P2

P1

Damper
Elements

Number of Nodes: 2
Coordinates:

Necessary for both nodes P1 and P2 , may be identical.

Discretisation:

Nonlinear force/velocity characteristic for rotation about the damper axis.
No damping with respect to translations and to rotations perpendicular to the
damper axis.

D. O. F. Types:

DISP

Definition of Element System:
Damper axis and local x′ -axis are always identical.
If the element nodes have different locations in space, the damper axis points from
node P1 to node P2 .
If the element nodes have identical coordinates, the local element system has to be
defined using three points, see page 4-411.

Remarks:
1. The element does not refer to any material property.
2. The nonlinear part of the element force is restricted to direct or modal transient response
analysis. For any other kind of linear analysis only the linearized element characteristic
(constant viscous damping coefficient) is taken into account.
3. Since the element has no temperature degrees of freedom, it is ignored in thermal analysis.

4.12 Viscoelastic Solid Elements
4.12

Viscoelastic Solid Elements

Overview on Available Viscoelastic Solid Elements:
HEXVE8

8 Noded Viscoelastic Solid Hexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-444

HEXVR8

8 Noded Viscoelastic Solid Hexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-448

Viscoelastic elements represent a Maxwell model, i.e. elastic and viscous part in series. The
submatrices of the elastic part are identical to the matrices of the corresponding solid elements,
i.e. for the HEXVE8 element the matrices of the HEXE8 element etc.. To achieve a generalized Maxwell or Biot model, one or more viscoelastic solid elements are added to one standard
(basic) solid element, forming a so-called Prony series. The standard translational degrees of
freedom of all those viscoelastic elements belonging to one basic element must be coupled,
either by identical element node lists (HEXVR8 elements) or coupled by MPCs (HEXVE8 elements). The non-standard degrees of freedom of HEXVE8 elements, representing the viscous
part, remain uncoupled.

Viscoelastic Solid
Elements

For all viscous solid elements, the positive face normal is directed outwards and does not
depend on the sequence of corner nodes of the face.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4.13

Load Carrying Membrane Elements

Overview on Available Load Carrying Membrane Elements :
LOADA4

4 Node Quadrilateral Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . 4-457

LOADA8

8 Node Quadrilateral Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . 4-460

LOADA9

9 Node Quadrilateral Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . 4-463

LOADA3

3 Node Triangular Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-466

LOADA6

6 Node Triangular Load Carrying Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-469

The load carrying membrane elements can be classified with respect to their geometry and
order of their shape functions. In terms of geometry there are two types of elements:
• The Quadrilateral elements LOADA4, LOADA8 and LOADA9.
• The Triangular elements LOADA3, LOADA6.
In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified :
• Elements with linear shape functions: LOADA3, LOADA4.
• Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: LOADA8.
• Elements with quadratic shape functions: LOADA6, LOADA9.
The element with the same order of shape function are fully compatible with each other whenever they match face to face. When the faces do not match completely (e.g. when two triangles
are mated with a quadrilateral), the full kinematic compatibility is lost.
All load carrying membrane elements have three degree of freedoms per node. They are used
solely for the definition of surface loads which act on solid elements. In addition they are able
to calculate the stresses on the boundary of solid elements, plain stress conditions assumed.
Hence evaluation of stresses on surfaces loaded by out-of-plane loads will give wrong results,
since the effect of stresses normal to the surface is ignored. In any case the material property
of the elements must be identical to the underlying solid elements. They do not contribute to
stiffness, damping or mass matrix.
• LOADA3 elements are compatible with the surfaces of TET4, PYRA5 and PENTA6.
• LOADA4 elements are compatible with the surfaces of PYRA5, PENTA6 and HEXE8.
• LOADA6 elements are compatible with the surfaces of TET10, PENTA15 and PENTA18.
• LOADA8 elements are compatible with the surfaces of PENTA15 and HEXE20.
• LOADA9 elements are compatible with the surfaces of HEXE27.

Definition of local element systems, element corner nodes Ci and element edges Ei for
triangular and quadrilateral membrane elements
For the print–out of stresses the local element system for triangular elements is defined as
follows:
1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.
2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.
3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.
For the print–out of stresses the local element system for quadrilateral elements is defined in
the following way:
1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.
2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
corner node).
3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.
4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
the reference surface.

If necessary, local element systems for special elements are defined using three points R1 , R2
and R3 as follows:
1. The xR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .
2. The yR -axis is perpendicular to the xR -axis, pointing to the third point R3
3. The zR -axis forms a right hand system with the xR - and yR -axis.
4. The local element system (x′ , y ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (xR , yR , zR ) with
its origin at the first element node.
