CONTROL3

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w, ϕx , ϕy , ϕz ) at each node

General Description:

Fx′ = f (xi ),

i = 1, n

with

1 ≤ n ≤ 18

where up to 18 of the element nodal point displacements or corresponding velocities
may be used as independent variables. Rotated node bases are taken into account,
i.e. displacements and velocities used as independent variables refer to local node
bases. A positive element force Fx′ acts at the first element node P1 in positive
x′ -direction, and at the second element node P2 in negative x′ -direction. The third
element node is used to carry degrees of freedom and may be located anywhere in
space.
Furthermore, for Harmonic Balance, there may be forces acting on the third node,
defined by the field HYSTFUN. In this case the DOFs of the third node may act as
internal variables of a hysteresis law, for example. Since the element has no linear
stiffness, it will introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
explicitly unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions.

Stresses:
No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

Stress Resultants:
Method:

Direct evaluation of element forces at nodes, referring to local element system.

Stored in book RSFR.DISP: (Nx′ , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0) at both element nodes
Printed stress resultants: (Nx′ , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 , 0) at both element nodes

Element Loads:
No distributed loads available.

The matrix input is done columnwise, for diagonal matrices only the diagonal, for symmetric matrices only the upper triangle is input. Trailing zeroes may be omitted. The
symmetric part of the stiffness matrix must be positive (semi-)definite.
8. The structural damping matrix is established by multiplying each element of the stiffness
matrix by the corresponding structural damping factor. Therefore, the following rules must
be fulfilled:
• Input of structural damping factors is possible if and only if the constant stiffness
matrix is specified.
• The kind of the structural damping matrix (diagonal, symmetric or quadratic) is always the same as the kind of the stiffness matrix, i.e. it is given by stf knd.
For analyses in time domain, e.g. for time history analysis, structural damping is converted to equivalent viscous damping by

4-483

Special
Elements

5. For elnid = 0, the following node-indendent data may be inserted as independent variables:

CONTROL6

4 Element Atlas

10. For dynamic response or complex eigenvalue analyses, constant stiffness or damping
matrix elements may be replaced by frequency and/or rotational speed dependent functions. To do so, the following rules must be observed:
• Field STIFFFUN with stiffness function identifiers may be specified if and only if
constant stiffness matrix is given in field STIFFLIN.
• Field DAMPFUN with viscous damping function identifiers may be specified if and
only if constant viscous damping matrix is given in field DAMPLIN.

Special
Elements

• Field GFUN with structural damping factor function identifiers may be specified if and
only if constant stiffness matrix is given in field STIFFLIN. Field G, however, may be
missing.
• The sequence of function identifiers in fields STIFFFUN, DAMPFUN and GFUN corresponds to the sequence of matrix elements in fields STIFFLIN and DAMPLIN, i.e.
the i-th function identifier in field STIFFFUN replaces the i-th matrix element in field
STIFFLIN etc.. Function identifiers equal zero are ignored.
• Stiffness and viscous damping functions may be frequency and/or speed dependent,
structural damping factor functions only frequency dependent. The independent variables frequency and rotational speed must be declared by means of fields VAR.
• If a field VAR specifies frequency as independent variable, all specified stiffness,
viscous damping and structural damping factor functions must be frequency dependent. If a field VAR specifies rotational speed as independent variable, all specified
stiffness and viscous damping functions must be speed dependent. The sequence
of frequency and speed specification by fields VAR fixes the sequence of those independent variables for stiffness and viscous damping functions, and all other independent variables declared in the remaining fields VAR are ignored for those functions.
11. For time history analysis, the nonlinear force functions in field FUNCTION determine the
complete natural element forces. If, for any natural degree of freedom, no nonlinear force
function is defined, then the corresponding natural force is calculated from stiffness and
damping matrices, if those matrices are input.
12. If frequency is specified as independent variable, the value is determined according to
following rules:
• If the UCI-command provides the specification of a reference frequency, the reference frequency is specified by the command.
• For time history analysis, the reference frequency must be input in the aligned result
variant by parameter RFREQTHA, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-1055.
• For analyses in the frequency domain where the solution procedure performs a loop
over excitation frequency, the actual excitation frequency is used.
13. If rotational speed is specified as independent variable, its value must be input within the
aligned result variant by a data block $ROTSPEED (see page 3-1066 ff.) with one value.
If, however, the solution procedure performs a loop over rotational speeds (e.g. MODAL
ROTATING (see page 2-231 ff.)), then the actual rotational speed is used instead.

For other dynamic analyses, including time history analyses where nonlinear force
functions are missing, frequency and/or speed dependent matrices are evaluated
for fixed reference values. If necessary (e.g. in time domain), structural damping is
replaced by equivalent viscous damping.
Optionally with rigid lever arms from nodal points to elastic center. If the offset is not
defined, the elastic center is always at the first element node.
A positive element force Fx′ acts at the first element node P1 in positive x′ -direction,

4-486

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

and at the second element node P2 in negative x′ -direction etc.
The third element node is used only to carry degrees of freedom and may be located
anywhere in space. Since its degrees of freedom have no linear stiffness, they will
introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed explicitly unless
there is sufficient support by adjacent elements, MPCs or boundary conditions.

No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

General Description:
Discrete three-term controller element (proportional plus reset plus derivative controller). Whereas the proportional part is always included, integral and differential
part may be omitted. The element force is acting on the element x′ -axis between
nodes P1 and P2 . The nominal value u0 must be given (e.g.prescribed) at degree of
freedom 11 at node P5 . The actual value u is given by
u = u′′4 − u′′3
where u′′3 and u′′4 are the displacements at nodes P3 and P4 in x′′ -direction.
A positive element force F tends to elongate the element along the x′ -axis, i.e. it
tries to increase u′2 − u′1 , and it acts on the structure at the first element node in
positive, at the second element node in negative x′ -direction. The stress resultant
component Nx′ at the second element node is equal to the element force F
As long as nominal value u0 is prescribed or coupled to other degrees of freedom,
the non-standard degrees of freedom do not introduce redundant degrees of freedom.

No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

Stress Resultants:
Method:

Direct evaluation of element forces at nodes P1 and P2 , referring
to local element system.

Printed stress resultants: (Nx′ , 0 , 0) at both element nodes

No distributed loads available.

decimally. A value greater than zero means that the corresponding functionality is taken

0.... Position controller entirely omitted.

3. According to the selection of controller functions, the input values for a cascade controller
must fulfill the following conditions:
• If the position controller is included, its proportional factor KP d must be greater than
zero.
• The velocity controller must be always included, and its proportional factor KP v must
be greater than zero.
• If the integral response part of the velocity controller is included, the reset time TN v
must be greater than zero.
• If the current controller is omitted, it is replaced by an internal connection without
any influence.
• If the current controller is included, its equivalent time constant TE must be greater
than zero.
• Mass m used for normalization must be greater than zero.
• If nominal velocity is requested, the proportional factor of velocity feedforward Kvv
must be greater than zero, if field CSCADD is specified, else Kvv is set to 1.0.
• A proportional factor for velocity feedforward Kvv > 0 is possible only if nominal
velocity is requested.
• First order delay of nominal displacement is only possible if position controller is
included and nominal displacement is requested.
• If specified, the time constant TSd for first order delay of nominal displacement must
be greater or equal zero where zero means no delay.
• If specified, the time constant Tdif f for first order delay of actual velocity must be
greater or equal zero where zero means no delay.
• For a low pass filter, the eigenfrequency f0 and the damping ratio D or DB resp.
must be greater than zero.
• For a band stop filter, the center frequency f0 and the pass bandwidth DB must be
greater than zero whereas the stop bandwidth BZ must be greater or equal zero.
4. There are different filters available in the cascade controller, which may be selected by
the corresponding filter type selection switch f ltreq:

General Description:
The element is intended to represent a linearized formulation of any controller in
state space. To this end, a quadratic stiffness matrix as well as a quadratic damping
matrices are defined by calling a user supplied function, i.e. a FORTRAN subroutine. The expected matrices of dimension (30,30) refer to the following vector of
local element degrees of freedom
̺′ = { u′1 z1 z2 z3 u′2 z4 z5 z6 u′′3 z7 z8 z9 · · ·
u′′4 z10 z11 z12 u′′′
z13 z14 z15 u′′′
z16 z17 z18 · · ·

It is intended that the element force is acting on the element x′ -axis between nodes P1 and P2 . The nominal displacement or velocity values u0 or u̇0 resp may
be given (e.g.prescribed) at degree of freedom 11 of nodes P7 or P8 . The actual
displacement or velocity values may be extracted e.g. by
u = u′′4 − u′′3
where u′′3 and u′′4 are the displacements at nodes P3 and P4 in x′′ -direction, and

The internal degrees of freedom z1 to z22 may be used to represent the internal
state variables of the controller. To avoid redundant degrees of freedom, the standard symmetric stiffness matrix is generated automatically which is zero-filled but
with 1.0 on the diagonal for each internal degree of freedom zi . So, as long as nominal values u0 and v0 are prescribed or coupled to other degrees of freedom, the
non-standard degrees of freedom do not introduce any redundant degree of freedom.

Discretisation:

Nonlinear force acting in the direction of element axis and (optionally) in the
two transversal directions.
The third node can carry up to three hysteresis parameters.

D. O. F. Types:

DISP

Definition of Element System:
Local x′ -axis is from node 1 to 2 if no reference system is defined.
In this case, the local y ′ -axis and z ′ -axis depend on the position of the third node.
Alternatively, the element axis may be defined using a local reference system. If the
element nodes P1 and P2 have different locations in space, the element axis points
from node P1 to node P2 .
If the element nodes P1 and P2 have identical coordinates, the local element system
has to be defined using three points, see page 4-473.

General Description:

Special
Elements

If the fields FUNCTION and HYSTFUN are given, the following applies: Nonlinear force acting in the direction of the three element axis. The element forces are
defined by
Fx′ = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
Fy′ = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
Fz ′ = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
The evolution of the three hysteresis parameters z1 , z2 and z3 is given by
R1 = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
R2 = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
R3 = F (u′ , u̇′ , v ′ , v̇ ′ , w′ , ẇ′ , z1 , ż1 , z2 , ż2 , z3 , ż3 )
Both element forces and displacements are given in the local coordinate system. A
positive element force Fx′ acts at the first element node P1 in positive x′ -direction,
and at the second element node P2 in negative x′ -direction. The third element node
is used to define the local y ′ and z ′ directions. Alternatively the local coordinate
system may be defined with a reference system.
If the field ELAPLAST is given, a one-dimensional elasto-plastic material behaviour
is modeled with the Bouc-Wen hysteresis model. The force in x′ direction is given
by
Fx′ = k2 u′ + (k1 − k2 )z1
and the forces Fy′ and Fz ′ direction are zero. The residual force is given by

CA1ZERF3

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

General Description:
Discrete equilibrium model with three translational stiffnesses in direction of element
axes. No stiffness with respect to rotations.
The element is intended to overcome static rigid body modes that will be supported
by later contact forces. I.e. the CA1ZERF3 stiffnesses help to avoid singularities
during the decomposition of the stiffness matrix, but is not a support by itself – if the
corresponding motion is not supported by adequate contact forces the unsupported
rigid body mode will still result in an infinite movement ! For more details on the
theory we refer to section 4.1.10 of [um550].

Special CA
Elements

Stresses:
No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

Stress Resultants:
Method:

Direct evaluation of element forces (linear force plus inner contact
correction force) at node, referring to local element system.

Stored in book RSFR.DISP: (Nx′ , Ny′ , Nz ′ ) at element node
Printed stress resultants: (Nx′ , Ny′ , Nz ′ ) at element node

Element Loads:
No distributed loads available.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:

(u, v, w) at each node

Discrete equilibrium model with translational stiffness in direction of element axis.
No stiffness with respect to transverse displacements or rotations.
The element is intended to overcome static rigid body modes that will be supported
by later contact forces. I.e. the CA2ZERF1 stiffness helps to avoid singularities
during the decomposition of the stiffness matrix, but is not a support by itself – if the
corresponding motion is not supported by adequate contact forces the unsupported
rigid body mode will still result in an infinite movement ! For more details on the
theory we refer to section 4.1.10 of [um550].
Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the
element may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
explicitly.

Stresses:
No element stresses available, no contribution to averaged nodal stresses.

Stress Resultants:
Method:

Direct evaluation of element forces (force resulting from constant
CA resulting from contact analstiffness k11 plus correction force R11
ysis) at nodes, referring to local element system.

Stored in book RSFR.DISP: (Nx′ , 0 , 0) at both element nodes
Printed stress resultants: (Nx′ , 0 , 0) at both element nodes

Element Loads:
No distributed loads available.

The element is intended to overcome static rigid body modes that will be supported

6 Noded Solid Pentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-551

The plot elements are pure dummy elements which do not contribute in any way to the system
matrices. They are intended to be used as display or plot device e.g. for
• Display of overall displacements of a fine mesh using a connected simplified mesh of plot
elements
• Visualization of ’invisible’ mesh properties like orientation of local systems etc.
There are no geometrical data for 2d-plot elements. Furthermore, plot elements do not refer to
any material property, therefore no material has to be assigned.

4.17

Line Convection Elements

Overview on Available Line Convection Elements:
CONAL2

2 Noded Straight Edge Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-554

CONAL3

3 Noded Curved Edge Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-559

CONL2

2 Noded Straight Line Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-564

CONL3

3 Noded Curved Line Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-569

Line convection elements are used to include convective heat transfer at the edges of membranes and shells (edge convection) or along rods and beams (line convection) in thermal
analysis. In addition, the heat capacity of the convective film may be taken into account.
Line convection elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored in any other kind
of analysis.

4.18

Surface Convection and Radiation Elements

CONA3

3 Noded Triangular Surface Convection and Radiation Element . . . . . 4-577

9 Noded Quadrilateral Surface Convection and Radiation Element . . . . 4-597

3 Noded Triangular Shell Surface Convection and Radiation Element . . 4-602

CONS4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Shell Surface Convection and Radiation Element . 4-607

CONS6

6 Noded Triangular Shell Surface Convection and Radiation Element . . 4-612

CONS8

8 Noded Quadrilateral Shell Surface Convection and Radiation Element . 4-617

CONS9

9 Noded Quadrilateral Shell Surface Convection and Radiation Element . 4-622

Surface convection and radiation elements are used to include radiation and convective heat
transfer at the surfaces of membranes, shells and solids in thermal analysis. Especially for shell
elements, shell surface convection and radiation elements are available which take into account
the temperature difference between upper and lower surface of the element. In addition, the
heat capacity of the convective film may be taken into account.
Surface convection and radiation elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored
in any other kind of analysis.

Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The surrounding
temperature must be defined as element load.

Convection
Elements

data list is assigned to the upper element surface and the second data list to the lower

4.18 Surface Convection and Radiation Elements

CONS3

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type TEMP:
Degrees of Freedom:

( T, ∆T ) at each node

General Description:
First order surface convection and radiation element with linear temperature field,
convective heat flows normal to element surface and radiation, separated for upper
and lower surface. Intended to be placed on triangular surfaces of first order shell
elements, taking into account the temperature difference between upper and lower
surface of shell. Optional rigid lever arms.
The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient for upper and lower
surface are possible:
Formula
α = α0
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )

where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The temperature
at the upper surface is given by
Tupper,i = Ti + 0.5∆T i
and at the lower surface by
Tlower,i = Ti − 0.5∆T i
The surrounding temperatures must be defined as element loads.
Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
COMPTEMP.
The surrounding temperatures for radiation may be defined as element loads.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type TEMP:

Degrees of Freedom:

( T, ∆T ) at each node

General Description:
First order surface convection and radiation element with bilinear temperature field,
convective heat flows normal to element surface and radiation, separated for upper
and lower surface. Intended to be placed on quadrilateral surfaces of first order
shell elements, taking into account the temperature difference between upper and
lower surface of shell. Optional rigid lever arms.
The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient for upper and lower
surface are possible:
Dependencies
- no dependency Temperature
Temperature, time
Temperature, time, space

Formula
α = α0
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )

Convection
Elements

where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The temperature
at the upper surface is given by
Tupper,i = Ti + 0.5∆T i
and at the lower surface by
Tlower,i = Ti − 0.5∆T i
The surrounding temperatures must be defined as element loads.
Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
COMPTEMP.
The surrounding temperatures for radiation may be defined as element loads.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type TEMP:
Degrees of Freedom:

( T, ∆T ) at each node

General Description:
Second order isoparametric surface convection and radiation element with quadratic
temperature field, convective heat flow normal to element surface and radiation ,
separated for upper and lower surface. Intended to be placed on triangular surfaces
of second order shell elements, taking into account the temperature difference between upper and lower surface of shell. Optional rigid lever arms.
The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient for upper and lower
surface are possible:
Formula
α = α0
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )

where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The temperature
at the upper surface is given by
Tupper,i = Ti + 0.5∆T i
and at the lower surface by
Tlower,i = Ti − 0.5∆T i
The surrounding temperatures must be defined as element loads.
Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
COMPTEMP.
The surrounding temperatures for radiation may be defined as element loads.

radiation, separated for upper and lower surface. Intended to be placed on quadrilateral surfaces of second order shell elements, taking into account the temperature
difference between upper and lower surface of shell. Optional rigid lever arms.
The following dependencies of the convective film coefficient for upper and lower
surface are possible:
Formula
α = α0
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i )
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t)
α = α0 f(Ti , TF,i , t, xi , yi , zi )

where Ti is the nodal point temperature and TF,i the corresponding temperature of
the surrounding fluid, t is the actual time in transient analysis and xi , yi , zi are the
Cartesian coordinates of node i referring to component system. The temperature
at the upper surface is given by
Tupper,i = Ti + 0.5∆T i
and at the lower surface by
Tlower,i = Ti − 0.5∆T i
The surrounding temperatures must be defined as element loads.
Temperature-dependent input data usually require a nonlinear analysis.
If a linear analysis is performed, the nodal point temperature Ti is assumed to
be the component temperature as defined by the system variant $PARAMETER
COMPTEMP.
The surrounding temperatures for radiation may be defined as element loads.

Overview on Available Fluid Elements:

FLHEX20

20 Noded Fluid Hexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-634

6 Noded Fluid Pentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-640

FLPENT18

18 Noded Fluid Pentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-646

5 Noded Fluid Pyramid . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-649

4 Noded Fluid Tetrahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-652

FLTET10

10 Noded Fluid Tetrahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-655

The fluid elements can be classified with respect to their geometry or the order of their shape
functions. In terms of geometry there are four types of elements:
• The Brick elements FLHEX8, FLHEX20 and FLHEX27

• The Tetrahedron elements FLTET4, and FLTET10.
• The Pyramid element FLPYR5
Although tetrahedron elements are sufficient to mesh any geometry, better results are obtained
when brick elements are used whenever possible, restricting the use of wedges, tetrahedrons
and pyramids to those parts of the mesh where they cannot be avoided.
In terms of their order of shape functions, three types of elements are identified:
• Elements with linear shape functions: FLHEX8, FLPENT6, FLTET4 and FLPYR5.
• Elements with incomplete quadratic shape functions: FLHEX20 and FLPENT15.
• Elements with quadratic shape functions: FLHEX27, FLPENT18 and FLTET10.

The element with the same order of shape function are fully compatible with each other whenever they match face to face. When the faces do not match completely (e.g. when two triangles
are mated with a quadrilateral), the full kinematic compatibility is lost.
All fluid elements carry one pressure degree of freedom per node.

elements as 3d absorber elements. All applicable material input options for fluid elements are

4.20 Fluid Structure Interface Elements
4.20

Fluid Structure Interface Elements

Overview on Available Fluid Structure Interface Elements:
FSINTA3

3 Noded Triangular Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-661

FSINTA4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-664

FSINTA6

6 Noded Triangular Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-667

FSINTA8

8 Noded Quadrilateral Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-670

FSINTA9

9 Noded Quadrilateral Fluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-673

The fluid structure interface elements are used to couple solid and fluid domains for coupled
analysis. In addition, they may be used to include boundary absorption in the fluid domain.
Each node carries three displacement degrees of freedom and one pressure degree of freedom. For a pure fluid analysis without structure the displacement degrees of freedom are
ignored, for a pure structural analysis the interface elements are ignored at all.
If two fluid regions are separated by a thin wall idealized by shell elements (doubly wetted
surface), the problem arises that for one shell node with one set of displacement degrees of
freedom there are two different pressure values, one for each fluid region. Therefore for each
fluid region one interface element is necessary, the first one with the same nodal points as the
corresponding shell element, and the second one with different nodes at the same position in
space and the displacement degrees of freedom joined by multipoint constraints.

Fluid
Elements

The orientation of interface elements must be such that the element normal points from the
fluid to the solid.
The local element system for triangular elements is defined as follows:
1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.
2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.
3. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ - and y ′ -axis.
For quadrilateral elements the local element system is defined in the following way:
1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.
2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
corner node).

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4-659

4 Element Atlas
3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.
4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
the reference surface.

Fluid
Elements

Fluid structure interface elements have isotropic fluid material. Beside the properties of an
inviscid fluid, surface absorption data may be added to describe absorption at the fluid boundary, and volumetric drag may be added to describe absorption within the fluid. All applicable
material input options for fluid elements are summarized in the following table:

4.21 Surface Wave Elements
4.21

Surface Wave Elements

Overview on Available Surface Wave Elements:
FLWAVEA3

3 Noded Triangular Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-679

FLWAVEA4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-682

FLWAVEA6

6 Noded Triangular Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-685

FLWAVEA8

8 Noded Quadrilateral Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-688

FLWAVEA9

9 Noded Quadrilateral Surface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-691

The surface wave elements are used to idealize free surfaces of the fluid where the pressure
at the surface is balanced by the weight of surface waves.
Surface wave elements carry one pressure degree of freedom.
Surface wave elements are always placed on the boundary of the fluid perpendicular to the
direction of gravity acceleration. The orientation of the element normal is meaningless. The
gravity acceleration value itself must be inputted by parameter GFLWAVE within the system
variant, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.
The local element system for triangular elements is defined as follows:
1. The x′ -axis points from first to second corner node.
2. The y ′ -axis is normal to the x′ -axis, pointing to the third corner node.

For quadrilateral elements the local element system is defined in the following way:
1. The element system is defined at the crossing point of the two diagonals in the reference
plane which is spanned by the midside points of the four edges.
2. The x′ -axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
rectangular shape the x′ -axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
corner node).
3. The y ′ -axis lies also in the reference surface bisecting the complementary angle between
the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
rectangular shape the y ′ -axis is parallel to the second edge.
4. The element normal forms a right hand system with the x′ -and y ′ -axis, i.e. it is normal to
the reference surface.

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4.23 Two–Dimensional Infinite Elements
4.23

Two–Dimensional Infinite Elements

Overview on Available Two-Dimensional Infinite Elements:
INFFLA2

2 Noded Straight Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-701

INFFLA3

3 Noded Curved Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-704

INF2QAM4

4 Noded Straight Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-707

INF2QAM8

8 Noded Curved Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-710

INF2QAM9

9 Noded Curved Infinite Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-713

The Infinite Elements are special elements to model the unbounded domain. Yet they are only
available for electromagnetic and acoustic/fluid problems. Pay attention to the following features
(see also theoretical manual) :
• The first part of the name ’INF’ indicates the element as an INFINITE element, the second
part ’FLA2’ names the element, which is used as the modeling element (here a FLA2
element).
• The geometry of the Infinite Elements tends to infinity and is described with singular
functions.
• The geometry of the Infinite Elements will be changed through the program and depends
on the position of the pole.
• The nodes at infinity are not modeled since they are thought to be suppressed (”automatic
Dirichlet boundary condition”), but they have influence on the interpolation–functions.
• The degrees of freedom (e. g. potential) are interpolated with the standard functions, e.
g. INFFLA2 with the QUAM4 interpolation–functions without the ones, which belong to
the nodes lying at infinity.
• The material is always isotropic and homogeneous. No local element system is necessary.
• The geometrical datas are always valid for all nodes.
• Rotated basis is not allowed.
• The user has to choose an expansion pole which is always opposite to the infinity side of
the element.

• Because the infinite elements are modeled with iso–parametric elements, higher order
infinite elements must have their greatest geometrical extension after the modeling in
infinite direction, otherwise they can not be recognized as an infinite element in the right
manner.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4-699

2D-Infinite
Elements

• All Infinite Elements can carry only nodal point loads ($CONLOAD).

4 Element Atlas
• Infinite elements are suitable for static and first order time–changing problems. For the
second order time–changing wave equation added mass problems can be treated. Infinite
elements can not handle the full wave equation in the unbounded domain. For those
problems absorbing boundary condition elements must be used.
Infinite elements have isotropic fluid material to emphasize their property of modelling the unbounded domain. All applicable material input options for infinite elements are summarized in
the following table:

Three–Dimensional Infinite Elements

Overview on Available Three–Dimensional Infinite Elements:
INF3QAM4

4 Noded Straight Infinite Solid element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-719

INFPNT18

18 Noded Curved Infinite Solid element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-760

The Infinite Elements are special elements to model the unbounded domain. Yet they are only
available for electromagnetic and fluid structure problems. Pay attention to the special features
(see also theoretical manual) explained on page 4-699.

4.25 Three–Dimensional Bayliss–Turkel RBC Elements
4.25

Three–Dimensional Bayliss–Turkel RBC Elements

Overview on Available Three–Dimensional Bayliss-Turkel RBC Elements:
RBCBT1A3

3 Noded Triangular Element with Straight Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-767

RBCBT1A6

6 Noded Triangular Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-771

RBCBT1A4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Element with Straight Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-775

RBCBT1A8

8 Noded Quadrilatral Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-779

RBCBT1A9

9 Noded Quadrilatral Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-783

RBCBT2A3

3 Noded Triangular Element with Straight Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-787

RBCBT2A6

6 Noded Triangular Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-791

RBCBT2A4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Element with Straight Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-795

RBCBT2A8

8 Noded Quadrilatral Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-799

RBCBT2A9

9 Noded Quadrilatral Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-803

The RBC (radiation boundary condition) elements are special elements to construct an artificial
boundary and to impose conditions on this surface to simulate an infinite domain. The Bayliss–
Turkel RBC elements are based on the mode annihilating approximation technique. The idea
is to absorb the modes of the far field expansion of outgoing propagating solution to the (wave)
equation (the Sommerfeld condition annihilates the first mode of plane waves). For further
details of the theory see (†† ) (‡‡ ). The RBC elements of first order annihilate the first mode
of the far field expansion, the elements of second order the first two modes. In general the
elements of second order are more accurate than those of first order.
The theory of Bayliss–Turkel in three dimensions is based on a far field solution in a spherical
coordinate system. Thus the RBC elements must be placed onto the surface of a Finite Element
mesh which is of spherical shape only. With the RBC elements the influence of the unbounded
domain is taken into account and the problem is well posed too. So no additional boundary
conditions for the unbounded domain are necessary.

††

A. Bayliss, E. Turkel : Radiation boundary conditions for wave–like equations, Commun. Pure Appl. Math., Vol.
23, S. 707–725, 1980
‡‡
A. Bayliss, M. Gunzberger, E. Turkel : Boundary conditions for the numerical solution of elliptic equations in
exterior regions, SIAM J. Appl. Math., Vol. 42, S. 430–451, 1982

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4-765

3D-RBC (B-T)
Elements

4 Element Atlas
The Bayliss–Turkel RBC elements are available until now for static electromagnetic, wave propagation and direct fluid frequency problems. The elements of second order are frequency
dependent for wave propagation and direct fluid frequency problems. For wave problems the
artificial boundary should be placed about one wavelength away from sources or scatterers to
reduce reflections from the artificial boundary sufficient. Of course this is dependent on the
specified problem and should not be seen as a constant.
Only isotropic fluid material is applicable to three-dimensional RBC elements, and the appropriate material input type is GENERAL. The applicable material input options are summarized
in the following table:

4.26 Three–Dimensional Engquist–Majda RBC Elements
4.26

Three–Dimensional Engquist–Majda RBC Elements

Overview on Available Three–Dimensional Engquist–Majda RBC Elements:
RBCEM1A3

3 Noded Triangular Element with Straight Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-809

RBCEM1A6

6 Noded Triangular Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-813

RBCEM1A4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Element with Straight Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-817

RBCEM1A8

8 Noded Quadrilateral Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-821

RBCEM1A9

9 Noded Quadrilateral Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-825

RBCEM2A3

3 Noded Triangular Element with Straight Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-829

RBCEM2A6

6 Noded Triangular Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-833

RBCEM2A4

4 Noded Quadrilateral Element with Straight Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-837

RBCEM2A8

8 Noded Quadrilateral Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-841

RBCEM2A9

9 Noded Quadrilateral Element with Curved Edges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-845

The RBC (radiation boundary condition) elements are special elements to construct an artificial boundary and to impose conditions on this surface to simulate an infinite domain. The
Engquist–Majda RBC elements are based on the one way wave equation approximation technique. The idea is to permit on an outer boundary only wave motions which are travelling
outward from the range of interest. For further details of the theory see (* ) († ). The RBC elements of first order approximate the pseudo–differential equation with a Taylor approximation
of first order, the elements of second order use a Taylor approximation of second order. In general the elements of second order are more accurate than those of first order. On a rectangular
boundary, the elements of first order lead to the Sommerfeld condition for plane waves.
The theory of Engquist–Majda used here is based on plane waves. Thus the RBC elements
must be placed onto the surface of a Finite Element mesh which is of rectangular shape only.
With the RBC elements the influence of the unbounded domain is taken into account and the
problem is well posed too. So no additional boundary conditions for the unbounded domain are
necessary.

* B. Engquist, A. Majda :

Absorbing boundary conditions for the numerical simulation of waves, Math. Comput.,
Vol. 31, S. 629–651, 1977
†
B. Engquist, A. Majda : Radiation boundary conditions for acoustic and elastic wave calculations, Commun. Pure
Appl. Math., Vol. 32, S. 312–358, 1979

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

4-807

3D-RBC (E-M)
Elements

4 Element Atlas
The Engquist–Majda RBC elements are available until now for wave propagation and direct
fluid frequency problems. The elements of second order are frequency dependent for wave
propagation and direct fluid frequency problems. For wave problems the artificial boundary
should be placed about one to two wavelengths away from sources or scatterers to reduce
reflections from the artificial boundary sufficient. Of course this is dependent on the specified
problem and should not be seen as a constant.
Only isotropic fluid material is applicable to three-dimensional RBC elements, and the appropriate material input type is GENERAL. The applicable material input options are summarized
in the following table:

Available Material Input Options for Engquist-Majda-3D Elements

4.27 Axisymmetric Flange Elements
4.27

Axisymmetric Flange Elements

RINGX

Single-node axisymmetric Flange Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-851

The axisymmetric flange elements are displacement models that are fully compatible with the
axisymmetric membrane elements QUAX and TRIAX. Their main application is thus the modelling of enforcements (flanges, stringers, prestressing cables) in axisymmetric problems.
Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the axisymmetric flange elements may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
explicitly.
All matrices and forces are with respect to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).
Axisymmetric flange elements may have, according to their nature, only homogeneous isotropic
material, therefore a homogeneous material has to be defined with TYPE = ISO (default). The
appropriate material property type is GENERAL. All applicable material input options for axisymmetric flange elements are summarized in the following table:

V 19.00.287

Material Properties

RINGX

4 Element Atlas
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:

Degrees of Freedom:

(r, w) at each node

axisymmetric
Flanges

General Description:
Discrete displacement model carrying only axisymmetric loads. No bending, torsion or shear stiffness. Unless the element is sufficiently supported by adjacent
elements or constraints, it will introduce redundant degrees of freedom which must
be suppressed explicitly.

Stresses:
Method:

Normal stress in circumferential direction only

Stored in book SIG.DISP: σtt (uniaxial stress) at center of element
Printed element stresses: σtt for node P1

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type POTE:

Degrees of Freedom:

axisymmetric
Flanges

(Ar , Az , Aφ , φ) at each node

General Description:
Discrete electromagnetic potential model. Element has no contribution for the electric scalar potential. Unless the element is sufficiently supported by adjacent elements or constraints, it will introduce redundant degrees of freedom for the vectorpotential which must be suppressed explicitly.

Field Quantities:
See page 1-24 for general description of available electromagnetic field quantities.
The element is capable to calculate the following field quantities :
∇t A, Bφ , Hφ , E, D, J .

The scalarpotential does not contribute to the electric field strength E, and thus not
to D and J. The electric charge ρ is always Zero.
Method:

Direct calculation in the nodal point.

Stored in books xxxx.POTE: In the nodal point.
Printed field quantities:

In the nodal point.

$DISLOAD, and page 3-693 for general description of distributed loads defined at structural

4.28

Axisymmetric Membrane Elements

FLAX2

2 Noded Axisymmetric Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-859

FLAX3

3 Noded Axisymmetric Membrane Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-865

The axisymmetric membrane elements are displacement models that are fully compatible with
the axisymmetric solid elements QUAX and TRIAX. They can carry only axisymmetric loads.
The local element system for axisymmetric membrane elements is defined as follows:
1. The r ′ -axis direction is determined through the tangential direction of the cross-section
geometry.
′

2. The z ′ -axis is the cross product from the r ′ -axis with the φ axis.
′

3. The φ axis is identical with the global φ axis.

the element geometry.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type POTE:

axisymmetric
Solids

(Ar , Az , Aφ , φ) at each node

General Description:
Axisymmetric first order isoparametric potential model with bilinear potential field
and straight edges, carrying axisymmetric loads only.

Field Quantities:
See page 1-24 for general description of available electromagnetic field quantities.
The element is capable to calculate the following field quantities :
∇t A, B, H, E, D, J, ρ.

For ELECTROstatic and STEADY ELECTRIC CURRENT problems the electric charge
will be Zero, since the second derivative of the scalarpotential is Null in a (bi–) linear
element.
Method:

Calculation in one (central) Gauss–Point. All nodal points will have
identical values.

Stored in books xxxx.POTE: In the nodal points.
Printed field quantities:

4-878

In the nodal points.

4.30 Axisymmetric Shell Elements
4.30

Axisymmetric Shell Elements

QUABX2K

Axisymmetric Harmonic Thin Shell Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-911

The geometry of axisymmetric elements is fully described by its intersection with the global
r, z-plane where the z-axis is the axis of symmetry (rotational axis for the body of revolution).
All matrices and forces refer to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).
The local coordinate system (m′ t′ n′ ) within axisymmetric shell elements is defined as follows:

1. The m′ -axis is tangential to the local meridian and points from the edge where the first
element point is located to the second one.
2. The t′ -axis is tangential to the circumferential direction and parallel to the global φ-direction.
3. The n′ -axis is normal to the shell surface. (m′ t′ n′ ) form a right-hand system.
4. The n′ -axis defines upper and lower surfaces of the shell, since it points from the lower to
the upper one.

Geometrical data for different geometry types

2. For axisymmetric shells elements, equally spaced stiffeners in meridian and/or circumferential direction may be taken into account which are described by some additional
geometrical data (see picture below):
• The number of stiffeners in meridian direction (parallel to the global z-axis) is given
by 360/dϕ which must be an integer number.
• The distance of stiffening rings in circumferential direction is given by dc , measured
on the reference surface of the shell element.
• The eccentricities em , ec define the distance of center of gravity of the stiffeners section area from the reference surface of the shell element.
• The bending moments of inertia are assumed to be given with respect to axes
through the center of gravity of the stiffeners section area, parallel to the circumferential direction for Im and parallel to the meridian direction for Ic

4.31 Axisymmetric Spring Elements
4.31

Axisymmetric Spring Elements

SPRINGX1

Axisymmetric Translational Spring . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-921

SPRINGX2

Axisymmetric Spring with Two Translational Stiffnesses . . . . . . . . . . 4-925

SPRINGX3

Spring with Two Translational and One Rotational Stiffnesses . . . . . . . 4-929

All matrices and forces are with respect to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).
The same is true for spring element properties like stiffness, mass or volume.
If necessary, local element systems for spring elements are defined using two points R1 and
R2 located in the r, z-plane as follows:
1. The rR -axis points from the first point R1 to the second point R2 .
2. The zR -axis together with the rR -axis form a plane system in the r, z-plane.
3. The local element system (r ′ , z ′ ) is parallel to the reference system (rR , zR ) with its origin
at the first element node.

Stress Resultants and Initial Deformations
For spring elements only stress resultants instead of stresses are available. They are calculated for both nodes, referring to the local element coordinate system (r ′ z ′ ), and can be easily
interpreted as the forces acting on the element in order to produce the elastic deformations.
The latter are represented by the difference of total element deformations and element initial
deformations. For SPRINGX1 and SPRINGX2 elements corresponding stress resultants at
both nodes are antivalent (equal magnitude, opposite direction), with positive values at the second node for positive elastic elongations ∆ui = ui,P 2 − ui,P 1 .
In analogy to the stress resultants, the initial strains which can be specified for spring elements
are initial deformations, referring to the local element coordinate system:
δ1

Elongation along the r ′ -axis.

δ2

Elongation along the z ′ -axis.

δ3

Twist about the t′ -axis.

When all degrees of freedom at the first element node P1 are suppressed, a positive elongation
will move the second element node P2 in the direction of the corresponding local coordinate
axis, and a positive twist will rotate node P2 in a positive sense of rotation around the respective
local coordinate axis.

CONALAX

Single Node Axisymmetric Edge Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-934

CONLAX

Single Node Axisymmetric Line Convection Element . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-939

Axisymmetric line convection elements are used to include convective heat transfer at the
edges of axisymmetric membrane (edge convection) or along axisymmetric flange (line convection) in thermal analysis. In addition, the heat capacity of the convective film may be taken
into account.
Axisymmetric line convection elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored in
any other kind of analysis.
All matrices and forces are with respect to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).
If the heat capacity of the convective film should be taken into account, a homogeneous
isotropic material has to be defined with TYPE = ISO (default) and material property type GENERAL. All applicable material input options for axisymmetric line convection elements are summarized in the following table:

4.35 Axisymmetric Fluid Structure Interface Elements
4.35

Axisymmetric Fluid Structure Interface Elements

FSINTSX3

3 Noded Curved Axisymmetric Harmonic Fluid Structure Interface Element4-963

The axisymmetric fluid structure interface elements are used to couple axisymmetric solid and
fluid domains for coupled analysis. In addition, they may be used to include boundary absorption in the fluid domain.
Fluid structure interface elements carry displacement degrees of freedom as well as pressure
degree of freedom. For a pure fluid analysis without structure the displacement degrees of
freedom are ignored, for a pure structural analysis the interface elements are ignored at all.
The geometry of axisymmetric elements is fully described by its intersection with the global
r, z-plane where the z-axis is the axis of symmetry (rotational axis for the body of revolution).
All matrices and forces refer to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).
The orientation of axisymmetric interface elements must be such that the element normal points
from the fluid to the solid. The local element system for axisymmetric interface elements is
defined as follows:
1. The m′ -axis is tangential to the local meridian and points from the edge where the first
element point is located to the second one.
2. The t′ -axis is tangential to the circumferential direction and parallel to the global φ-direction.
3. The n′ -axis is normal to the element surface. (m′ t′ n′ ) form a right-hand system.

4.36 Axisymmetric Surface Wave Elements
4.36

Axisymmetric Surface Wave Elements

FLWAVEX3

3 Noded Curved Axisymmetric Harmonic Surface Wave Element . . . . . 4-968

The axisymmetric surface wave elements are used to idealize free surfaces of the axisymmetric
fluid where the pressure at the surface is balanced by the weight of surface waves.
Axisymmetric surface wave elements carry one pressure degree of freedom.
Axisymmetric surface wave elements are always placed on the boundary of the fluid perpendicular to the direction of gravity acceleration. The orientation of the element normal is meaningless. The gravity acceleration value itself must be inputted by parameter GFLWAVE within
the system variant, see data block $PARAMETER, page 3-549.
The geometry of axisymmetric elements is fully described by its intersection with the global
r, z-plane where the z-axis is the axis of symmetry (rotational axis for the body of revolution).
All matrices and forces refer to a sector of 360 degrees (full axisymmetric body).
Axisymmetric surface wave elements have isotropic fluid material, and only fluid density is used.
All applicable material input options for axisymmetric surface wave elements are summarized
in the following table:

5.1 General

5 Design Element Atlas
Important notice: This chapter provides a detailed description and a complete list of general
purpose design element types. For any other type please refer to 3-62 ff.

General

For design optimization purpose, all parts of the structure which may be modified are assigned
to so-called Design Elements. They are used to define possible modifications for elements
and nodes belonging to the design element, and are intended for simple and clear description
of interpolation within the design element (interpolation is not yet provided in current version).
Design elements are used according to following rules:
• Each design element contains one or more finite elements by unique assignment. Together with the elements, all nodal points connected to those elements are associated to
the design element.
• Each design element may have any number of design variables, at least one. All possible
modifications within the design element are defined dependent on those design variables.
• Each design element has a fixed number of design nodes, a defined geometry and corresponding interpolation functions. Design nodes are needed for interpolation within the
design element and shape optimization only, and may be omitted elsewhere.
• Each design element has a fixed type of Geometrical Data Record. For optimal sizing
problems only elements with matching Geometrical Data Record may be assigned.
• For optimal sizing problems property dependencies may be defined for the whole design
element. They are valid for all corresponding finite elements, independent on its location
within the design element. Design nodes are not used and may be omitted.
• For interpolation of properties within the design element, property dependencies are defined at the design nodes of the design element; then the property is interpolated according to the interpolation function of the design element and the location of the element
within the design element. For that case, the design nodes of the design element must
be inputted.
Interpolation of properties is not yet available in current version.
• For shape optimization the coordinates of the design nodes are made dependent on the
design variables, and the coordinates of all nodal points associated to the corresponding
design element are modified according to the design element interpolation functions.

Primary Results
6.1.1

6 Results

Primary Results Overview

This overview holds all primary results and all results, where the amount of data depends on
the highest DOF at all nodes.
For mechanical analysis:
DISPlacement: Nodal point displacements
VELOcity: Nodal point velocities
ACCEleration: Nodal point accelerations
REACtion DOFTYPE=DISP: Nodal point reaction forces
REACD DOFTYPE=DISP: Nodal point reaction forces on dependent DOFs
RESIdual DOFTYPE=DISP: Nodal point residual forces
RIGID MODES DOFTYPE=DISP: Nodal point rigid body modes
For thermal analysis:

Results

TEMPerature: Nodal point temperatures
REACtion DOFTYPE=TEMP: Nodal point reacting heat flux
REACD DOFTYPE=TEMP: Nodal point reacting heat flux on dependent DOFs
RESIdual DOFTYPE=TEMP: Nodal point residual heat flux
RIGID MODES DOFTYPE=TEMP: Nodal point zero temperature modes
For fluid analysis:
PRESsure: Nodal point pressures
REACtion DOFTYPE=PRES: Nodal point reac
REACD DOFTYPE=PRES: Nodal point reac on dependent DOFs
RESIdual DOFTYPE=PRES: Nodal point residual
RIGID MODES DOFTYPE=PRES: Nodal point constant pressure modes
For electromagnetical analysis:
MPOTEntial: Nodal point magnetic potentials
EPOTEntial: Nodal point electric potentials
REACtion DOFTYPE=POTE: Nodal point reac
REACD DOFTYPE=POTE: Nodal point reac on dependent DOFs

Verification Results
6.1.2

6 Results

Verification Results Overview

With the GO command in the UCI EXPORT section additional verification results from the
analysis are exported to the postprocessor together with the standard results obtained by the
pure analysis if the DEFAULT switch VERIFICATION is set to RESULTS (or ON).
Also in UCI sections PRINT and EXPORT those results can be explicitly requested with the
ITEM command.
Selectable results without setting the VERIFICATION switch:
The results below can be printed or exported by an explicit ITEM selection without setting the
VERIFICATION switch. The results will be exported automatically, if the VERIFICATION switch
is set to RESULTS or ON and they are available.

6.1 General

Please refer to the indicated examples for further information.
Remarks:
1. The IVOLVEC verification result is the vector from the dependent node to the coordinate
derived from the calculated position in parameter space. Distorted elements and/or extrapolation due to OUTTOL may lead to differences between true and calculated position.
The IVOLINF verification result consists of 2 columns (2 scalar results):
col1 : element identifier of guiding element as real number
col2 : Flag: found (0), found with OUTTOL (2), not found (3)

6-5

Contact Results
6.1.3

6 Results

Contact Results Overview

With the GO command in the UCI EXPORT section additional results from the contact analysis
are exported to the postprocessor together with the standard results obtained by the pure static
analysis. Also in UCI sections PRINT and EXPORT those results can be explicitly requested
with the ITEM command. All contact results are based on nodal points, i.e. are scalar values
or vectors at contact nodes.
According to the solution step in which the data is generated, the contact analysis results may
be separated in 4 groups:
Scanning results (verification of model):
Directly after the model’s input and consolidation (e.g. after task scanning with TASK STORE)
some load-independent* contact results are available for model verification:

Results

INITIAL CONTACT DEFinition
Initial contact definitions with 3-6 scalar values per node: the definition counter, the definition type, the family type of the involved guiding CA-DOFs and, for surface contact, an
isolation-indicator, the patch kink angles before smoothing and an indicator for doubled
contact pairs
INITIAL CONTACT GEOmetry
It is the nadir vector (geometrical gap vector from node to surface nadir) as a result of the
neighborhood search
INITIAL CONTACT SYStem
It contains 3 normalized vectors building the axes of the contact system, i.e. the contact
normal (Nx ) and frictional y/z (Fy /Fz ) direction respectively
Precheck results (verification of loads):
For a verification of the contact loads the following results are already available after the use
of a STATIC TO PRECHECK (hence, may be exported after a test-run without costly calculations). Of course, the simple STATIC command also includes the precheck. This results are
only exported if explicitly requested (or if the UCI DEFAULT switch VERIFICATION is set to
DEFAULT SET VERIFICATION = RESULTS):
INITIAL CONTACT STATUS
It is a single scalar value for each contact node in each load pattern indicating the geometrical situation prior to simulation, i.e. basically the sign of the input gap width given by
$CONTACT LOAD (see page 3-567 ff.)
INITIAL GAP [WIDTH]
The initial gap δ0norm is only a signed scalar value of the normal part: open gap if > 0,
penetration if < 0

* In the post-processor the load-independent results may show up under load pattern zero.

6-6

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

6.1 General

Contact Results

INITIAL GAP VECtor
The initial gap width vector δ 0 (x, y, z) itself is split into a normal δ 0norm (x,y,z) and tangential δ 0tang (x,y,z) vector part according to the local contact system
Standard results:

CONTACT STATUS
Contact status (decimal coded)
CONTACT FORCE
Normal RCnorm (x,y,z) and frictional RCf ric (x,y,z) force
CONTACT PRESsure
Scalar contact pressure and shear vector
CONTACT PRESsure VECtor
Contact pressure vector and shear vector
GAP [WIDTH]
Final gap δnorm (signed scalar value): open gap if > 0, penetration if < 0
GAP VECtor
Final gap vector in normal δ norm (x,y,z) and tangential δ tang (x,y,z) direction
GAP DISPlacement
Relative gap displacement in normal ∆r norm (x,y,z) and tangential ∆r tang (x,y,z) direction
GAP VELOcity
Relative gap velocity in normal ∆v norm (x,y,z) and tangential ∆v tang (x,y,z) direction
CONTACT INTERference
Contact interference (linear dependent CA-DOFs)
CONTACT RESIdual
Residuum in gap displacements in normal εnorm (x,y,z) and tangential εtang (x,y,z) direction
CONTACT FORCE RESIdual
Residuum in contact forces for contact zero-force (CA0) and gaskets (GSK) DOFs
FRICTION ENergy
Dissipative frictional energy
FRICTION ENergy DENsity
Dissipative frictional energy density
FRICTION RATIO
Frictional coefficients, saturation and slip-force declination angles
CONTACT DEFinition
Is linked to INITIAL CONTACT DEFinition for calculations without geometrical update

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

6-7

Results

After the contact analysis the contact reaction forces RC the contact pressure pC the final
gap width δ, the relative displacements ∆r, the relative velocities ∆v, and the contact residuals
ε are directly available. Each of the six results is split into a normal and tangential vector (or
scalar) according to the local contact system. The vector values are given with respect to the
global coordinate system. In case of slipping also the scalar frictional energy density Φslip is
available as a result.

Contact Results

6 Results

CONTACT GEOmetry
Is linked to INITIAL CONTACT GEOmetry for calculations without geometrical update
CONTACT SYStem
Is linked to INITIAL CONTACT SYStem for calculations without geometrical update
Also an ’accumulated’ contact status is calculated as a single scalar value for each node. And
if slipping occurs the frictional energy dissipation and some frictional coefficients like saturation
and declination angle are calculated.
Geometry update results:

Results

CONTACT DEFinition
Contact definitions. It contains 1-2 scalar values per node: the family type of the involved
guiding CA-DOFs and, for surface contact, an isolation-indicator
CONTACT GEOmetry
It shows the nadir vector (geometrical gap vector from node to surface nadir) as a result
of the neighborhood search
CONTACT GEOmetry UPdate
Contact geometry update displacements
CONTACT SYStem
Contact coordinate system (Nx / Fy / Fz )

Default Selection for Export
The default for the EXPORT GO command is to export all the above scanning results (i.e. CONTACT DEFinition / GEOmetry / SYStem) and standard results CONTACT STATUS / FORCE /
PRESsure, GAP WIDTH, and FRICTION ENergy DENsity. Thus usually an explicit ITEM request is only needed for additional PRINTs or for exporting the precheck results or the standard
results not listed above.

6.1 General

Pressfit Results

6.1.4 Pressfit Results Overview
With the GO command in the UCI EXPORT section additional results from the analysis are
exported to the postprocessor together with the standard results obtained by the pure analysis.
Also in UCI sections PRINT and EXPORT those results can be explicitly requested with the
ITEM command. All pressfit results are based on nodal points, i.e. are scalar values or vectors
at pressfit nodes.
According to the solution step in which the data is generated, the pressfit analysis results may
be separated in 2 groups:
Scanning results (verification of model):

PRESSFIT DEFinition
It contains 2–3 scalar values per node: the definition type, the dependency type and, for
pressfit surfaces, an isolation-indicator, see page 6-145
PRESSFIT GEOmetry
It shows the nadir vector (geometrical gap vector from node to surface nadir) as a result
of the neighborhood search
PRESSFIT SYStem
It contains 3 normalized vectors building the axes of a node-local pressfit system according to the coupling partners and PREDIR direction
Standard results:
After the analysis the pressfit reaction forces † RC are directly available.
PRESSFIT FORCE
Pressfit coupling forces
PRESSFIT FORCE VECtor
Pressfit coupling forces
PRESSFIT OVERLAP
Pressfit overlap value

Default Selection for Export
The default for the EXPORT GO command is to export all the above scanning results (i.e.
PRESSFIT DEFinition / GEOmetry and SYStem) and standard result PRESSFIT FORCE (if

* In the post-processor the load-independent results may show up under load pattern zero.
†

In case of NLMATERIAL an additional GENerate REACtion or GENerate RESIdual is necessary to generate
the pressfit reaction forces (not needed for STATIC).

6.1 General

Pretension Results

6.1.5 Pretension Results Overview
With the GO command in the UCI EXPORT section additional results from the analysis are
exported to the postprocessor together with the standard results obtained by the pure analysis.
Also in UCI sections PRINT and EXPORT those results can be explicitly requested with the
ITEM command. All pretension results are based on nodal points, i.e. are scalar values or
vectors at pretension nodes.
According to the solution step in which the data is generated, the pretension analysis results
may be separated in 2 groups:
Scanning results (verification of model):

PRETENsion DEFinition
It contains 2–3 scalar values per node: the definition type, the dependency type and, for
pretension surfaces, an isolation-indicator, see page 6-154
PRETENsion GEOmetry
It shows the nadir vector (geometrical gap vector from node to surface nadir) as a result
of the neighborhood search
PRETENsion SYStem
It contains 3 normalized vectors building the axes of a node-local pretension system
according to the coupling partners and PREDIR direction
THREAD SYStem
It contains 3 normalized vectors building the axes of a node-local flank system, based on
the $PRETENSION THREAD parameters ALPHA and PITCH
Standard results:
After the analysis the pretension reaction forces † RC are directly available.
PRETENsion FORCE
Pretension coupling forces

Default Selection for Export
The default for the EXPORT GO command is to export all the above scanning results (i.e. PRETENsion DEFinition / GEOmetry / SYStem & THREAD SYStem) and standard result PRETENsion FORCE (if generated). Thus usually an explicit ITEM request is only needed for additional
PRINTs or for exporting the precheck results or the standard results not listed above

* In the post-processor the load-independent results may show up under load pattern zero.
†

In case of NLMATERIAL an additional GENerate REACtion or GENerate RESIdual is necessary to generate
the pretension reaction forces (not needed for STATIC).

Surface Results
6.1.6

6 Results

Surface Results Overview

With the GO command in the UCI EXPORT section additional results from the analysis are
exported to the postprocessor together with the standard results obtained by the pure analysis.
Also in UCI sections PRINT and EXPORT those results can be explicitly requested with the
ITEM command. All surface results are based on nodal points, i.e. are scalar values or vectors
at surface nodes.
Scanning results:
Directly after the model’s input and consolidation (e.g. after task scanning with TASK STORE)
some load-independent* surface results are available for model verification:
SURFACE DEFinition
It contains 4 scalar values per node: the definition type, border type, area and kink angle
SURFACE SYStem
Is linked to INITIAL SURFACE SYStem for calculations without geometrical update
SURFACE SMOOTHING
It contains the surface smoothing vector

Results

Geometry update results:
SURFACE SYStem
It contains the surface normal vector

Default Selection for Export
The default for the EXPORT GO command is to export all the above scanning andgeometry
update results, if the DEFAULT SET VERIFICATION = RESULTS is set. Thus usually an explicit
ITEM request is only needed for additional PRINTs.

* In the post-processor the load-independent results may show up under load pattern zero.

6.2 Result Items
6.2.10

Contact Geometry Update

Contact Geometry Update

Contact geometry update
• Type: Vector at contact nodes (for each load pattern or time step)
• Available after static contact analysis with contact geometry update
• Result Label: UCAGEOUP
• GENERATE: n/a (automatically generated)
• EXPORT:

ITEM CONTACT GEOMETRY UPDATE

• Export Rule: Default Result
• POST,HDF:

$DATA CAGEOUP, CONTACT GEOMETRY UPDATE

• PRINT:

ITEM CONTACT GEOMETRY UPDATE

• XYDATA:

n/a

• Related DAT keywords: $CONTACT, $CONTACT LOAD, $NLLOAD, etc.
CAGEOUP, CAGEOUPMAX, CAGEOUPTOL

The contact geometry update contains the final displacements before the last contact geometry
update for the corresponding load pattern or time step. This displacement before the last update
step is used as the reference geometry for the last contact iteration. Thus the contact geometry
update can be used to check the influence of the last contact geometry update step.
It is only available for the setting CAGEOUP=ON. If the contact geometry update steps did not
reach the tolerance criterion CAGEOUPTOL, the result is exported in any case, otherwise only
if it is addressed by the user.

Contact Interference
6.2.11

6 Results

Contact Interference

Contact interference
• Type: Vector at contact nodes (for each load pattern or time step)
• Available after static contact analysis
• Result Label: UCALDEP
• GENERATE: n/a (automatically generated)
• EXPORT:

ITEM CONTACT INTERFERENCE

• Export Rule: Default Result
• POST,HDF:

$DATA CALDEP, CONTACT INTERFERENCE

• PRINT:

ITEM CONTACT INTERFERENCE

• XYDATA:

n/a

• Related DAT keywords: $CONTACT, $CONTACT LOAD, $NLLOAD, etc.

Results

Contact interference is a nodal point vector with a vector length > 0 for linear dependent CADOFs, i.e. singularities in the active flexibility matrix (if any). The vector direction corresponds
to the CA-DOF in question. The length of the vector shows the ’degree’ of linear dependency:
= 0.0: No singularities (or no active contact).
> 0.0: Node is part in some duplicated CA-Definition or over-constrained by MPCs and/or
boundary conditions.
= n.0: Number of iteration steps where the interference is active.
= n.x: Partial/interpolated dependency.
The result is not generated if all active CA-DOFs are linearly independent.

6.2.12

6 Results

Contact Pressure

Contact pressure
• Type: Scalar and vector values at contact nodes (for each load pattern or time step)
• Available after static contact analysis
• Result Label: UCAPRESS
• GENERATE: n/a (automatically generated)
• EXPORT:

ITEM CONTACT PRESSURE

• Export Rule: Default Result
• POST,HDF:

$DATA CAPRES, CONTACT PRESSURE

• PRINT:

ITEM CONTACT PRESSURE

• XYDATA:

ITEM CONTACT PRESSURE (PRINT/EXPORT TYPE = CPRES)

• Related DAT keywords: $CONTACT, $CONTACT LOAD, $NLLOAD, etc.
• Related UCI switches:

CALINEWIDTH, CAPOINTAREA

Results

Normal pressure (scalar or vector) and frictional shear vector are area-related nodal point results which can be printed/exported in two variants:
a) ITEM CONTACT PRESsure
Maximum normal pressure (as scalar) and shear vector with maximum norm at each node
(e.g. appears as ’Contact Pressure’ and ’Contact Shear’ respectively in Medina postprocessor).
This is a default export item, i.e. exported with a simple GO command already.
Compared to the next item this result type has the following advantages/disadvantages:
⊕ Shows critical maximum for nodes with several contacts (e.g. edges or sandwich
contacts).
⊕ Sign of normal pressure indicates pressure/tension (e.g. for fixed contacts).
⊕ Enables simultaneous view of contact pressure and shear as color and vector in a
single plot.
p
2 + R2 .
⊖ No summation, e.g. edge contact shows Max(Rc1 ,Rc2 ) instead of Rc1
c2
⊖ No vector information for normal direction (user must know about normal direction
or compare to surface respectively ITEM CONTACT SYStem).
b) ITEM CONTACT PRESsure VECtor
Normal pressure vector (sum) and average shear vector (sum) at each node (e.g. ’Contact
PressVec’ and ’Contact ShearVec’ in Medina). This item is only exported if explicitly requested.
Compared to the previous item this result type has the following advantages/disadvantages:
⊕ Normal direction as vector information.
⊕ Vector sum at edges and for multi-contact nodes.

Contact Pressure

Contact Pressure

Figure F6-3: Normal pressure (left) and normal pressure with shear vector (right)

Theory:
In contrast to the calculation of stresses the calculation of contact pressure is not a derivative of
the element displacements, but is done by a direct mapping of the discrete contact forces taking
into account the areas and shape-functions of the neighboring element faces. This approach
has several advantages:
• Contact pressure is available for all element faces, i.e. even for elements which do not
have any elasticity in normal direction (e.g. shell, membrane or plot elements).

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

6-33

Contact Pressure

6 Results

• Contact pressure is also available for rigid surfaces, e.g. for elements with suppress,
prescribed or dependent nodes.
• Unique separation of normal and tangential pressure for nodes with multiple contacts.
• Pressure values are calculated at the contact nodes directly (no gauss point extrapolation).
Remarks
1. The area-related contact pressure and shear result use as reference surface all element
faces moistened by the corresponding contact definition. I.e. the reference surface is
derived from the adjacent finite-element mesh and not taken from a surface definition
used in the contact definition !
This makes the reference surface independent of the contact definition type, so that this
area-related results are available for simple nodal point contacts as well as for both sides
of a surface-to-node or surface-to-surface contact !
For line-like contacts the length of the moistened element edges are multiplied by the
value of the UCI switch CALINEWIDTH (default 1.0) to get a reference area. For singular
node-to-node contacts the value of UCI switch CAPOINTAREA is taken as a reference
area (default 0.0).

Results

2. For incompatible meshes an additional balancing between both sides of contact is applied, taking into account the local mesh size. For equally sized meshes this means just
an average determination, but for ample different meshes local details of the finer side
are not smeared by a coarse partner mesh.
3. Contact forces as well as contact pressure often show very high gradients at the border
of the contact region – especially at geometrical sharp edges (edge pressure). This is not
a simulation or discretization error, but meets the correct progression also known from
analytical press-fit solutions. Depending on the geometrical characterstics a very fine
meshing of a sharp edge might even lead to singular effects with almost infinite stress
values.†
4. The direct mapping algorithm used for the calculation of area-related contact results is
suited for elements with linear, quadratic or incomplete quadratic shape functions. However, mixed-case elements with a linear shape function in normal and a quadratic shape
function in tangential direction (i.e. thick shell elements TRIMS6 and QUAMS8/9 or
quadratic gasket elements GKPNT15/18 and GKHEX20/27) may show a slightly discontinuous pressure distribution from mid to corner nodes – similar to the non-smooth contact
forces at quadratic shaped elements.
5. At the symmetry border of cyclic symmetric models only one half of the effective reference
area can be derived from the contact adjacent element faces (the second half acts via the

†

In praxis edges of real parts mostly show small roundings or peak stress values at sharp edges are lowered by
microscopic small areas of plastification wihtout affecting the part’s function. Hence, for the outer most series
of nodal points it is often acceptable to tolerate a STATIC contact pressure above the material’s limit of elasticity
without this demanding a more expensive NLMATERIAL calculation.

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

6.2 Result Items

Contact Pressure

Results

symmetry-joins on the other side of the symmetry plane, but without direct connectivity
to the contact nodes). Therefore contact nodes at the border of cyclic symmetry usually
show a doubled contact pressure although the contact forces are correct.
Standard symmetry is not impaired by this effect. Notwithstanding contact pairs along
the border of this symmetry also see only half the effective reference area, but as the
very same nodes also get only half the contact forces this effect is compensated and the
contact pressure at the border of symmetry is correct, too.

The contact residuals indicate the numerical error for all relative contact displacements, i.e. the
numerical error in the final gap width (δ norm , δ f ric ) as well as in the relative gap displacements
(∆r norm , ∆r f ric ).
Of course, this is an error estimation for the contact iteration only. The overall accuracy may be
worse, see the Pro-File Accuracy Limit, Load Check and overall residual forces RESI.
Equally, for a nonlinear load history $NLLOAD the contact residuals of each LPAT include the
sum of all previous load patterns (summarized residuals).
