6.2 Result Items

Contact Status

If a node is part of several contact definitions the final status value is build by a decimal coding
of all corresponding contact status. The status values are collected in descending order with
the decimal point after the first status value. E.g. if an edge node participates in 2 contact
definitions, one of them passive (status 1) and the other one slipping (status 4) then the final
contact status of that node will be CA-Status = 4.1 !
As surface contact allows the contact between incompatible meshes each node on a surface
may be influenced by several (partially inherited) status values:
• The primary contact status value reflects the contact situation directly at the node’s location, e.g. contact of node with a patch of the opposing surface (i.e. the standard contact
status at that node).†
• A surface node may inherit an additional secondary contact status from the nearest nadir
point of an ’opponent’ contact node.*
Optionally this secondary contact status may
be shifted with -0.5 by setting the UCI switch CASURFST=SHIFT, see page 2-33. This
setting helps to clearly distinguish between primary and secondary status values.

• Moreover all orphan contact nodes, i.e. contact nodes for which no contact partner was
found (see also isolation type) get a status value of 0.0. Nodes not belonging to any
contact definition will get no status value.

Figure F6-5: Contact Status for example CA4 (surface-to-node).

†

A surface node in a surface-to-node contact has no primary status.

* The distance up to which a secondary contact from a patch contributes to a node’s contact status is controlled by

the UCI switch CASURFMSR, see page 2-33.

Cutting Flux

Internal heat flow at nodes
• Type: Scalar at nodes (for each load pattern or time step)
• Available after a temperature analysis
• Result Label: UBL1
• GENERATE: CUTTING FLUX
• EXPORT:

ITEM CUTTING FLUX

$DATA CUTTINGFLUX, CUTTING FLUX

• PRINT:

ITEM CUTTING FLUX

• XYDATA:

n/a

• Related DAT keywords: $ESET, $NSET

Results

CUTTING FLUX computes the internal heat flow if at least an element set filter is ACTIVE. The
result is given in units of power.
A boundary may be described by defining an active node set in addition, connected to the
elements of the element set. In this case the result represents the flow through the boundary.
The element set defines which side of the boundary and therefore the sign of the flow values.
The sum of the calculated flow values at nodes is written automatically to the result file. The
calculation of the internal heat flow may be invoked several times, previous results will be
overwritten.

The data sets "Effective frictional coefficient" and "Saturation of sticking forces" allow to evaluate how far a sticking contact area from the slipping state is. The data sets "Slip saturation
deficit" and "Slip force declination angle" lead the information about a quality of a frictional
contact solution.
1. Effective frictional coefficient
µef f =

|Rf ric |
|Rnorm |

(E6-1)

Obviously, it must hold for sticking contact area µef f ≤ µ0 , for slipping contact area µef f =
µ (see the picture F6-6).

2. Saturation of sticking forces
Sat. =

|Rf ric |
100%
µ0 |Rnorm |

(E6-2)

Obviously, saturation of sticking forces must be no bigger than 100%.
3. Slip saturation deficit
The Coulomb friction law says |Rslip | = µ |Rnorm |. The quality of its fulfilment is shown by
slip saturation deficit value.
Sat. = 1 −

|Rf ric |
µ |Rnorm |

100%

(E6-3)

Ideally, the value of the deficit must be zero.
4. Slip force declination angle

The Coulomb friction law prescribes the direction of the frictional force relative to slip
displacement vector. The value of the slip force declination angle shows the declination
of the frictional force from its direction calculated based on the slip displacement vector.
For isotropic friction law the declination angle can be found as
∠(−Rslip , r slip )

(E6-4)

I.e. the frictional force must point in an opposite direction to the slip displacement vector.
It does not hold for the orthotropic friction !
Ideally, the value of the declination must be zero. Note that for the small force or displacement values (with values close to an accuracy limit), the directions can be only badly
defined. In such cases for the very accurate solution, the declination values can be quite
large.

For all considered vector quantities the normal part, e.g. δ norm , and the tangential part, e.g.
δ tang , is exported, see 6.1.3. We remark that the tangential part is only exported, if friction
is used. If a node is part of several contact definitions the [initial] gap vector and the gap
displacement are the vector sum of the vectors at each contact definition. The scalar valued
gap width is the minimum gap of the involved contact definitions.
Please note, that for a non-linear load history $NLLOAD (see page 3-838 ff.), respectively a
non-linear analysis, the initial gap width δ 0 always refers to the undeformed state. It does not
correspond to the value listed as ’Starting Gapwidth’ in the contact results table of a time step
in the result file. In cases where the initial gap width between time tn−1 and tn is constant the
’Starting Gapwidth’ for time step tn is simply identical to the final gap width of tn−1 . If the initial
gap width is changed in time, then the ’Starting Gapwidth’ for time step tn is obtained by:
δstart (tn ) = δ(tn−1 ) − δ0 (tn−1 ) + δ0 (tn )
Equally, for a nonlinear load history $NLLOAD the gap displacement ∆r gives the relative
movement with reference to the undeformed mesh – not with reference to the previous time
step !

If a node is part of several contact definitions the final definition type is build by a decimal coding of all corresponding definition types. The definition types are collected in
descending order with the decimal point after the first status value. E.g. if an edge node
participates in 2 contact definitions, in one of them on the node side (value 2) and in the
other one on the surface side (value 1) then the final definition type of that node will be
2.1 !

3. The DOF family type of the involved guiding CA-DOFs. Dependent, prescribed or suppressed DOFs may introduce additional constraints to the mobility of contact nodes. If
those constraints include physical inconsistencies (like mutual dependent or over-constrained contacts) they may be a source for bad convergence or ’clamped contact’ warnings. Therefore the DOF family type allows the verification of all contact definitions which
are based on non-local DOFs:
= 1 : Contact node whose contact definitions are based on local DOFs only (standard
L).
= 2 : Contact node which introduces dependent DOFs as a base for contact definitions
(L+D).
= 3 : Contact node which introduces dependent and external/prescribed/suppressed
CA-DOFs (L+D+E/P/S).
= 4 : Contact node which introduces external/prescribed/suppressed CA-DOFs (L+E/P/S).
= 5 : Contact node which is based on dependent CA-DOFs only (D, no locals).
= 6 : Contact node which is based on dependent/external/prescribed/suppressed CADOFs only (D+E/P/S, no L).
= 7 : Contact node which is based on external/prescribed/suppressed CA-DOFs only
(E/P/S, no locals).

Initial Contact Definition

6. The contact doublet indicator* shows which contact pairs were removed from a contact
definition. Values 2 and 3 indicates a doubled contact pair whose definition was removed,
because a dublicate contact pair (value 1) was established already at the same position.
Value 4 indicates a contact pair that was not taken into account in the current analysis.
= 0 : Unique contact region (nil value if no contact)
= 1 : Full valid contact pair.
= 2 : Doubled (geometrical) contact pair automatically removed from a surface-to-surface
contact definition due to (local) mesh compatibilities.†
= 3 : Dependent doubled contact pair automatically removed from a $SURFACE or a
$NODE contact definition. ‡
= 4 : Contact pairs which are automatically removed due to the COMPLEMENT parameter in a surface-to-surface definition. No parent contact pair with value 1 exists.
Export results will be also generated at all contact points, but the contact points with
value > 1 will not appear in the contact iteration and result tables printed to Log-, Proand Res-File respectively.

Results
Figure F6-20: Duplicate contact pairs in S2S contact due to local mesh compatibilities

* Note that this contact doublet indicator is not available if all contact pairs are unique, i.e. is only generated if there

is at least one duplicate CA-Pair.
†

The exact criterion is as follows: If a point NA from surface A establishes a contact with surface B and the distance
from the nadir of this contact to a patch point NB is less than 10∗TOLNOD then any contact pair arising from node
NB with surface A will be ignored if the nadir of that contact would also lie in 10∗TOLNOD distance to node NA .

‡

The exact criterion is as follows: If the corresponding contact point NA of a contact pair has only dependent
degrees of freedom and if there exists another contact point NB in the same contact definition nearly at the same
position (tolerance CATOLDUPDEP) without any dependent degrees of freedoms (which is assumed to be the
guiding node) the contact pair at point NA will be ignored.

EXPORT of laminate stresses is only supported for the PERMAS postprocessor. The usual

MPC Definition
6.2.78

6 Results

MPC Definition

Verification result; MPC definition types & properties
• Type: Scalar values at MPC nodes
• Available after the model’s input and consolidation if VERIFICATION is set
• Result Label: MPCVER
• GENERATE: n/a (automatically generated)
• EXPORT:

ITEM MPC DEFINITION

• Export Rule: Default Result
• POST,HDF:

$DATA MPCDEF, MPC DEFINITION

• PRINT:

ITEM MPC DEFINITION

• XYDATA:

n/a

• Related DAT keywords: $MPC
• Related UCI switches:

VERIFICATION, MPCDISTOL, MPCOUTTOL

Results

This load-independent result is available for model verification directly after the model’s input
and consolidation (e.g. after task scanning with TASK STORE), if default switch VERIFICATION
is set.
The MPC definition contains 7 scalar values for each MPC node. If printed, the information
is shown in readable form, whereas the postprocessing result uses coded values (shown in
parentheses).
DefCount : Number of MPCs the node is connected to
MPCType: Type of MPC (coded value not documented)
DepType : Guiding (1), Dependent (2) or Both (3)
DofMask : Dependent degrees of freedom (binary coded, e.g. 1,2,4 as 11)
IsoType : Verification of neighborhood search (if applicable)
Found — Guiding (0), found — In (1), found by OUTTOL — Out (2), not found —
Orphans (3)
DepLevel : Level of dependency starting with zero, values greater zero indicate hierarchical
MPC
Distance : Length of projection vector to guiding patch (or line) or distance guiding - dependent node
For orphan nodes no further information is given. If nodes participate in several MPCs, specific
information is given for the first MPC only.

This load-independent result is available for model verification directly after the model’s input

distance vector between each dependent node and the center of its corresponding guiding nodes.

multiple MPC definitions with different dofs may be misleading since the result shows the superposition of all contributing definitions.

6.2.81

MPC System

MPC System

Verification result; Coupling coordinate system
• Type: Coupling coordinate system at dependent nodes (load-independent result)
• Available after the model’s input and consolidation if VERIFICATION is set
• Result Label: MPCCSYS
• GENERATE: n/a (automatically generated)
• EXPORT:

ITEM MPC SYSTEM

• Export Rule: Default Result
• POST,HDF:

$DATA MPCSYSTEM, MPC SYSTEM

• PRINT:

ITEM MPC SYSTEM

• XYDATA:

n/a

• Related DAT keywords: $MPC
VERIFICATION, MPCDISTOL, MPCOUTTOL

This load-independent result is available for model verification directly after the model’s input
and consolidation (e.g. after task scanning with TASK STORE), if default switch VERIFICATION
is set. Please note that the result shows only one coupling system at each node.
Constraint conditions are enforced at dependent degrees of freedom with respect to a local
coupling coordinate system. In general, the coupling system coincides with the (possibly) rotated basis, defined by $ROTB, at each dependent node. An explicit system specification is
available for some MPC types by the parameter DPSYS, e.g. $MPC ISURFACE.

For linear elements (geometry and material) the strain energy is calculated from element displacements ρ and element forces P as

Results

1
Es = ρT P
2
For nonlinear elements the volume specific elastic, plastic and creep strain energy densities are
integrated over the load history at the integration points. The strain energy is then the integral
over the element volume of the sum of these energy densities.

6.2.106

Pressfit Definition

Pressfit Definition

Pressfit definition types & properties
• Type: Scalar Values at pressfit nodes
• Available after the model’s input and consolidation (e.g. after task scanning with TASK
STORE)
• Result Label: UPFDEF0
• GENERATE: n/a (automatically generated)
• EXPORT:

ITEM PRESSFIT DEFINITION

• Export Rule: Default Result
• POST,HDF:

$DATA PFDEF, PRESSFIT DEFINITION

• PRINT:

ITEM PRESSFIT DEFINITION

• XYDATA:

n/a

• Related DAT keywords: $PRESSFIT
PFDISTOL, PFOUTTOL

This load-independent* result is available for model verification directly after the model’s input
and consolidation (e.g. after task scanning with TASK STORE). The pressfit definition contains
2–3 scalar values for each pressfit node:
1. The pressfit definition type may be used to verify that the proper kind of coupling definition
was used:
= 1 : Pure surface partner, i.e. an adjacent patch at the node participates in a pressfit
surface, but the node itself is not a pressfit node (surface node from a $PRESSFIT
surface-to-node coupling).
= 2 : Standard pressfit node, i.e. the node itself is the base of a local coupling pair from
a $PRESSFIT node-to-node or surface-to-node coupling.
= 3 : Master guiding node (gid)
2. With the pressfit dependency type one can verify which nodes where introduced as dependent or guiding nodes in MPCs internally generated by the $PRESSFIT def.:
= 1 : Guiding nodes (usually 1st partner)
= 2 : Dependent nodes (usually 2nd partner)
3. The pressfit isolation type is provided in order to verify the neighborhood of pressfit
couplings. Values > 1 indicate an orphan coupling situation (also see UCI switches
PFDISTOL and PFOUTTOL on page 2-43 of this manual):

* In the post-processor the load-independent results may show up under load pattern zero.

6.3.1

SPR Procedure

SPR: Smooth
[Zienkiewicz].

Patch

Recovery

method,

• Evaluate stress at “superconvergent”
points.
• Build element patches:
For each interior corner node an element
patch is build consisting of those elements sharing this corner node, which is
denoted the patch node. Patch nodes
must not be located on boundaries, on
property interfaces or on mesh interfaces.

integration point
superconvergent point
element patch
patch node

Results

• Least square fit:
To approximate the stress inside the
patch a polynomial stress ansatz is used.
The polynomial coefficients are determined via a least square fit to the stresses y
at the “superconvergent” points.
x
• Nodal values from patches:
The nodal stress values are determined
as arithmetic mean of the evaluated polynomials from the contributing patches.
Each SPR patch contributes to its interior
nodes. If the patch includes boundary nodes it also contributes to this nodes.
In order to have consistent patches, the model has to be partitioned due to certain rules. This is
performed internally within the SPR computation so that no manual action is needed. However,
some settings are available to influence the automatic SPR model partitioning.
• No SPR patch nodes at MPC interfaces, i.e. MPC interfaces are treated like exterior
boundaries regarding the SPR procedure. Hence, e.g. at an MPC ISURFACE between
a HEXE8 and TET10 volume mesh, SPR stresses will be generated for both volume
meshes separately. I.e. there will be no SPR patch with HEXE8 and TET10 elements.
• Split model due to element families.
• Material borders are also separators (except e.g. short fibre materials).

6.3.2 Absolute Error Indicator (AEI)
The Absolute Error Indicator (AEI) σAEI is a scalar measure of the discretization error in terms
of stress within one element. It is defined as
σAEI = max kσ FE − σSPR k ,
V

where V denotes the element volume, σFE is the standard element stress
√ and σ SPR the SPR
stress. The stress difference is measured in the Frobenius norm kAk = A : A. Because the
AEI is based on the SPR stress the same restrictions apply regarding mesh partitioning and
boundaries.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

6-199

AEI

6 Results

The AEI is an indicator for the discretization error in terms of stress and must not be mixed
up with the exact error in the stress. The purpose of the AEI is to identify those mesh regions
where the mesh quality should be improved and/or the mesh should be refined in order to
reduce the error in the stresses. Note that at stress singularities like at corners, the error will
not be reduced by a mesh refinement.
Example example LS19 on page 2-243 ff. of [um550] shows an application of SPR stresses
and the AEI.

7.1 General
7.1

General

Default result item selection
The export process has a default result selection rule in order to avoid explicit selections for
many cases. The rule is as following:
1. Primary results are always selected.
2. Each secondary result which is generated explicitly is selected as far as the postprocessor
is able to support the item. (Exceptions are documented in the corresponding output door
sections.)
3. Verification item if "DEFAULT SET MODEL = verification" is selected. Verification item
should only be used for testing purpose in conjunction with TASK STORE.

Explicit result item selections
Using the EXPORT ITEM (see page 2-373 ff.) command, further selections may be done in
addition to the default selection. If only explicit selections are desired, the default selection
must be cleared previously.

The naming convention for the postprocessing files is designed to be as common for the different postprocessors as possible. The specific naming rules are documented for each postprocessor separately. Of course, the names are machine dependent. Some restrictions are
documented for each postprocessor, too.
There are several parameters influencing the result file names:
1. Project name
2. Component (in case of substructuring)
3. Situation (if several variants are used)
4. Export mode (direct/combined)
5. Exported result item (for several postprocessors)
6. Task loop

7.2 Export to PERMAS
7.2

Export to PERMAS

7.2.1 General
Model and result output can be generated in the EXPORT (see page 2-363 ff.) section of
PERMAS. The generated output is written in PERMAS ( ref. chapter 3 ) input format. Therefore
this output may be used as model/result input for a subsequent PERMAS run or for other
postprocessing purposes.
For easy processing the output file is written in a fixed format.

7.2.4 Binary File Framework

HDF Data Model
• The HDF format has two primary objects
Group

: is like a directory of a file system

Dataset : is like a file of a file system
• and Attributes to annotate data.
Each result item is stored in a HDF Group named according to the item name, e.g. ’ELEMENT
STRESS’ and may contain several HDF Datasets corresponding to e.g. LPATs or xy-curves.
All result items belong to a HDF Group named like the situation they belong to. This group is
the Situation Group. The situation belongs to a HDF Group according to the component name,
and if the model has a multilevel configuration, this component belongs to a HDF Group with
the configuration (top component) name.

Export to
PERMAS

/.File Header
/[configuration/]component/
/[configuration/]component/situation/
/[configuration/]component/situation/.Analysis
/[configuration/]component/situation/.Model
/[configuration/]component/situation/item
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/.ColDes
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/.RowDes
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/Column1
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/Column2
/[configuration/]component/situation/item
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/.Abscissae
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/.Label
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/Curve1
There is a ’.File Header’ HDF Dataset in the HDF Root Group of the binary file. This dataset is
written as a ’string’ datatype with a fixed length of 80 characters and several lines.
The Situation Group contains one additional HDF Dataset named ’.Analysis’. This dataset is a
’string’ datatype with a fixed length of 40 characters, containing the analysis command of the
situation, e.g. ’STATIC’. It can also contain the Postprocessing Model as a HDF Dataset named
’.Model’.
Each right-hand side of a result item is stored in a HDF Dataset named ’Columni’ with the
column index i of the item. The value (e.g. LPAT, TIME or FREQUENCY) of the Column is
stored in the HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’ at the position i. The label of the result position (node,
element, ...) is stored in the HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

7-21

7 Export Formats
If an item consists of curves, the ordinate values are stored in a HDF Dataset named ’Curvei’
with the curve index i. The label of the curve is stored in the HDF Dataset ’.Label’ at the position
i. The independent values (e.g. LPAT, TIME or FREQUENCY) of the Curve are stored in the
HDF Dataset ’.Abscissae’.
The description of the dimensions and the dimensionality is done in FORTRAN notation. The
indices start with 1, and the first index is running fastest.
Each result HDF Dataset is a two dimensional array for real data and a three dimensional array
in the case of complex data. The result data components (e.g. DOFs) are stored in the first
dimension and the datapoints (nodes, elements, ...) in the second dimension of the real data
array. Complex values are stored as real and imaginary part of the complex data in the first
dimension of the three dimensional array. The result data components are stored in the second
dimension and the datapoints are stored in the third dimension of the three dimensional data
array.
All nodal point results and element results with result data at elements or result data at center
of elements have a HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’ which is a vector with the nodal point IDs or the
element IDs. The values are 64 bit values.
The column description HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’ is a vector with load pattern IDs, column IDs,
time values, frequencies or a text description. The values are 64 bit values, the strings have a
fixed length.

Column Descriptor ’.ColDes’
The HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’ is a vector containing the right-hand side description. The IDs are
64 bit values or strings with a length of 40 characters. The type depends on the analysis:
integer

: The value is an integer for all results with LPAT or COLUMN as descriptor

float

: The value is a float for all other results e.g TIME, FREQUENCY . . .

string

: A string used for a better readability of some verification results e.g. ’Surface Normal’ of the ’Surface System’.

The vector length matches the number of HDF Dataset ’Columns’. The position in the vector
belongs to the ’Column’ with the ID of the position (we start the counting at ONE).
Position 7 belongs to Column7
The column descriptor may have an attribute named Label which contains the column type
label as a string with a length of 12 characters. Its content can be ’LPAT’, ’Time’, ’Frequency’,
. . ..

The Result HDF Group can have some attributes:

7 Export Formats
Column Attributes
The columns also can have some attributes.
Original Column ID: This attribute contains the Column ID of the result column. This is
important for e.g. an eigenvalue analysis, or if not all columns are written on the
HDF file.
Column type label: The Column type label attribute is introduced to have an additional easy
access to the same data as in the column descriptor. Its name is taken from the
contents of the column descriptor attribute ’Label’ (e.g. LPAT . . .). The value is the
value from the HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’.
Result Items for Nodal Point Data
The HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’ is a vector with the nodal point IDs. The IDs are 64 bit integer
values.
All columns have the same dimension. The values are 32 or 64 bit values according the default
setting
DEFAULT SET HDF_DATASIZE = 32 or 64
specified at the beginning of the UCI-file by DEFAULT (see page 2-66 ff.). They are, according
to the analysis result:
real

Export to
PERMAS

: It is a two dimensional HDF Dataset. The result data columns are the first dimension and the nodes are the second dimension. The second dimension matches
with the dimension of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.

complex : It is a three dimensional HDF Dataset. The first dimension is two and contains
the real and imaginary part of the complex value. The result data columns are
the second dimension and the nodes are the third dimension. The third dimension
matches with the dimension of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.
Result Items for Constant Element Data
The HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’ is a vector with the element ids. The ids are 64 bit integer values.
All columns have the same dimension. The values are 32 or 64 bit values according the default
setting
DEFAULT SET HDF_DATASIZE = 32 or 64
specified at the beginning of the UCI-file by DEFAULT (see page 2-66 ff.). They are, according
to the analysis result:
real

7-24

: It is a two dimensional HDF Dataset. The result data columns are the first dimension and the elements are the second dimension. The second dimension matches
with the dimension of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

V 19.00.287

7.2 Export to PERMAS
complex : It is a three dimensional HDF Dataset. The first dimension is two and contains
the real and imaginary part of the complex value. The result data columns are the
second dimension and the elements are the third dimension. The third dimension
matches with the dimension of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.
Result Items for Distributed Element Data
The HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’ is two dimensional with the element IDs, which are 64 bit integer
values. The first dimension is THREE. The first value is the element ID, the second the row
pack value and the third the start pointer to the column data.
All columns have the same dimension. The values are 32 or 64 bit values according the default
setting
DEFAULT SET HDF_DATASIZE = 32 or 64
specified at the beginning of the UCI-file by DEFAULT (see page 2-66 ff.). They are, according
to the analysis result:
real

: It is a one dimensional HDF Dataset. The result data columns are stored in the
second value of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.

complex : It is a two dimensional HDF Dataset. The first dimension is two and contains the
real and imaginary part of the complex value. The result data columns are stored
in the second value of the ’.RowDes’ HDF Dataset.

Code C2 : This attribute contains the row pack rule for ’.RowDes’ column 2 (e.g. 2.3.2.5). It
is a decimal coded value with following meaning described from right to left. Each
field shows the width of its decimal portion. The ’Most Right’ value ’Pos 1’ must be
used to get the correct data length. The other values can be used for displaying the
data.
P os1 : This portion is (in this example) 5 digits wide and holds the number of values
for this element.
P os2 : This portion is (in this example) 2 digits wide and holds the dimension of
ONE data point, e.g. 6 for Tensor, 3 for vector, 1 for scalar.
P os3 : This portion is (in this example) 3 digits wide and holds the number of layer
or ZERO if not layered.
P os4 : This portion is (in this example) 2 digits wide and holds the data point code
for data display.
0
: No explicit position
1
: Data at center of element
2
: Data at element nodes
3
: Data at layer center
4
: Data at all layer for all nodes
5
: Data at all nodes for all layer

The lines of the PERMAS output file are written in a fixed format. Therefore each line may be
processed with a specific format.
Some useful information are given as comment lines starting with "!#."
The following format descriptions are in the sense of FORTRAN format statements. For other
programming languages the appropriate definitions must be used.

!#
!#------------------------------------------------------------------------------

7-333

7 Export Formats

Export to
PERMAS

C*($) RDLINE ........RDLINE ........RDLINE ........RDLINE ........
SUBROUTINE RDLINE (IUNIT,FORM,NLINES,NCOL,
*
N O P O E L , D A T A , L I N E , E N D )
C--X-------------------------------------------------------------------C
# Entry # to Permas 5 Data file processing
C
C Read one data line from result file
C
C --> IUNIT : FORTRAN unit number
C --> FORM
: Format specification
C --> NLINES : Number of lines to process
C --> NCOL
: Number of columns in data line
C <-- NOPOEL : Nodal point or element number
C <-- DATA
: Numerical values
C <-- LINE
: Last line if end of block was found (character*80)
C <-- END
: .TRUE. if end of data line was found
C----------------------------------------------------------------------C (C) Copyright INTES GmbH, Stuttgart, Germany
C!----------------------------------------------CHARACTER*(*) FORM,LINE
LOGICAL
END
DIMENSION
DATA(*)
CHARACTER*80 LINES(100)
C----------------------------------------------------------------------C
C
... Read in line and test for end of block
READ(IUNIT,’(A80)’)LINES(1)
IF( LINES(1)(1:1) .EQ. ’$’)THEN
END = .TRUE.
LINE = LINES(1)
GOTO 999
ENDIF
C
C Next line found get rest of data
IF( NLINES .GT. 1 )THEN
DO 10 I=2,NLINES
READ(IUNIT,’(A80)’)LINES(I)
10
CONTINUE
ENDIF
C
C Convert data
READ(LINES,FORM)NOPOEL,(DATA(I),I=1,NCOL)
END = .FALSE.
C---999 CONTINUE
RETURN
END

SUBROUTINE RDBLOC (IUNIT,
*
N A M O B J , T E X T , L I N E S , F O R M )
C--X-------------------------------------------------------------------C
# Entry # to Permas 5 Data file processing
C
C Get information from data comment block
C
C --> IUNIT : FORTRAN unit with connected input file
C <-- NAMOBJ: Name of data object
C <-- TEXT : Description text from data object
C <-- LINES : Number of lines for one data item
C <-- FORM : Fortran format to convert data
C----------------------------------------------------------------------C (C) Copyright INTES GmbH, Stuttgart, Germany
C!----------------------------------------------CHARACTER*(*) NAMOBJ,TEXT,FORM
CHARACTER
INAM*13,ITEXT*40,FFORM*65
C----------------------------------------------------------------------C
NAMOBJ = ’ ’
TEXT
= ’ ’
FORM
= ’ ’
C
C Get book name and text
READ(IUNIT,’(16X,A13,7X,A40)’)INAM,ITEXT
NAMOBJ = INAM
TEXT
= ITEXT
C
C Get number of lines
READ(IUNIT,’(11X,I9)’)LINES
C
C Get format for data line
READ(IUNIT,’(10X,A65)’)FFORM
FORM = FFORM
C
C Skip next line
READ(IUNIT,’(A65)’)FFORM
C---RETURN
END

7.4

Export to HyperView

The standard export is done with the HyperView Version 11 Library.

7.4.1 File Management
The output of the selected items (see page 2-373 ff. of the PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)
) to the HyperView interface is done on one file. The default parameter POSTCAT (DEFAULT
(see page 2-66 ff.)) has no influence on the export process.

Naming rule for export files:

Parameter

Type

Explanation

< project >

name

name

used, the name is build as S_<icount> instead of the complete name.
Component name.
Part of the filename in case of substructure analysis. If the standard
name (DFLT_COMP) is used, the name is build as C_<icount> instead of the complete name.

Only in case of substructuring as appendix to the component name
(_C).

2. ASCII and compressed (.gz) output are not supported.

the TASK LOOP. (e.g. 100 leads to a 3 digit task identifier).

and in HyperView u = r ∗ cos(ωt − ϕ).

7.5.1 File Management
The output of the selected items (see page 2-373 ff. of the PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)
) to the I-DEAS universal file may be done on one or several files, depending on the setting of
default parameter POSTCAT (DEFAULT (see page 2-66 ff.))
Naming rule for POSTCAT = ON
output of model and results (as selected) on one result file.

7 Export Formats
Parameter

Type

sum-files

Explanation
Each SUM item is written on a separate File. The file extension for the
SUM items are shown on page 7-13

Remarks:
1. The file extension may be written in upper or lowercase letters, depending on the actual
machine.
2. Binary and compressed (.gz) output are not supported.
3. The standard names for a PERMAS situation and component are assigned if a foreign
input door contains no explicit specification of the names.
4. The number of digits of the task loop identifier is evaluated from the number of loops in
the TASK LOOP. (e.g. 100 leads to a 3 digit task identifier).
5. Modal Masses are written for normal mode analysis if the mode normalization is switched
off (see SET MODENORM command on page 2-40 of PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)).

Naming rule for POSTCAT = OFF
Output of model and each result item for each column (as selected) on separate result files.

Naming rule for export files:

(< project >)(< sit >)(< comp >)(< combine >)(< task >)(. < item >)

with ”BLOCKF ORM = value” parameter.

7.9 Export to VAO
UGV File Format
The UGV File is a binary file with a maximum size of 2 GByte. The first five words are the file
descriptor.
1. Magic ID (is currently 948250943)
2. VAO version (is currently 2)
3. Number of data for each nodal point (number of planes). Is 6 for displacements and 1 for
pressures.
4. Number of nodal points on UGV file
5. Number of modes on UGV file
The UGV file is written in several parts, if the total size of the modes is larger than 2 GB. All
files contains all modes of a number of nodes. The matrix is split in row direction on the UGV
files. The extensions are UGV1, UGV2 . . .UGVi.

7.11.4

Static correction modes

As long as modal synthesis ( Craig-Bampton method ) is not supported in PERMAS the following procedure is used for generating static correction modes for ADAMS interface.
• Static correction modes are calculated for degree of freedom which are declared $EXTERNAL
(see page 3-109 ff.)
For the calculation of elastic modes in a single component EXTERNAL degrees of freedom are
fixed. Therefore the result is the same as if the degrees of freedom are SUPPRESSED.

Restriction
The following restriction must be respected for the calculation of static correction modes:
• No substructuring is supported
• No constraint variant for EXTERNAL degrees of freedom possible ( EXTERNAL declaration belongs to the basic module of the component)

Export to
ADAMS

• Calculation of static correction modes is done by the ADAMS interface

8.1 Degree of Anisotropy

8 Material Description (Theory)
8.1

Degree of Anisotropy

The degree of anisotropy is a fundamental property of all types of material. In many practical
applications the material behavior can be considered as isotropic and only few constants are
needed to describe it, but some types of material, e.g. fiber-reinforced plastics, wood or reinforced concrete show a distinct anisotropic behavior which has to be taken into account. The
description of general anisotropic behavior is an expensive task, so e.g. for the constitutive matrix C which relates stresses and strains in linear elasticity twenty-one independent constants
are needed. Fortunately most anisotropic materials have any planes of symmetry for their behavior, reducing the number of independent constants and so the amount of work to describe
it. For user convenience different types of anisotropic behavior are implemented in PERMAS,
identified by their so-called degree of anisotropy.
The simplest case is isotropic material behavior. No dependency on orientation of material in
space exists, there is an infinite number of planes of material property symmetry.
In contrast, if there is not any plane of material property symmetry, the material is called (general) anisotropic or triclinic.
If there is only one plane of material property symmetry the material is called monoclinic.
If there are two orthogonal planes of material property symmetry, symmetry will exist also relative to a third mutually orthogonal plane. The intersections of the three planes define the
principal directions of the material. Using the principal directions to establish the stress-strain
relation leads to a so-called orthotropic material.

Material

If there is one plane in which all material properties are equal in all directions the material is
called transversely isotropic.

V 19.00.287

PERMAS User’s Reference Manual (EDU)

8 Material Description (Theory)

8.5 Heat Capacity
8.5

Heat Capacity

Material

The amount of heat required to raise the unit volume of the material by 1 degree in temperature
is called heat capacity per unit volume κ, and is used in transient thermal analysis. Since heat
capacity is a scalar quantity, the input does not depend on the degree of anisotropy of the
material.
Heat capacity may be a function of temperature. For each kind of homogeneous material one
heat capacity value or one heat capacity function may be input, using the data block header
$HEATCAP.

8.9 Structural Damping
8.9

Structural Damping

Structural or material damping describes dissipative forces in the material which are proportional to the strains and in opposite direction to the motion, i.e.
FD ∼ − sgn(ε̇)ε
If and only if the motion is harmonic, elemental structural damping forces in a linear system
may be formulated according to
F D,E = − igE kE ρE
where kE is the elemental stiffness matrix, gE the structural damping factor of the element and
ρE are the elemental displacements. This leads to a complex elemental stiffness matrix
k̄E = (1 + igE )kE
The structural damping factor gE may depend on frequency. Complex stiffness matrices containing structural damping forces can be processed in frequency response analysis. To include
structural damping forces in transient response analysis, equivalent viscous damping forces
are calculated with the elemental viscous damping matrix
dg,E =

gE
kE
2πfE

where fE is the element reference frequency. For a harmonic motion with frequency f = fE the
equivalent viscous damping forces are equal to the structural damping forces, for f > fE the
equivalent viscous damping forces are higher, for f < fE lower than the corresponding structural damping forces. If the structural damping factor is a function of frequency, for calculation
of the equivalent viscous damping forces the function is evaluated for f = fE .

Material

The structural damping factor gE is assumed to be a scalar quantity, therefore the input does
not depend on the degree of anisotropy of the material. For each kind of homogeneous material one damping value or one damping function may be input, using the data block header
$DAMPING.

expansion which in differential form is defined as increment of length in a unit length per temperature increment, i.e.

εϑ (T1 ) = αd (T1 − T0 )

temperature-dependent coefficients is calculated according to
εϑ (T1 ) = α(T1 , Tref )(T1 − Tref ) − α(T0 , Tref )(T0 − Tref )

F-5

Appendix

1. The name rule for complex arithmetics is as follows:
< label >
basic label with amplitude data.
< label >F to store the phase data.
< label >R for the real part.
< label >I
for the imaginary part.

F Table of Result Data Object Labels
The label has at most 7 characters.
For example, USAR is the real part of the acceleration result.
2. For STEADY STATE results, by default the labels are built by adding SST to the standard
labels of the corresponding item, leading to following labels:
Item

etc.

Note, that these label names are only defaults and may be changed using RESULT =
parameter. Therefore, they have to be selected explicitly for export.

< label >SD
< label >RS

1. Of course, other matrices may be input, but will not be used to replace standard data
object labels within PERMAS, hence no computation time is saved.

G Table of Standard Input Data Object Labels
2. If the cholesky factor is being input, it is expected that also all other stiffness matrices are
being input.
3. The content of structural damping matrices is solution-dependent. For analyses in frequency domain, the matrices must contain structural damping as imaginary stiffness
parts, for analyses in time domain the corresponding equivalent viscous damping matrices are expected.
